Efficient Division Strategy Current research [62], [63] indicates that diffusion models initially generate coarse outlines and shapes of objects, progressively refining details (e.g., style) as the denoising process continues. Accordingly, our method leverages this characteristic to divide our denoising process into two stages for improved performance. We introduce a hyperparameter η ∈(0, 1) to split the total timestep [0, T] into [0, ηT] and [ηT, T], and then we focus on enhancing the structural fidelity of the inpainted content in [ηT, T], while emphasizing stylistic harmony between the masked and unmasked regions in [0, ηT]. This design significantly reduces the computational cost during inference. V. EXPERIMENTS A. Experimental Settings 1) Implementation Details: Our method is implemented on top of SDI and operates without additional training. We set the classifier-free guidance scale [32] to 7.5 and use 50step DDIM [31] sampling. For the division strategy, we set parameters as follows: τ = 0.1, λ = 1.4, and η = 0.6. SelfAttention Masking Strategy (SAMS): is applied to layers 2-6 of the U-Net, while the Mask-Adjusted Key-Value Strategy (MAKVS) is employed in the final 8 layers. 2) Competitors: We compare our method with several stateof-the-art text-guided inpainting methods, including Blended Latent Diffusion (BLD) [4], Control Net Inpainting (CNI) [1], Stable Diffusion Inpainting (SDI) [6], Brush Net (BN) [2], and Power Paint (PP) [3]. For CNI, BN, and PP, we use their official pretrained models. All competitors are evaluated with their default settings. 3) Test Benchmarks: Commonly used datasets for image inpainting, such as MSCOCO [64], Open Images [65], and Image Net [66], are primarily designed for natural images and do not suit our aim of testing harmonized inpainting across diverse styles. Therefore, we created a Stylized-COCO dataset by selecting 50 reference images in various styles from Wiki Art [67] and applying Style ID [61] to transform MSCOCO images into different artistic styles. The dataset includes both segmentation masks and bounding box masks, with MSCOCO captions as text conditions. Additionally, we generated a Stylized-Open Images dataset following the same procedure, using Open Images as the base. 4) Evaluation Metrics: Traditional inpainting metrics, such as FID [68] and KID [69], fail to adequately capture the diversity and style harmonization required in our setting [70]. Instead, we evaluate performance using CLIP Score (CS) [71], Image Reward (IR) [72], Aesthetic Score (AS) [34], and CLIP Maximum Mean Discrepancy (CMMD) [70]. CS measures the alignment between inpainted content and the provided text prompt. IR, a human preference-based model designed for text-to-image tasks, assesses structural fidelity. AS quantifies stylistic harmony using a linear model trained on real imagequality scores. CMMD evaluates distributional differences between the reference and generated image sets by computing the squared MMD distance between their CLIP embeddings. B. As λ increases, the style of the “cake” progressively aligns with that of the unmasked region, achieving visual harmony at λ = 1.4. However, increasing λ beyond this point causes the self-attention layer to overemphasize style information, which interferes with content generation. Our experiments show that setting τ = 0 (hard mask) leads to noticeable boundary artifacts. In contrast, values of τ within the range 0.1 to 0.6 strike an optimal balance, yielding high-quality, well-controlled inpainting results. General Inpainting Although our method is primarily designed for stylized image inpainting, it also performs effectively on general inpainting tasks, as shown in Fig. 10. Unlike stylized images, natural images lack a distinct artistic style, yet achieving visual harmony still requires careful attention to lighting and color consistency. To address this, we set λ to 0.8, allowing the diffusion model to capture subtle visual attributes while minimizing stylistic interference from the unmasked region. The results align with the text descriptions while maintaining a realistic and cohesive appearance, demonstrating the versatility of our approach. Notably, while prior methods struggle to adapt to both stylized and natural image inpainting, our method excels in both scenarios without requiring additional modifications. VI. CONCLUSIONS, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE WORK In this paper, we propose Harmon Paint, a diffusion-based inpainting framework capable of producing harmonious and structurally coherent results across diverse styles without requiring additional training. Harmon Paint effectively preserves structural fidelity and ensures stylistic consistency between inpainted and unmasked regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate its robustness under various mask types and its applicability to natural images. 9 Input Ours “house” Fig. 11: When the image is more than 90% missing, especially when only one edge remains, although we can use text to complete the masked content, it is difficult to achieve Harmonized Inpainting due to the insufficient style information provided outside the mask. While our method performs well for small to medium missing regions, its effectiveness degrades when the masked area exceeds 90% of the image, as shown in Fig. 11. This limitation arises from the reliance on the remaining unmasked content as the primary source of style cues, which becomes insufficient in extreme cases. In future work, we plan to explore strategies to infer stylistic information directly from text descriptions or to incorporate external references to improve performance in scenarios with large missing regions. APPENDIX A USER STUDY We conduct a user study to evaluate the performance of our method against competing approaches. A total of 20 incomplete images are randomly selected, and their inpainting results using our method and other methods are compiled into a questionnaire with two evaluation criteria: Q1) “Which image better aligns with the given text description?” and Q2) “Which image exhibits stronger style consistency and visual harmony?” The study is completed by 40 participants independently, without prior knowledge of the methods used. Scores are computed as the proportion of times each method is selected for the two questions, with results summarized in Tab. IV. Our method achieves the highest scores in both questions, demonstrating its ability to ensure strong text alignment and structural fidelity simultaneously. While methods such as Brushnet and Power Paint performed well in Q1, they scored lower in Q2 due to insufficient consideration of stylistic harmony. Harmon Paint addresses this limitation using the Mask-Adjusted Key-Value Strategy (MAKVS) to transfer style information from unmasked regions into the masked areas, ensuring visual coherence. 2507.16612v1.title: CTSL: Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning for Accurate Non-Contrast Cardiac Risk Prediction Using Cine MRIs
2507.16612v1.abstract: CTSL: Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning for Accurate Non-Contrast Cardiac Risk Prediction Using Cine MRIs Haoyang Su1,2,4, Shaohao Rui2,3,4, Jinyi Xiang3, Lianming Wu3, and Xiaosong Wang4(B) 1 Fudan University, Shanghai, China 2 Shanghai Innovation Institute, Shanghai, China 3 Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China 4 Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China Abstract. Accurate and contrast-free Major Adverse Cardiac Events (MACE) prediction from Cine MRI sequences remains a critical challenge. Existing methods typically necessitate supervised learning based on human-refined masks in the ventricular myocardium, which become impractical without contrast agents. We introduce a self-supervised framework, namely Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning (CTSL), that learns dynamic, spatiotemporal representations from raw Cine data without requiring segmentation masks. CTSL decouples temporal and spatial features through a multi-view distillation strategy, where the teacher model processes multiple Cine views, and the student model learns from reduced-dimensional Cine-SA sequences. By leveraging codebook-based feature representations and dynamic lesion self-detection through motion cues, CTSL captures intricate temporal dependencies and motion patterns. High-confidence MACE risk predictions are achieved through our model, providing a rapid, non-invasive solution for cardiac risk assessment that outperforms traditional contrast-dependent methods, thereby enabling timely and accessible heart disease diagnosis in clinical settings. Keywords: Motion-aware Multi-view Distillation · Temporal-Spatial Feature Disentangling · Non-contrast Survival Prediction 1 Introduction The application of MACE in survival analysis within cardiology is of paramount importance, serving as a critical indicator of long-term cardiac health and treatment outcomes [3, 27, 26]. In this context, Cine cardiac MRI imaging is widely accessible, while its prognostic efficacy is significantly hindered by the inherent intricacy of myocardial tissue and the entanglement of its temporal and spatial dynamics [24]. Classical methods [5, 15, 21], modeled through electronic health records (EHR) or radiomics, purely rely on manual interpretations of structural and functional abnormalities [1, 2], which are subject to inter-observer variability and often fail to capture subtle, yet crucial, prognostic features. Though the ar Xiv:2507.16612v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 2 H. Su et al. landscape of state-of-the-art survival models for 3D medical imaging is vast, limitations still persist. XSurv [19], which utilizes multi-modal data such as PET and CT scans, struggles with the scarcity of paired samples and the challenges of data co-registration. Ada MSS [20], which requires physician-driven lesion refinement, is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Furthermore, models specialized in pathology [29, 25, 13, 11] are limited by their reliance on 2D imaging, resulting in poor generalization to high-dimensional images. As a result, while Cine imaging is a commonly available modality, its integration of multi-dimensional data, including multi-chamber dynamics from short-axis and longitudinal views of cardiac morphology over time, still remains a challenge in survival analysis. In this work, we first present a self-supervised pre-training scheme, denoted as CTSL, which operates independently of heart masks or contrast imaging data. The framework mainly comprises two stages: motion-aware multi-view model distillation and spatiotemporal disentangling. Initially, we extend the classical distillation learning paradigm, DINOv2 [23], from a patient-level perspective, innovatively incorporating multi-view Cine sequences as input for the distillation, i.e., injecting the information from other views than short-axis (SA) images into the pre-trained model. In this stage, motion queries extracted through SA Cine sequences are treated as myocardium-oriented key tokens by the student network, which aligns with long-axis Cine tokens from the teacher network via Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [17]. Subsequently, drawing upon the latent space discretization techniques of VQVAE [22], we extract query tokens from the preceding KL-aligned student model and design trainable temporal and spatial codebook embeddings, disentangling the spatiotemporal representations from the compressed 4D Cine data. Finally, a survival prediction framework is presented using the learned image tokens from CTSL and EHR features to perform MACE-based survival analysis. Our contributions in the proposed framework are threefold: 1) We demonstrate the feasibility of adopting contrast-free imaging techniques together with EHR for the MACE survival analysis. 2) We introduce a self-supervised framework, CTSL, that learns codebook-based spatiotemporal representations from raw Cine data via a motion-aware multi-view model distillation module and a spatiotemporal feature disentanglement module. 3) We evaluate the proposed survival analysis framework on three private datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to prior arts. 2 Method We propose the CTSL framework shown in Fig. 1, which operates through a two-stage self-supervised learning paradigm, followed by a final survival prediction stage. In stage I, multi-view cine sequences are processed independently by teacher and student networks, where KL loss LKL aligns SA dynamics with long-axis anatomical patterns, while motion-aware distillation is enforced via motion contrastive loss LMCL. CTSL: Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning 9 4 Conclusion This study introduces a self-supervised framework for non-contrast cardiac risk prediction, integrating motion-aware model distillation with codebook-based spatiotemporal disentanglement. By eliminating manual annotations, our approach effectively captures intrinsic myocardial dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that CTSL not only enhances prognostic accuracy but also improves model interpretability by transforming raw 4D Cine sequences into relevant image biomarkers. These findings highlight the potential of routine imaging for risk stratification, laying the groundwork for future advancements in personalized therapeutic planning through dynamic motion trajectory modeling. 2507.16612v1.full_text: CTSL: Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning for Accurate Non-Contrast Cardiac Risk Prediction Using Cine MRIs Haoyang Su1,2,4, Shaohao Rui2,3,4, Jinyi Xiang3, Lianming Wu3, and Xiaosong Wang4(B) 1 Fudan University, Shanghai, China 2 Shanghai Innovation Institute, Shanghai, China 3 Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China 4 Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China Abstract. Accurate and contrast-free Major Adverse Cardiac Events (MACE) prediction from Cine MRI sequences remains a critical challenge. Existing methods typically necessitate supervised learning based on human-refined masks in the ventricular myocardium, which become impractical without contrast agents. We introduce a self-supervised framework, namely Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning (CTSL), that learns dynamic, spatiotemporal representations from raw Cine data without requiring segmentation masks. CTSL decouples temporal and spatial features through a multi-view distillation strategy, where the teacher model processes multiple Cine views, and the student model learns from reduced-dimensional Cine-SA sequences. By leveraging codebook-based feature representations and dynamic lesion self-detection through motion cues, CTSL captures intricate temporal dependencies and motion patterns. High-confidence MACE risk predictions are achieved through our model, providing a rapid, non-invasive solution for cardiac risk assessment that outperforms traditional contrast-dependent methods, thereby enabling timely and accessible heart disease diagnosis in clinical settings. Keywords: Motion-aware Multi-view Distillation · Temporal-Spatial Feature Disentangling · Non-contrast Survival Prediction 1 Introduction The application of MACE in survival analysis within cardiology is of paramount importance, serving as a critical indicator of long-term cardiac health and treatment outcomes [3, 27, 26]. In this context, Cine cardiac MRI imaging is widely accessible, while its prognostic efficacy is significantly hindered by the inherent intricacy of myocardial tissue and the entanglement of its temporal and spatial dynamics [24]. Classical methods [5, 15, 21], modeled through electronic health records (EHR) or radiomics, purely rely on manual interpretations of structural and functional abnormalities [1, 2], which are subject to inter-observer variability and often fail to capture subtle, yet crucial, prognostic features. Though the ar Xiv:2507.16612v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 2 H. Su et al. landscape of state-of-the-art survival models for 3D medical imaging is vast, limitations still persist. XSurv [19], which utilizes multi-modal data such as PET and CT scans, struggles with the scarcity of paired samples and the challenges of data co-registration. Ada MSS [20], which requires physician-driven lesion refinement, is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Furthermore, models specialized in pathology [29, 25, 13, 11] are limited by their reliance on 2D imaging, resulting in poor generalization to high-dimensional images. As a result, while Cine imaging is a commonly available modality, its integration of multi-dimensional data, including multi-chamber dynamics from short-axis and longitudinal views of cardiac morphology over time, still remains a challenge in survival analysis. In this work, we first present a self-supervised pre-training scheme, denoted as CTSL, which operates independently of heart masks or contrast imaging data. The framework mainly comprises two stages: motion-aware multi-view model distillation and spatiotemporal disentangling. Initially, we extend the classical distillation learning paradigm, DINOv2 [23], from a patient-level perspective, innovatively incorporating multi-view Cine sequences as input for the distillation, i.e., injecting the information from other views than short-axis (SA) images into the pre-trained model. In this stage, motion queries extracted through SA Cine sequences are treated as myocardium-oriented key tokens by the student network, which aligns with long-axis Cine tokens from the teacher network via Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [17]. Subsequently, drawing upon the latent space discretization techniques of VQVAE [22], we extract query tokens from the preceding KL-aligned student model and design trainable temporal and spatial codebook embeddings, disentangling the spatiotemporal representations from the compressed 4D Cine data. Finally, a survival prediction framework is presented using the learned image tokens from CTSL and EHR features to perform MACE-based survival analysis. Our contributions in the proposed framework are threefold: 1) We demonstrate the feasibility of adopting contrast-free imaging techniques together with EHR for the MACE survival analysis. 2) We introduce a self-supervised framework, CTSL, that learns codebook-based spatiotemporal representations from raw Cine data via a motion-aware multi-view model distillation module and a spatiotemporal feature disentanglement module. 3) We evaluate the proposed survival analysis framework on three private datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to prior arts. 2 Method We propose the CTSL framework shown in Fig. 1, which operates through a two-stage self-supervised learning paradigm, followed by a final survival prediction stage. In stage I, multi-view cine sequences are processed independently by teacher and student networks, where KL loss LKL aligns SA dynamics with long-axis anatomical patterns, while motion-aware distillation is enforced via motion contrastive loss LMCL. The proposed model was developed utilizing the Py Torch framework and trained on a single NVIDIA-H100 GPU with CUDA 12.2. The optimization process utilized the Adam optimizer [16], with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5 and weight decay set to 1 × 10−5. A batch size of 16 was employed, and training was conducted over 50 epochs with the Step LR scheduler. To evaluate the robustness of our framework, we design ablation experiments at three levels: (1) Model CTSL, which is obtained through the complete workflow; (2) Model Uniformer(Distilled), whose representation aggregated from motion queries directly without employing the discrete spatiotemporal codebook for refinement; (3) Model Uniformer(Image Net), which does not undergo distillation or codebook discretization, and instead relies solely on pretrained Image Net [6] weights as a feature extractor. While achieving marginally lower performance in cohort RJCCM, Stage II’s disentangled spatiotemporal representations achieve statistically an overall performance improvement (mean ∆C-index: +0.078 vs. Stage I). This cross-cohort consistency quantitatively validates the robustness of our latent space learning paradigm against anatomical variability. CTSL: Codebook-based Temporal-Spatial Learning 9 4 Conclusion This study introduces a self-supervised framework for non-contrast cardiac risk prediction, integrating motion-aware model distillation with codebook-based spatiotemporal disentanglement. By eliminating manual annotations, our approach effectively captures intrinsic myocardial dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that CTSL not only enhances prognostic accuracy but also improves model interpretability by transforming raw 4D Cine sequences into relevant image biomarkers. These findings highlight the potential of routine imaging for risk stratification, laying the groundwork for future advancements in personalized therapeutic planning through dynamic motion trajectory modeling. 2507.16663v1.abstract: Self-Contradiction as Self-Improvement: Mitigating the Generation-Understanding Gap in MLLMs Yujin Han1,8∗, Hao Chen2, Andi Han3,4, Zhiheng Wang5,6, Xinyu Lin7 Yingya Zhang8, Shiwei Zhang8†, Difan Zou1† 1The University of Hong Kong, 2Carnegie Mellon University, 3University of Sydney, 4RIKEN AIP, 5Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, 6Shanghai Jiao Tong University,7Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, 8Alibaba Group Abstract Despite efforts to unify multimodal generation and understanding tasks in a single model, we show these MLLMs exhibit self-contradiction where generation produces images deemed misaligned with input prompts based on model’s own understanding. We define a Nonunified score that quantifies such self-contradiction. Our empirical results reveal that the self-contradiction mainly arises from weak generation that fails to align with prompts, rather than misunderstanding. This capability asymmetry indicates the potential of leveraging self-contradiction for self-improvement, where the stronger model understanding guides the weaker generation to mitigate the generation–understanding gap. Applying standard posttraining methods (e.g., SFT, DPO) with such internal supervision successfully improves both generation and unification. We discover a co-improvement effect on both generation and understanding when only fine-tuning the generation branch, a phenomenon known in pre-training but underexplored in post-training. Our analysis shows improvements stem from better detection of false positives that are previously incorrectly identified as prompt-aligned. Theoretically, we show the aligned training dynamics between generation and understanding allow reduced promptmisaligned generations to also improve mismatch detection in the understanding branch. Additionally, the framework reveals a potential risk of co-degradation under poor supervision—an overlooked phenomenon that is empirically validated in our experiments. Notably, we find intrinsic metrics like Nonunified score cannot distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement, which highlights the necessity of data quality check. Finally, we propose a curriculum-based strategy based on our findings that gradually introduces harder samples as the model improves, leading to better unification and improved MLLM generation and understanding. 1 Introduction Recently, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in both image understanding and generation tasks [1–6]. Understanding tasks often rely on high-level semantic from image data, while generation tasks require more pixel-level details for accurate reconstruction [7–10]. Despite the difference in information granularity, unified pre-training approaches, such as shared tokenizers and autoregressive model architectures, have been actively explored [3, 4, 8]. Unlike prior work compares generation and understanding separately on disjoint-modal data [15] or focuses on single-task performance [16, 17], self-contradiction emphasizes internal inconsistency: as shown in Figure 1, a model’s generated image may be deemed misaligned with the prompt by its own understanding branch. This phenomenon not only indicates imperfect unification between generation and understanding, but also reveals an asymmetry in their capabilities. Over 85% of these cases are attributable to weak generation, where understanding branch correctly rejects prompt-misaligned outputs. To address the above question, we first quantify selfcontradiction and provide a systematic analysis of its origins. Specifically, we introduce the Nonunified score (detailed in equation 1), defined as the proportion of cases where the understanding branch judges the generated outputs as prompt-misaligned. Ideally, a fully unified MLLM would have a Nonunified score of zero. However, as shown in Figure 2, models such as Janus-Pro-7B [18] exhibit clear self-contradiction with nonzero Nonunified scores, i.e., the nonunified scores range from 10% to 40% across different concepts. To further analyze these contradictions, we leverage the strong external model Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct [19] to assess the accuracy of the understanding branch’s evaluations of generated outputs. Figure 2 indicates that most misalignments stem from weak generation rather than misunderstanding, with incorrect rejections of correct generations by the understanding branch accounting for less than 15%. These findings indicate that promoting MLLM unification can be achieved by having the stronger understanding branch guide the weaker generation branch, enabling a fully self-improvement method without external supervision. We first explore classical post-training techniques such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) [20, 21] and direct preference optimization (DPO) [22], treating the understanding branch as an internal reward model to construct post-training data for the generation branch. Experi2 ments on Janus-Pro-7B validate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding significant improvements in both generation and unification of MLLMs. Alongside improvements in both generation and unification, we also observe a co-improvement effect between the generation and understanding branches: during post-training that targets generation, not only does the generation branch improve, but the understanding branch is also enhanced. While coimprovement between generation and understanding has been widely observed during pre-training [23– 26], it remains underexplored in the post-training stage [15]. To understand this phenomenon, we analyze the improvement in understanding primarily comes from the model’s enhanced ability to recognize false-positive samples, namely generations that were incorrectly considered promptaligned. By extending the learning dynamics framework [27] to the multimodal setting, we formalize how generation and understanding behaviors evolve for each image–prompt pair (x, y) during self-improvement and reveal both branches tend to follow consistent learning trajectories. This helps explain the improvement in understanding, as shared training dynamics allow generation-side optimization to reduce the probability of producing prompt-misaligned outputs also enhance the understanding branch’s ability to recognize such misalignments. Interestingly, our learning dynamics analysis also indicates the potential for co-degradation, especially when low-quality post-training data, such as corrupted images misaligned with prompts, are introduced. We confirm this risk on Janus-Pro-1B [18]: fine-tuning with completely corrupted SFT labels results in a synchronized decline in both branches. Notably, intrinsic MLLM metrics like the Nonunified score fail to distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement, as both scenarios manifest as improved unification. These findings highlight the necessity of pre-validating data quality, e.g., using external models, prior to initiating self-improvement. Finally, we explore whether the synchronized mechanism between generation and understanding can further enhance self-improvement in MLLMs. The observed co-improvement effect motivates us to introduce curriculum learning [28, 29] in post-training by gradually incorporating harder samples that were initially excluded due to limited generation or understanding abilities. This online strategy leverages the evolving capabilities of both branches to progressively expand the training data based on sample difficulty and further improve both the performance and unification of MLLMs. 2 Nonunified Generation and Understanding of MLLMs Takeaway on self-contradiction MLLMs such as Janus-Pro-7B exhibit a self-contradiction phenomenon, reflecting a disparity between generation and understanding capabilities. Further analysis reveals that the selfcontradiction is primarily attributed to weak generation strength, while the understanding branch correctly identifies prompt-misaligned images. Notably, on Texture dataset, the score reaches over 43%, indicating for 43% of prompts, the generated images are judged by its own understanding branch as failing to align the given prompts. The results suggest Janus-Pro-7B exhibits self-contradiction, where generation and understanding fail to demonstrate unified behavior. Figure 2 shows that the majority of misalignments (over 85%) fall into the first type, where Janus Pro’s understanding branch correctly rejects prompt-misaligned generations. These results suggest that mitigating unification issues in MLLMs through self-improvement can be achieved by leveraging the stronger understanding branch to guide the weaker generation branch. 3 Co-Improvement of Generation and Understanding in Post-Training In this section, we apply classical post-training strategies to enable self-improvement in MLLMs (Section 3.1) and examine whether these strategies can promote unification. We then further investigate how generation-targeted self-improvement influences the understanding branch (see Section 3.2,Section 3.2.2 and Section 3.2.3), which provides insights into better mitigating the generation–understanding gap. 3.1 Leveraging Self-Contradiction for MLLMs’ Self-Improvement Takeaway on self-improvement In self-improvement of MLLMs, we find: • Leveraging self-contradiction by using the understanding branch as an internal reward model can effectively improve generation and promote unification. • Generation-targeted self-improvement also enhances model’s understanding, indicating co-improvement between generation and understanding exists in post-training as well. We consider classical post-training strategies, such as DPO and SFT. Specifically, using DPO as an example, we construct preference pairs as follows: for a given image generation prompt y, the MLLM πθ first generates N candidate images {xi}N i=1 = πθ(y). Next, each candidate images in {xi}N i=1 is paired with the question “Does this image describe y?” and passed back into πθ for an understanding task. The model then selects images that align with the prompt (chosen image) and those that do not (rejected image), forming preference data (y, xchosen, xrejected) for DPO on the generation branch. For SFT, only the chosen samples are used for supervised fine-tuning. Better Generation and Unification . We consider Janus-Pro-7B on 3D Spatial subtask and report two metrics: generation quality, evaluated by Uni Det score [31] and unification between generation and understanding, measured by Nonunified score. Figure 3a shows generation quality improves with a 5% increase in Uni Det score, while Nonunified score decreases by 10%, demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging self-contradiction to enhance both MLLM generation and unification without any external signals. This is facilitated by aligned training dynamics between generation and understanding, where reducing prompt-misaligned generations helps the understanding branch better identify such misalignments. • Co-degradation: This phenomenon is particularly likely to occur under poor post-training data quality or when using smaller-scale models. Notably, internal metrics such as the Nonunified score are unable to distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation. We observe an interplay mechanism, i.e., co-improvement, between the reward model (understanding) and the fine-tuned model (generation) during self-improvement. The reward model evolves alongside the fine-tuned model is unique to MLLMs’ post-training, in contrast to traditional post-training settings where the reward model and the fine-tuned model are structurally decoupled [32–34]. Motivated by this observation, we pose the following questions: (1) Cause of co-improvement: why does generation-targeted self-improvement result in co-improvements in both branches? (2) Co-degradation: Does the synergy between generation and understanding manifest only as coimprovement, or can both branches also degrade together? 3.2.1 Learning Dynamics Theory of Generation and Understanding To address these questions, we need to understand the interplay mechanism between generation and understanding. We adopt the learning-dynamics framework [27] and extend it to the multimodal setting. To empirically validate the above theoretical insights, we compare two settings: one using correct SFT labels (i.e., the better image from DPO), and the other using corrupted labels—assigning the same corrupted image with a fixed image token ID as the SFT label for each prompt. More setting details are provided in Appendix A.3. Figure 9 presents performance in generation (Uni Det score), understanding (Win Rate), and unification (1 - Nonunified score) for two model sizes (1B and 7B) under both training settings. We observe: • Low-quality corrupted labels degrades MLLM performance. For the 1B model, corrupted supervision leads to significant co-degradation. • The occurrence of co-degradation is closely related to the model’s priors. Specifically, the 1B model exhibits a strong co-degradation effect whereas the 7B model shows degradation primarily in generation, while understanding remains more stable. Additionally, Figure 5a issues a warning: although the 1B model exhibits simultaneous degradation in both generation and understanding, its unification score still improves. This observation reveals a core limitation: without external supervision, internal metrics like unification cannot distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation. This phenomenon parallels findings in LLMs, where reliance on internal signals, such as self-critique, can result in model collapse [35, 36]. A straightforward way to avoid co-degradation is to pre-validate data quality using external models (e.g., Qwen). For instance, Qwen can reliably identify corrupted samples, thereby preventing the use of low-quality data during self-improvement. However, this approach still depends on stronger external models. An interesting direction is to explore whether any internal signals within MLLMs can be used to detect such risks, an open question we leave for future work. 4 Curriculum-based Self-Improvement: Leveraging Co-Improvement for Better MLLMs We next discuss how to further leverage the synergy between generation and understanding to promote self-improvement in MLLMs. While co-degradation is possible, it predominantly occurs in smaller models such as Janus-Pro-1B when trained with severely corrupted fine-tuning data. In contrast, larger models like Janus-Pro-7B (Figure 5b) are more robust to noisy supervision and less likely to produce low-quality data for self-improvemnet. This motivates us to further enhance the offline fine-tuning strategy by introducing a Curriculum Learning-based Online (CLO) post-training approach. Specifically, taking the construction of DPO data as an example, training prompts can be categorized into three types based on whether they can be utilized by the generation or understanding branches during post-training: 49.7% 48.3% 2.0% 89.5% 9.7% 0.9% Figure 6: Outer ring shows only 49.7% of prompts (Ideal Set) are usable in pre-trained model. After SFT, improved generation and understanding allow 9.7% (inner ring) of previously FC/FR sets to be incorporated. • Ideal Set: the candidate generations contain both samples that satisfy and not satisfy the prompt by the understanding branch—these are ideal for constructing preference pairs. • Fully Rejected (FR) Set: all candidate generations are considered to fail the prompt—this may indicate that the prompt is too complex for the generation branch. • Fully Chosen (FC) Set: all candidate generations are considered to satisfy the prompt—this could mean the prompt is simple for the generation branch, or that incorrect generations are too hard for the understanding branch to distinguish. For the 3D Spatial subtask, Figure 6 shows that with the pre-trained Janus-Pro model, the standard offline post-training strategy can only utilize 49.7% of the available data (the ideal set), while a substantial portion remains unusable due to generation or understanding failures, namely, the FC and FR sets. After SFT, we observe that 9.7% of these previously unusable FC and FR samples become usable again, driven by the co-improvement in generation and understanding. This observation further validates the rationale for introducing curriculum learning into the post-training process, enabling dynamic expansion of the training set as model capabilities improve. Figure 7 accordingly proposes a CLO-based fine-tuning strategy, in which both the training data and MLLM are updated during the post-training process. The curriculum is constructed in a prompt complexity-wise manner: training samples are introduced progressively from simple to difficult, starting with Ideal prompts and gradually incorporating FR and FC prompts. This training order naturally aligns with the evolving capabilities of generation and understanding, only when the model’s capacity improves can it extract useful training signals from FR and FC prompts. Moreover, it reflects the well-established principle of curriculum learning: learning from easy to hard examples, a strategy that has been proven effective in both human and machine learning [29, 37, 38]. 10 {!! We also evaluate T2I-R1 model3, which enhances Janus-Pro-7B’s generation capability by treating its understanding branch as a prompt-expansion tool and fine-tuning it with external reward models. We observe that the self-improved model performs competitively on T2I-R1 and even achieves better results in understanding. A possible reason is T2I-R1 relies on external rewards, while selfimprovement leverages internal signals from the understanding branch. An interesting direction for future work is to explore whether internal and external rewards induce different (synergistic) mechanisms between generation and understanding. Notably, self-improvement and external rewards are not mutually exclusive: self-improved models can be further improved using T2I-R1 techniques. 5 Related Work Prior work typically focuses on enhancing specific capabilities of MLLMs, such as generation [16, 39], rather than emphasizing unification between generation and understanding. In these work, understanding branch primarily serves to provide additional details for generation prompt expansion. By combining enriched prompts with external reward models (e.g., BLIP [40], Human Preference Model [41, 42]), these studies improve generation quality of MLLMs. In contrast, we center on mitigating internal inconsistency within MLLMs, rather than merely improving single3To ensure consistency with the evaluation protocol, we generate images directly from the original prompts without using the understanding branch for prompt expansion. 11 task performance and aim to uncover why generation and understanding can co-improve during post-training, and leverages this property to better enhance alignment without any external signal. Additionally, some studies [15, 17, 43] have explored self-improvement for MLLMs by applying methods such as SFT, DPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [44]. However, these methods do not explicitly explore the synergy between generation and understanding. Instead, they often treat them as separate tasks to be co-optimized, typically relying on external reward models or additional data construction. In contrast, our work focuses on self-improvement in MLLMs without relying on any external signals, and aims to explain the interaction mechanism that arises from the shared architecture between the generation (post-trained model) and understanding (reward model) branches, which has been overlooked in prior work. More importantly, our approach is not in conflict with existing methods. Instead, it can be viewed as a complementary and cost-free enhancement: once self-improvement is achieved, techniques such as Chain-of-Thought prompting [16, 45, 46] or QA-based supervision [17] can be further applied to boost MLLM performance. 6 Conclusion and Future Work This work serves as an exploratory prelude, offering a systematic investigation into the selfimprovement capabilities of MLLMs. We show that the inherent asymmetry between generation and understanding offers a unique opportunity to improve both performance and unification of MLLMs. For future work, we plan to extend our analysis to a broader range of models and benchmarks. Specifically, we aim to: (1) compare self-contradiction and self-improvement behaviors across more unified architectures, such as Show-O [1]; and (2) investigate the effectiveness of internal versus external reward signals in driving co-improvement of generation and understanding. Furthermore, the current learning dynamics framework introduced in Section 3.2.1 primarily focuses on single-token SFT scenarios. We plan to generalize it to multi-token settings and explore its applicability to a wider set of post-training strategies, including DPO. We fine-tune Janus-Pro-7B using 700 samples from the 3D Spatial training subset of T2I-Comp Bench. For DPO, we adopt a common practice of using the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss over the preferred response in each pair to enhance training stability and performance. In both the SFT and DPO settings, we perform full-parameter fine-tuning on the autoregressive branch of Janus-Pro for 120 epochs, which requires approximately 13 hours on 4 A800 GPUs. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule with a peak value of 1e-7. We save checkpoints every 20 epochs and report the checkpoint that yields the lowest Nonunified Score in Table 3. A.2 Details of Co-improvement Analysis Understanding Improvement. While Section 3.2.2 analyzes the proxy ∆Gt, in this section we directly compute ∆Gt and show that it exhibits the same trend in generation probability change, consistent with the prediction of Proposition 1. Following Table 1, we divide the post-training samples into two groups based on ground truth (GT): GT = 0 and GT = 1. Specifically, samples with label transitions (GT, Base, Post) = (0,1,0) and (1,0,1) are considered understanding-improved. Specially, given a prompt y, we first generate the image token sequence x = πpre(y) = (x1, . . . , x L) using the pre-trained model. We then define the direct generation probability change as: ∆Gt(x | y) := 1 L L X i=1 log πpost(xi | x<i, y) −log πpre(xi | x<i, y), (4) which measures how the likelihood of reproducing the original image x changes after post-training. Figure 8 compares two pairs of groups: (0,1,0) vs. (0,0,1) and (1,0,1) vs. (1,1,0), corresponding to the understanding-improved and baseline comparison groups, respectively. According to Proposition 1, we can predict the expected direction of change in generation probability, and mark the theoretically improving group with the Expected label. As shown in Figure 4, the directly computed ∆Gt exhibits a trend consistent with its proxy counterpart, further supporting the hypothesis of synchronized learning dynamics between generation and understanding. However, unlike the proxy metric which shows clear group-wise differences ∆Gt reveals only marginal numerical differences between groups, making the comparison less distinguishable. Generation Improvement. To analyze improvements in generation, we focus on samples whose Qwen scores change from 0 to 1 before and after post-training. Proposition 1 indicates if the generation branch reduces the probability of producing an incorrect image x given a prompt y, then the understanding branch is also less likely to judge that the incorrect image x satisfies the prompt y. For samples where the MLLM initially assigns a score of 1 to a misaligned image x and continues to do so after self-improvement, ∆Ut is expected to be negative. Conversely, for samples consistently scored as 0, the log-probability should increase, i.e., ∆Ut > 0, even the score changes from 1 to 0. To compute ∆Ut, we first identify the subset of prompts for which the Qwen score changes from 0 to 1. Next, the pre-trained MLLM is used to generate images corresponding to these prompts. Both the pre-trained and post-trained MLLMs then perform the relevant understanding tasks on these samples, 16 and the corresponding ∆Ut values are calculated. As shown in Table 2, we observe that in nearly 60% of cases, the understanding trend (i.e., the direction of ∆Ut) aligns with the theoretical prediction. A.3 Details of Co-degradation Analysis Figure 9: Corrupted SFT objective with a fixed token 624. To verify whether improper fine-tuning data can lead to simultaneous degradation of generation and understanding in MLLMs, we conduct experiments using Janus-Pro-1B, a smaller model with weaker priors that is more susceptible to data corruption. Focusing on the 3D Spatial subtask, we apply standard SFT for fine-tuning, but replace all labels with a fixed target token ID of 624, meaning that each training sample is optimized to generate the same image as shown in Figure 9. We fine-tune the model for 120 epochs, saving a checkpoint every 20 epochs to track generation and understanding performance over time. Figure 9 reports the model’s performance at the checkpoint with the lowest nonunified score and shows that under an incorrect fine-tuning objective for the generation branch, both generation and understanding degrade simultaneously, with a notable drop in understanding accuracy. This supports the reasoning in Proposition 1 and underscores that self-improvement with low-quality data carries the risk of synchronized degradation alongside potential co-improvement. A.4 Details of Curriculum-based Post-training Details of Curriculum-based Post-training. In the online strategy, we continue using the 3D Spatial subtask and train the Janus-Pro-7B for 120 epochs with both SFT and DPO. We still set the maximum learning rate to 1e-7 with cosine learning schedule and perform full-parameter fine-tuning on the LLM component. Curriculum updates are introduced at epoch 60 to incorporate additional training samples that were previously unusable for fine-tuning due to the limited generation and understanding capabilities of the initial Janus model. Figure 6 illustrates the distribution of newly added training samples during curriculum learning. We follow the same evaluation protocol as Section 2, using the original image generation prompts from T2I-Comp Bench [30] without semantic expansions, which results in lower baseline generation scores compared to evaluations with prompt augmentation [16]. 2507.16663v1.full_text: Self-Contradiction as Self-Improvement: Mitigating the Generation-Understanding Gap in MLLMs Yujin Han1,8∗, Hao Chen2, Andi Han3,4, Zhiheng Wang5,6, Xinyu Lin7 Yingya Zhang8, Shiwei Zhang8†, Difan Zou1† 1The University of Hong Kong, 2Carnegie Mellon University, 3University of Sydney, 4RIKEN AIP, 5Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, 6Shanghai Jiao Tong University,7Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, 8Alibaba Group Abstract Despite efforts to unify multimodal generation and understanding tasks in a single model, we show these MLLMs exhibit self-contradiction where generation produces images deemed misaligned with input prompts based on model’s own understanding. We define a Nonunified score that quantifies such self-contradiction. Our empirical results reveal that the self-contradiction mainly arises from weak generation that fails to align with prompts, rather than misunderstanding. This capability asymmetry indicates the potential of leveraging self-contradiction for self-improvement, where the stronger model understanding guides the weaker generation to mitigate the generation–understanding gap. Applying standard posttraining methods (e.g., SFT, DPO) with such internal supervision successfully improves both generation and unification. We discover a co-improvement effect on both generation and understanding when only fine-tuning the generation branch, a phenomenon known in pre-training but underexplored in post-training. Our analysis shows improvements stem from better detection of false positives that are previously incorrectly identified as prompt-aligned. Theoretically, we show the aligned training dynamics between generation and understanding allow reduced promptmisaligned generations to also improve mismatch detection in the understanding branch. Additionally, the framework reveals a potential risk of co-degradation under poor supervision—an overlooked phenomenon that is empirically validated in our experiments. Notably, we find intrinsic metrics like Nonunified score cannot distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement, which highlights the necessity of data quality check. Finally, we propose a curriculum-based strategy based on our findings that gradually introduces harder samples as the model improves, leading to better unification and improved MLLM generation and understanding. 1 Introduction Recently, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in both image understanding and generation tasks [1–6]. Understanding tasks often rely on high-level semantic from image data, while generation tasks require more pixel-level details for accurate reconstruction [7–10]. Despite the difference in information granularity, unified pre-training approaches, such as shared tokenizers and autoregressive model architectures, have been actively explored [3, 4, 8]. We begin by highlighting that unified MLLMs are not truly unified in behavior, as evidenced by the phenomenon of self-contradiction, i.e., a mismatch between the generation and understanding ∗Email to: Yujin Han †Correspondence to: Shiwei Zhang and Difan Zou ar Xiv:2507.16663v1 [cs.CL] 22 Jul 2025 Generate an image: a plush lion toy in front of the mirror. In reality, the elephant's side of the seesaw would be firmly on the ground, and the mouse's side would be elevated high in the air. We find that a discrepancy exists within MLLMs: images produced by the generation branch are identified as incorrect by their own understanding branch, showing a lack of MLLM unification. branches. Unlike prior work compares generation and understanding separately on disjoint-modal data [15] or focuses on single-task performance [16, 17], self-contradiction emphasizes internal inconsistency: as shown in Figure 1, a model’s generated image may be deemed misaligned with the prompt by its own understanding branch. This phenomenon not only indicates imperfect unification between generation and understanding, but also reveals an asymmetry in their capabilities. Such asymmetry raises a question: Can stronger branch guide the weaker to achieve self-improvement of MLLMs without any external rewards? 0 10 20 30 40 Nonunified Score (%) 3D Spatial Color Shape Texture Complexity Weak Generation Weak Understanding Figure 2: Janus-Pro-7B exhibits notable generation-understanding contradiction, with Nonunified score ranging from 10% to 40%. Over 85% of these cases are attributable to weak generation, where understanding branch correctly rejects prompt-misaligned outputs. To address the above question, we first quantify selfcontradiction and provide a systematic analysis of its origins. Specifically, we introduce the Nonunified score (detailed in equation 1), defined as the proportion of cases where the understanding branch judges the generated outputs as prompt-misaligned. Ideally, a fully unified MLLM would have a Nonunified score of zero. However, as shown in Figure 2, models such as Janus-Pro-7B [18] exhibit clear self-contradiction with nonzero Nonunified scores, i.e., the nonunified scores range from 10% to 40% across different concepts. To further analyze these contradictions, we leverage the strong external model Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct [19] to assess the accuracy of the understanding branch’s evaluations of generated outputs. Figure 2 indicates that most misalignments stem from weak generation rather than misunderstanding, with incorrect rejections of correct generations by the understanding branch accounting for less than 15%. These findings indicate that promoting MLLM unification can be achieved by having the stronger understanding branch guide the weaker generation branch, enabling a fully self-improvement method without external supervision. We first explore classical post-training techniques such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) [20, 21] and direct preference optimization (DPO) [22], treating the understanding branch as an internal reward model to construct post-training data for the generation branch. Experi2 ments on Janus-Pro-7B validate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding significant improvements in both generation and unification of MLLMs. Alongside improvements in both generation and unification, we also observe a co-improvement effect between the generation and understanding branches: during post-training that targets generation, not only does the generation branch improve, but the understanding branch is also enhanced. While coimprovement between generation and understanding has been widely observed during pre-training [23– 26], it remains underexplored in the post-training stage [15]. To understand this phenomenon, we analyze the improvement in understanding primarily comes from the model’s enhanced ability to recognize false-positive samples, namely generations that were incorrectly considered promptaligned. By extending the learning dynamics framework [27] to the multimodal setting, we formalize how generation and understanding behaviors evolve for each image–prompt pair (x, y) during self-improvement and reveal both branches tend to follow consistent learning trajectories. This helps explain the improvement in understanding, as shared training dynamics allow generation-side optimization to reduce the probability of producing prompt-misaligned outputs also enhance the understanding branch’s ability to recognize such misalignments. Interestingly, our learning dynamics analysis also indicates the potential for co-degradation, especially when low-quality post-training data, such as corrupted images misaligned with prompts, are introduced. We confirm this risk on Janus-Pro-1B [18]: fine-tuning with completely corrupted SFT labels results in a synchronized decline in both branches. Notably, intrinsic MLLM metrics like the Nonunified score fail to distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement, as both scenarios manifest as improved unification. These findings highlight the necessity of pre-validating data quality, e.g., using external models, prior to initiating self-improvement. Finally, we explore whether the synchronized mechanism between generation and understanding can further enhance self-improvement in MLLMs. The observed co-improvement effect motivates us to introduce curriculum learning [28, 29] in post-training by gradually incorporating harder samples that were initially excluded due to limited generation or understanding abilities. This online strategy leverages the evolving capabilities of both branches to progressively expand the training data based on sample difficulty and further improve both the performance and unification of MLLMs. 2 Nonunified Generation and Understanding of MLLMs Takeaway on self-contradiction MLLMs such as Janus-Pro-7B exhibit a self-contradiction phenomenon, reflecting a disparity between generation and understanding capabilities. Further analysis reveals that the selfcontradiction is primarily attributed to weak generation strength, while the understanding branch correctly identifies prompt-misaligned images. We first propose the Nonunified score to quantify self-contradiction, i.e., the capability asymmetry between the generation and understanding. Specifically, consider an MLLM πθ and a prompt y ∈Y, where Y denotes the prompt space. The generation branch produces an image x = πgen θ (y), and the pair (x, q(y)), where q(y) := “Does this image describe y?”, is then passed into the understanding branch πund θ (·, ·). If the understanding branch deems x aligned with prompt y score 1; otherwise, score 0. We define the Nonunified score as the proportion of score 0, i.e., Nonunified score := 1 |Y| X y∈Y I  πund θ (x, q(y)) ̸= 1  . (1) We evaluate the Nonunified score of Janus-Pro-7B on T2I-Comp Bench [30] in Figure 2 and find that the Nonunified score is consistently greater than zero across all tasks. Notably, on Texture dataset, the score reaches over 43%, indicating for 43% of prompts, the generated images are judged by its own understanding branch as failing to align the given prompts. The results suggest Janus-Pro-7B exhibits self-contradiction, where generation and understanding fail to demonstrate unified behavior. To further investigate the causes of generation–understanding gap, we assign each generated image a ground-truth label s Qwen ∈{0, 1} based on scores from Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct. Among the cases where the Janus-Pro-7B understanding branch assigns a score of 0 (i.e., rejects the generation), we identify two types of misalignment: 3 • Weak Generation: Understanding branch correctly rejects a misaligned image produced by the generation branch. This corresponds to both Janus-Pro-7B and Qwen assigning a score of 0: Weak Generation := P �πund θ (x, q(y)) = s Qwen πund θ (x, q(y)) = 0  . • Weak Understanding: Generation branch produces a correct image, but understanding branch mistakenly rejects it. This occurs when Janus-Pro-7B assigns a score of 0 while Qwen assigns 1: Weak Understanding := P �πund θ (x, q(y)) ̸= s Qwen πund θ (x, q(y)) = 0  . Figure 2 shows that the majority of misalignments (over 85%) fall into the first type, where JanusPro’s understanding branch correctly rejects prompt-misaligned generations. These results suggest that mitigating unification issues in MLLMs through self-improvement can be achieved by leveraging the stronger understanding branch to guide the weaker generation branch. 3 Co-Improvement of Generation and Understanding in Post-Training In this section, we apply classical post-training strategies to enable self-improvement in MLLMs (Section 3.1) and examine whether these strategies can promote unification. We then further investigate how generation-targeted self-improvement influences the understanding branch (see Section 3.2,Section 3.2.2 and Section 3.2.3), which provides insights into better mitigating the generation–understanding gap. 3.1 Leveraging Self-Contradiction for MLLMs’ Self-Improvement Takeaway on self-improvement In self-improvement of MLLMs, we find: • Leveraging self-contradiction by using the understanding branch as an internal reward model can effectively improve generation and promote unification. • Generation-targeted self-improvement also enhances model’s understanding, indicating co-improvement between generation and understanding exists in post-training as well. We consider classical post-training strategies, such as DPO and SFT. Specifically, using DPO as an example, we construct preference pairs as follows: for a given image generation prompt y, the MLLM πθ first generates N candidate images {xi}N i=1 = πθ(y). Next, each candidate images in {xi}N i=1 is paired with the question “Does this image describe y?” and passed back into πθ for an understanding task. The model then selects images that align with the prompt (chosen image) and those that do not (rejected image), forming preference data (y, xchosen, xrejected) for DPO on the generation branch. For SFT, only the chosen samples are used for supervised fine-tuning. Better Generation and Unification . We consider Janus-Pro-7B on 3D Spatial subtask and report two metrics: generation quality, evaluated by Uni Det score [31] and unification between generation and understanding, measured by Nonunified score. Figure 3a shows generation quality improves with a 5% increase in Uni Det score, while Nonunified score decreases by 10%, demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging self-contradiction to enhance both MLLM generation and unification without any external signals. This is facilitated by aligned training dynamics between generation and understanding, where reducing prompt-misaligned generations helps the understanding branch better identify such misalignments. • Co-degradation: This phenomenon is particularly likely to occur under poor post-training data quality or when using smaller-scale models. Notably, internal metrics such as the Nonunified score are unable to distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation. We observe an interplay mechanism, i.e., co-improvement, between the reward model (understanding) and the fine-tuned model (generation) during self-improvement. The reward model evolves alongside the fine-tuned model is unique to MLLMs’ post-training, in contrast to traditional post-training settings where the reward model and the fine-tuned model are structurally decoupled [32–34]. Motivated by this observation, we pose the following questions: (1) Cause of co-improvement: why does generation-targeted self-improvement result in co-improvements in both branches? This observation reveals a core limitation: without external supervision, internal metrics like unification cannot distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation. This phenomenon parallels findings in LLMs, where reliance on internal signals, such as self-critique, can result in model collapse [35, 36]. A straightforward way to avoid co-degradation is to pre-validate data quality using external models (e.g., Qwen). For instance, Qwen can reliably identify corrupted samples, thereby preventing the use of low-quality data during self-improvement. However, this approach still depends on stronger external models. This motivates us to further enhance the offline fine-tuning strategy by introducing a Curriculum Learning-based Online (CLO) post-training approach. Specifically, taking the construction of DPO data as an example, training prompts can be categorized into three types based on whether they can be utilized by the generation or understanding branches during post-training: 49.7% 48.3% 2.0% 89.5% 9.7% 0.9% Figure 6: Outer ring shows only 49.7% of prompts (Ideal Set) are usable in pre-trained model. After SFT, improved generation and understanding allow 9.7% (inner ring) of previously FC/FR sets to be incorporated. • Ideal Set: the candidate generations contain both samples that satisfy and not satisfy the prompt by the understanding branch—these are ideal for constructing preference pairs. • Fully Rejected (FR) Set: all candidate generations are considered to fail the prompt—this may indicate that the prompt is too complex for the generation branch. • Fully Chosen (FC) Set: all candidate generations are considered to satisfy the prompt—this could mean the prompt is simple for the generation branch, or that incorrect generations are too hard for the understanding branch to distinguish. For the 3D Spatial subtask, Figure 6 shows that with the pre-trained Janus-Pro model, the standard offline post-training strategy can only utilize 49.7% of the available data (the ideal set), while a substantial portion remains unusable due to generation or understanding failures, namely, the FC and FR sets. After SFT, we observe that 9.7% of these previously unusable FC and FR samples become usable again, driven by the co-improvement in generation and understanding. This observation further validates the rationale for introducing curriculum learning into the post-training process, enabling dynamic expansion of the training set as model capabilities improve. Figure 7 accordingly proposes a CLO-based fine-tuning strategy, in which both the training data and MLLM are updated during the post-training process. The curriculum is constructed in a prompt complexity-wise manner: training samples are introduced progressively from simple to difficult, starting with Ideal prompts and gradually incorporating FR and FC prompts. This training order naturally aligns with the evolving capabilities of generation and understanding, only when the model’s capacity improves can it extract useful training signals from FR and FC prompts. Moreover, it reflects the well-established principle of curriculum learning: learning from easy to hard examples, a strategy that has been proven effective in both human and machine learning [29, 37, 38]. 10 {!! We observe that the self-improved model performs competitively on T2I-R1 and even achieves better results in understanding. A possible reason is T2I-R1 relies on external rewards, while selfimprovement leverages internal signals from the understanding branch. An interesting direction for future work is to explore whether internal and external rewards induce different (synergistic) mechanisms between generation and understanding. Notably, self-improvement and external rewards are not mutually exclusive: self-improved models can be further improved using T2I-R1 techniques. 5 Related Work Prior work typically focuses on enhancing specific capabilities of MLLMs, such as generation [16, 39], rather than emphasizing unification between generation and understanding. In these work, understanding branch primarily serves to provide additional details for generation prompt expansion. By combining enriched prompts with external reward models (e.g., BLIP [40], Human Preference Model [41, 42]), these studies improve generation quality of MLLMs. In contrast, we center on mitigating internal inconsistency within MLLMs, rather than merely improving single3To ensure consistency with the evaluation protocol, we generate images directly from the original prompts without using the understanding branch for prompt expansion. 11 task performance and aim to uncover why generation and understanding can co-improve during post-training, and leverages this property to better enhance alignment without any external signal. Additionally, some studies [15, 17, 43] have explored self-improvement for MLLMs by applying methods such as SFT, DPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [44]. However, these methods do not explicitly explore the synergy between generation and understanding. Instead, they often treat them as separate tasks to be co-optimized, typically relying on external reward models or additional data construction. In contrast, our work focuses on self-improvement in MLLMs without relying on any external signals, and aims to explain the interaction mechanism that arises from the shared architecture between the generation (post-trained model) and understanding (reward model) branches, which has been overlooked in prior work. More importantly, our approach is not in conflict with existing methods. Instead, it can be viewed as a complementary and cost-free enhancement: once self-improvement is achieved, techniques such as Chain-of-Thought prompting [16, 45, 46] or QA-based supervision [17] can be further applied to boost MLLM performance. 6 Conclusion and Future Work This work serves as an exploratory prelude, offering a systematic investigation into the selfimprovement capabilities of MLLMs. We show that the inherent asymmetry between generation and understanding offers a unique opportunity to improve both performance and unification of MLLMs. For future work, we plan to extend our analysis to a broader range of models and benchmarks. Specifically, we aim to: (1) compare self-contradiction and self-improvement behaviors across more unified architectures, such as Show-O [1]; and (2) investigate the effectiveness of internal versus external reward signals in driving co-improvement of generation and understanding. Furthermore, the current learning dynamics framework introduced in Section 3.2.1 primarily focuses on single-token SFT scenarios. We plan to generalize it to multi-token settings and explore its applicability to a wider set of post-training strategies, including DPO. We fine-tune Janus-Pro-7B using 700 samples from the 3D Spatial training subset of T2I-Comp Bench. For DPO, we adopt a common practice of using the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss over the preferred response in each pair to enhance training stability and performance. In both the SFT and DPO settings, we perform full-parameter fine-tuning on the autoregressive branch of Janus-Pro for 120 epochs, which requires approximately 13 hours on 4 A800 GPUs. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule with a peak value of 1e-7. We save checkpoints every 20 epochs and report the checkpoint that yields the lowest Nonunified Score in Table 3. A.2 Details of Co-improvement Analysis Understanding Improvement. While Section 3.2.2 analyzes the proxy ∆Gt, in this section we directly compute ∆Gt and show that it exhibits the same trend in generation probability change, consistent with the prediction of Proposition 1. Following Table 1, we divide the post-training samples into two groups based on ground truth (GT): GT = 0 and GT = 1. Specifically, samples with label transitions (GT, Base, Post) = (0,1,0) and (1,0,1) are considered understanding-improved. Specially, given a prompt y, we first generate the image token sequence x = πpre(y) = (x1, . . . , x L) using the pre-trained model. We then define the direct generation probability change as: ∆Gt(x | y) := 1 L L X i=1 log πpost(xi | x<i, y) −log πpre(xi | x<i, y), (4) which measures how the likelihood of reproducing the original image x changes after post-training. Figure 8 compares two pairs of groups: (0,1,0) vs. (0,0,1) and (1,0,1) vs. (1,1,0), corresponding to the understanding-improved and baseline comparison groups, respectively. According to Proposition 1, we can predict the expected direction of change in generation probability, and mark the theoretically improving group with the Expected label. As shown in Figure 4, the directly computed ∆Gt exhibits a trend consistent with its proxy counterpart, further supporting the hypothesis of synchronized learning dynamics between generation and understanding. However, unlike the proxy metric which shows clear group-wise differences ∆Gt reveals only marginal numerical differences between groups, making the comparison less distinguishable. Generation Improvement. To analyze improvements in generation, we focus on samples whose Qwen scores change from 0 to 1 before and after post-training. Proposition 1 indicates if the generation branch reduces the probability of producing an incorrect image x given a prompt y, then the understanding branch is also less likely to judge that the incorrect image x satisfies the prompt y. For samples where the MLLM initially assigns a score of 1 to a misaligned image x and continues to do so after self-improvement, ∆Ut is expected to be negative. Conversely, for samples consistently scored as 0, the log-probability should increase, i.e., ∆Ut > 0, even the score changes from 1 to 0. To compute ∆Ut, we first identify the subset of prompts for which the Qwen score changes from 0 to 1. Next, the pre-trained MLLM is used to generate images corresponding to these prompts. Both the pre-trained and post-trained MLLMs then perform the relevant understanding tasks on these samples, 16 and the corresponding ∆Ut values are calculated. As shown in Table 2, we observe that in nearly 60% of cases, the understanding trend (i.e., the direction of ∆Ut) aligns with the theoretical prediction. A.3 Details of Co-degradation Analysis Figure 9: Corrupted SFT objective with a fixed token 624. To verify whether improper fine-tuning data can lead to simultaneous degradation of generation and understanding in MLLMs, we conduct experiments using Janus-Pro-1B, a smaller model with weaker priors that is more susceptible to data corruption. Focusing on the 3D Spatial subtask, we apply standard SFT for fine-tuning, but replace all labels with a fixed target token ID of 624, meaning that each training sample is optimized to generate the same image as shown in Figure 9. We fine-tune the model for 120 epochs, saving a checkpoint every 20 epochs to track generation and understanding performance over time. Figure 9 reports the model’s performance at the checkpoint with the lowest nonunified score and shows that under an incorrect fine-tuning objective for the generation branch, both generation and understanding degrade simultaneously, with a notable drop in understanding accuracy. This supports the reasoning in Proposition 1 and underscores that self-improvement with low-quality data carries the risk of synchronized degradation alongside potential co-improvement. A.4 Details of Curriculum-based Post-training Details of Curriculum-based Post-training. In the online strategy, we continue using the 3D Spatial subtask and train the Janus-Pro-7B for 120 epochs with both SFT and DPO. We still set the maximum learning rate to 1e-7 with cosine learning schedule and perform full-parameter fine-tuning on the LLM component. Curriculum updates are introduced at epoch 60 to incorporate additional training samples that were previously unusable for fine-tuning due to the limited generation and understanding capabilities of the initial Janus model. Figure 6 illustrates the distribution of newly added training samples during curriculum learning. We follow the same evaluation protocol as Section 2, using the original image generation prompts from T2I-Comp Bench [30] without semantic expansions, which results in lower baseline generation scores compared to evaluations with prompt augmentation [16]. 2507.16405v1.title: Self-Supervised Inductive Logic Programming
2507.16405v1.abstract: Self-Supervised Inductive Logic Programming Stassa Patsantzis Abstract Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) approaches like Meta - Interpretive Learning (MIL) can learn, from few examples, recursive logic programs with invented predicates that generalise well to unseen instances. This ability relies on a background theory and negative examples, both carefully selected with expert knowledge of a learning problem and its solutions. But what if such a problem-specific background theory or negative examples are not available? We formalise this question as a new setting for Self-Supervised ILP and present a new MIL algorithm that learns in the new setting from some positive labelled, and zero or more unlabelled examples, and automatically generates, and labels, new positive and negative examples during learning. We implement this algorithm in Prolog in a new MIL system, called Poker. We compare Poker to state-of-the-art MIL system Louise on experiments learning grammars for Context-Free and L-System languages from labelled, positive example strings, no negative examples, and just the terminal vocabulary of a language, seen in examples, as a first-order background theory. We introduce a new approach for the principled selection of a secondorder background theory as a Second Order Definite Normal Form (SONF), sufficiently general to learn all programs in a class, thus removing the need for a backgound theory tailored to a learning task. We find that Poker’s performance improves with increasing numbers of automatically generated examples while Louise, bereft of negative examples, overgeneralises. Introduction In the Standard Setting (Nienhuys-Cheng and de Wolf 1997) for Inductive Logic Programming (Muggleton 1991) (ILP) a background theory B and positive and negative examples E+, E−are used as training data to learn a correct hypothesis H that accepts, in conjunction with B, all examples in E+, and no examples in E−. Typically, E+, E−are selected, and B programmed, manually by the user according to their background knowledge of the learning target (i.e. the logic program to be learned). B in particular is tailored to each learning target (Flener and Yilmaz 1999), and E− hand-picked to avoid over-generalisation. Given the right B, E+ and E−, recent ILP systems can learn correct hypotheses with recursive clauses and invented predicates. Copyright © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved. The ability to include background knowledge in training data is a desirable characteristic of ILP systems, but the practice of manually creating a target-specific background theory and selecting negative examples is a constant burden that limits the real-world application of ILP approaches. In this paper we present a new way to alleviate the aforementioned burden on the user with a new algorithm for Self Supervised ILP, more specifically, Self-Supervised Meta Interpretive Learning(Muggleton et al. 2014) (MIL). The new algorithm, implemented in a new MIL system called Poker1, is “self-supervised” in the sense that it learns from both labelled positive and unlabelled examples and it automatically generates new positive and negative examples during learning. Because it generates new negative examples, Poker can learn from a background theory that is not tailored to the learning target without over-generalising. Poker returns not only a hypothesis, but also a labelling of unlabelled, and automatically generated, examples. We illustrate the use of Poker in Table 1 where Poker is given 3 positive, labelled examples, E+, of the {1n0n : n > 0} (1n0n) Context-Free Language (CFL), and 30 unlabelled examples, E? of the {1n0m : n ≥m ≥0} (1n0m) CFL which includes 1n0n as a subset. Examples are atoms in Definite Clause Grammars (DCG) notation (Pereira and Shieber 1987) representing strings of 1n0n and 1n0m. The first-order background theory, B, consists of just the terminal vocabulary of both languages, {1, 0, ϵ}, defined as a set of DCG pre-terminals. 1n0n and 1n0m are more often denoted as anbn and anbm respectively, but replacing a, b with 1, 0 makes it possible for B to express any grammar with two terminal symbols suitably mapped to 1 and 0. B can also be constructed automatically from E+, E?. A second-order background theory, M, includes two metarules, Chain and Identity, Second-Order definite clauses with a set of constraints encoding a Second Order Definite Normal Form (SONF)2. The background theory B ∪M is thus sufficiently general to express, as a DCG, a Context Free Grammar (CFG) of any bit-string CFL or Regular language, i.e. one with a vocabulary of at most two characters and ϵ. 1Named after, not the game, but Wittgenstein’s Poker; a friendly dig at Popper (Cropper and Morel 2021). 2SONFs are formalised in the Framework Section. ar Xiv:2507.16405v1 [cs.AI] 22 Jul 2025 Self-supervised ILP with Poker Labelled examples E+:1n0n(n > 0) Unlabelled examples E?:1n0m(n ≥m ≥0) (21 of 100 for n ∈[0, 18]) s(11, 01). s(10, 00). s(13, 00). s(16, 00). s(19, 09). s(17, 07). s(16, 06). s(15, 03). s(12, 02). s(11, 00). s(14, 00). s(17, 00). s(18, 08). s(16, 01). s(15, 01). s(15, 05). s(13, 03). s(12, 00). s(15, 00). s(18, 00). s(17, 01). s(16, 02). s(15, 02). s(14, 01).
