These subscales are able to capture nuanced human perceptions of a robot’s sociability, relational behavior, and social presence, which are central to evaluating meaningful human-robot collaboration. We chose these subscales in particular for the following reasons: As socially assistive robots must design their processes in such a way that they are equally accessible and appropriate for all user groups without disadvantaging certain groups, procedural fairness makes a decisive contribution to HRC being perceived as successful, especially if humans with protected characteristics are involved. Interpersonal fairness focuses on the quality of interpersonal treatment during formal decision-making processes. Respect, appropriateness, and the avoidance of bias are particularly relevant when robots interact with people with different abilities and needs. The assessment of the perceived usefulness of the robot is fundamental to acceptance and intention to use. According to [46], perceived usefulness is a key factor in technology acceptance. For people with protected characteristics, the definition of usefulness may vary—for aged people or people with disabilities, this may 9 mean that the robot takes over or supports specific tasks that are difficult for them. The quality of interaction subscale measures the smooth and effective interaction between humans and robots. High-quality interaction is significant for users with special needs. [48] emphasizes the importance of fluency in human-robot collaboration, which can be especially crucial for people with disabilities or the elderly, as they may require more time or specific adaptations. System performance refers to the technical effectiveness and efficiency of the robot. A system designed to adapt to protected characteristics must deliver consistent performance that meets the user’s specific requirements. Evaluating system performance allows us to understand whether the robot meets the technical requirements necessary to support different user groups. The Positive Teammate Traits subscale measures the extent to which the robot is perceived as a positive and supportive teammate. When working with humans with different abilities and protected characteristics, it is crucial that the robot is seen as a helpful partner that adapts to individual needs. This dimension is particularly relevant as it reflects the social acceptance and integration of the robot into everyday life. Attitude Towards Using the Robot is based on the Technology Acceptance Model [46] and measures the general attitude of users towards the robot. Attitude can be strongly influenced by how well the robot adapts to specific needs, especially for people with protected characteristics. [49] extended this model to a unified view of technology acceptance, which is also relevant for our study. The GODSPEED III: Likeability and GODSPEED IV: Perceived Intelligence subscales from Bartneck et al. [50] measure how likeable and intelligent the robot is perceived to be. Our literature review of studies on HRC shows that likeability and intelligence are decisive factors for user acceptance. For people with protected characteristics, the robot must be not only perceived as intelligent enough to recognize individual needs, but also as socially comfortable to promote long-term acceptance. 3.2.2 Cognitive-Affective Mapping (CAM) The cognitive-affective maps that we collected for RQ-CAM function as independent variables in this study to investigate the potential of cognitiveaffective mapping as a reflection tool. We measured whether the ratings of the CAM group on the summed score of the scales listed in Table 3 differed significantly from those of the control group. In a subsequent study, we will examine the cognitiveaffective maps as a dependent variable and analyze them according to quantitative and qualitative standards. 3.3 Power Analysis and Participants 112 participants (56 each in the CAM and control groups and 14 per group according to the Latin square design) took part in the experiment. We determined the sample size for the between subject comparison CAM/control based on G*Power. For a medium effect size (d=0.5) in a one-tailed ttest with a standard .05 alpha error probability, we needed 51 participants per group to obtain a power of 0.8. Due to counterbalancing reasons, we collected data from 56 participants per group. This sample size per group (N=56) resulted in a power of 0.99 for the 2 × 2 ANOVA with the between subject factor group and the respective within subject comparisons with standard .05 alpha error probability when assuming medium effect sizes for the HRC-related hypotheses (correlation among repeated measures = .5 nonsphericity correction). Participants were recruited on prolific.co whereby we selected participants who are located in the US and are fluent in English. Participation was compensated with £ 11 per hour, which is approximately equivalent to the German minimum wage. To reach the target sample size of 56 participants per group, we finally had to recruit 61 participants in the control group (dropout rate: 8%) and 72 participants in the CAM group (dropout rate: 22%). 3.4 CAM Hypotheses To address RQ-CAM, we tested the following CAM-related hypotheses: H1: Reflecting on human-robot collaboration by drawing a CAM before completing a questionnaire leads to more pronounced ratings regarding 10 Table 3 Overview of the scales used in the user study. H3: In the ’no-handover’ conditions, mid Fluency (M) and max Fluency (F) are rated better than alternating items and antisocial for young humans (FY and MY). H4: In the ’no-handover’ conditions, max Fluency is rated worse than alternating items for disabled and aged humans (D and A). H5: In the ’no-handover’ condition, mid Fluency (M) is rated worse than alternating items (I) for disabled and aged humans (D and A). H6: Across all human conditions (FY, MY, D, and A), alternating items (I) and mid Fluency (M) are rated better in the ’handover’ conditions than in the ’no-handover’ conditions. H7: Across all human conditions (FY, MY, D, and A), max Fluency (F) is rated worse than the alternating items (I) and mid Fluency (M) conditions in the ’no-handover’ condition. H8: In the young human conditions (FY and MY), max Fluency (F) is rated worse in the ’handover’ condition than in the ’no-handover’ condition. H9: In disabled and aged humans (D and A), max Fluency (F) in the handover conditions is equally negatively rated as max Fluency (FH) in the ’no-handover’ conditions. In addition, we exploratorily analyzed whether handover and no-handover were rated significantly differently across all conditions. 3.6 Statistical Models As a data basis for the analyses with regard to RQ-CAM and RQ-HRC, we calculated the sum of the ratings on the individual scales and summed the scale values to an overall value. For the analysis of the CAM-related hypotheses (H1, H1.1, H1.2), we conducted independent samples t-tests. We tested whether the ratings of the CAM group differed from the control group on the scales that are more related to affective aspects, as well as overall across the sum of all scales. For the HRC-related hypotheses (H2–H8), we performed 2x2 ANOVAs, analyzing between subject factors by group and within subject comparisons according to the respective hypothesis. Additionally, we examined potential interactions between the group and the relevant conditions. For H9, we performed a 2 × 2 Bayes ANOVA, as we expected equal ratings between conditions. For the exploratory analysis of the handover/no-handover comparison, we used a paired samples t-test. 4 Results In the following, we present the statistical analysis (t-test) results for hypotheses H1, H1.1, and H1.2, which proposed that drawing a CAM influences the affective and cognitive subscales. These hypotheses examine how the creation of a CAM impacts participants’ responses on these specific dimensions, focusing on emotional and cognitive responses. Following this, we present the results of the statistical analyses (ANOVA and Bayesian ANOVA) for the hypotheses related to human-robot collaboration (H2–H9). These analyses investigate the effects of different robot behaviors and human conditions on the participants’ perception of collaboration, highlighting any significant differences and interactions between groups and conditions. 4.1 CAM-related Results Reflecting on human-robot collaboration by drawing a CAM before completing the questionnaire had no significant influence on the ratings on the affective or cognitive subscales (Table 3). This contradicts our original assumption that the CAM group would show more pronounced ratings in the affective subscales. Moreover, for H1.1, the data show no significant difference in the evaluation of ’antisocial’ robot behavior between the CAM and the control groups. Similarly, we found no evidence in the data that the CAM group would rate the non-antisocial, i.e., the basically acceptable robot behaviors (’mid Fluency’, ’max Fluency’ and ’alternating’) more positively than the control group, so that we also have to reject H1.2. 4.2 HRC-related Results Given the non-significant differences between the CAM group and the control group in the assessment of the human-robot collaboration (HRC), we decided to aggregate the data from both groups for 12 Table 4 Overview of hypotheses testing depending on the person Characteristics. The results are illustrated by a box plot (Figure 8) and a paired plot (Figure 9), which show the distribution of ratings in both conditions as well as the individual changes per participant. 5 Discussion We examined how participants assess a humanrobot collaboration from the observer’s perspective with regard to the combination of robot behavior and human physical characteristics. We investigated furthermore whether prior general reflection on human-robot collaboration using cognitiveaffective mapping (CAM) leads to differences in the assessment of the specific variants of human-robot collaboration. Fig. 8 Exploratory comparison of handover and nohandover for person Characteristics = aged. Fig. 9 Exploratory comparison of handover and nohandover for person Characteristics = aged. To answer RQ-HRC and test the corresponding hypotheses (H2 to H9), we aggregated the data from the CAM and control groups. In the following, we discuss the differences we observed in the assessments of the variants of the human-robot collaboration. Antisocial robot behavior was rated significantly lower than all other behaviors, supporting hypothesis H2. This can be attributed to the expectation that, regardless of the human partner, robots should engage in a manner that actively involves humans in the interaction, especially when collaboration is anticipated. Effective human-robot collaboration is often assessed through an efficiency lens, meaning that humans expect robots to facilitate task completion faster and more effectively. From this perspective, antisocial behavior 15 may be perceived as counterproductive, potentially hindering workflow and reducing overall task efficiency. Regarding the results of the hypothesis H3, it is possible to assume that participants believe that mid Fluency represents a smoother and more natural collaboration for young humans, as the robot provided enough time for the humans to complete the task without exerting pressure on them. This suggests that participants may prefer a balance between robotic assistance and human agency, rather than rigid alternation or highly autonomous robot behavior. Additionally, the fact that mid Fluency was rated more positively than alternating, even when compared to max Fluency, can indicate that excessive fluency might be perceived as too dominant or intrusive. For hypotheses H4, H5, H7, and H8, we found no significant differences. This can be due to the fact that the variations between the interactions presented in those conditions were not particularly noticeable or impactful. As a result, the participants may not have perceived the differences strongly enough to influence their judgments. The results provided partial support for H6. These findings suggest that, in general, observers preferred collaborations in the handover condition rather than the no-handover condition. This may be because the handover condition represents a more natural form of collaboration, allowing for more direct and intuitive interaction between humans and the robot. By engaging in physical exchange, participants may have felt a greater sense of involvement and control in the task, reinforcing the perception of effective teamwork. However, this result does not align with mid Fluency in the handover condition. This may be due to the interaction being influenced by the difference in the robot behavior resulting from the sorting scheme. Given that human-robot collaboration occurs in a direct way, the robot’s speed in completing the task might not match the pace at which the human participant is accustomed to working. This could have lead to the observing study participants perceiving a mismatch between the efficiency and fluency of the collaboration. Based on the results, we were also able to partially accept hypothesis H9. On the one hand, the difference found for the disabled and elderly human collaborator in the max Fluency condition in both the handover and no-handover conditions can be attributed to the type of person characteristic analyzed in the study. The disabled male was represented by a person walking with crutches, and since the task primarily involved hand usage, this kind of person characteristic might not face significant challenges when interacting with the robot under the max Fluency condition. Indeed, the videos of the disabled male indicated similar timing as young female and young male collaborators, and did not show any major obstacles in their collaboration with the robot. On the other hand, the negative ratings of the max Fluency condition in both the handover and no-handover conditions for the collaborations with the aged female may be influenced by the fact that, compared to all other conditions, the max Fluency condition demands the highest levels of efficiency and speed for the human collaborator. This could result in increased stress and pressure for the human partners. In the observing participants, the demand for quick decisions and actions in such a condition could therefore evoke feelings of discomfort, leading to a more negative perception of the interaction. From the perspective of the observing participants, it seems that a direct handover cannot outweigh the disadvantages of the max Fluency condition for older people. Overall, the participants rated the variations of the human-robot collaboration positively, with a mean sum score of 50.84 (with a possible maximum score of 66.00).6 The fact that some of our hypotheses, specifically those related to acceptability expectations, were not supported by the data highlights the inherent complexity of collecting social data to inform the development of assistive robots. It underscores the challenges of designing humanrobot collaborations that meaningfully reflect the diverse and context-dependent nature of interaction types between humans and machines. This outcome underscores how challenging it remains, even for interdisciplinary teams that integrate diverse perspectives, to develop methods that adequately reflect the preferences, expectations, and contextual needs of different user groups. Notably, during the planning phase of this study, collaboration with computer scientists played a key role in the development of realistic scenarios aimed 6To what extent our scenario text influenced the positive ratings was beyond the scope of our assessment. 16 at simulating more complex and natural forms of human-robot collaboration that could be trained with social data. However, despite these efforts, our findings suggest that aligning technical design with user-centered values in socially embedded contexts remains a critical and ongoing challenge in the field of social robotics. While the data did not confirm some of our initial hypotheses, the analysis nonetheless yielded valuable insights into how individuals’ preferences and perceptions can inform the development of robotic systems that are more adaptable, ethical, and responsive to users’ needs. Conducting this type of research requires in-depth analysis to uncover meaningful differences in robot behavior that are not always immediately apparent in everyday social contexts. A closer examination revealed subtle yet significant variations that can meaningfully guide the design of context-sensitive strategies for human-robot collaboration. Therefore, these nuanced findings underscore the challenges and importance of adopting a human-centered approach, one that captures behavioral specificities of robots that might otherwise go unnoticed by users in typical social settings. By identifying these less visible changes in robot behavior, researchers can develop more inclusive, responsive, and ethically grounded robotic systems that better reflect the realities and expectations of users. Regarding RQ-CAM, our results showed that drawing a CAM did not significantly change participants’ perceptions of the specific human-robot collaboration in general. However, the results of the exploratory analysis suggest that creating a cognitive-affective map prior to the assessment of the human-robot collaboration influences the perception depending on the combination of human condition and robot behavior, as well as some of the queried subscales. Affective and social subscales, such as interpersonal fairness and likability, were particularly affected. This suggests that CAM sensitizes participants with respect to social and interpersonal aspects of interaction, which can lead to more critical or differentiated judgments. Functional subscales such as System Performance or Perceived Usefulness were not influenced . The present exploratory analyses indicate that prior reflection on cognitive and affective aspects of human-robot collaboration through CAM might be linked to condition-specific differences in the assessment of human-robot collaboration tasks. The exploratory results suggest that for vulnerable groups such as older adults or people with disabilities, sensitization through CAM could potentially foster a more nuanced perception of fairness and appropriateness of robot use. These initial observations may provide valuable starting points for future confirmatory research and for informing the design of user studies and social robots adapted to different user groups. 6 Conclusion This study offers valuable insights into how human characteristics influence the perception and acceptance of collaborative robots on a specific scenario. By analyzing participant´s assessment of humanrobot collaboration across varying combinations of robot behavior and human physical conditions, we identified certain preferences for certain HRC conditions. Our main findings revealed that antisocial robot behavior was rated significantly more negatively than all other behaviors, that the protected personal characteristic ‘aged’ in the human collaboration partner predicted that participants were more sensitive in their ratings, and that the handover conditions were rated significantly more positively than the no-handover conditions. These findings suggest that humans may have distinct preferences when collaborating with robots, which can be influenced by the context of the interaction and the robot’s behavior. With this work, we aim to contribute to the field of social robotics from both a human-centered design method and an interdisciplinary perspective. By examining how different factors shape human-robot collaboration, we hope to offer valuable insights into designing more effective, ethical, user-friendly, and value-sensitive robotic systems. International Journal of Social Robotics 1, 71– 81 (2009) 08-0001-3 7 Supplementary Material In this section, we present the results of an exploratory analysis regarding RQ-CAM, in which we examined in detail the conditions of humanrobot collaboration that produced significant differences in specific subscales when comparing the CAM and control groups. 7.1 CAM-related Exploratory Analysis An exploratory analysis of the data revealed some significant and marginally significant differences, with medium to high effect sizes, on individual scales between the CAM and control groups, depending on single comparisons of the HRC. Table 6 gives an overview. Among the 14 conditions examined with young humans (female/male), 4 showed significant differences between the CAM and control groups. Notably, for the young men in the mid Fluency (MYM) condition in particular, the CAM group rated Interpersonal Fairness, Perceived Usefulness, and Likability of the robot significantly lower than the control group (e.g., Interpersonal Fairness: d = -0.892, p = 0.029). Young women in the alternating items (FYI) and mid Fluency handover (FYMH) conditions were also found to have lower values for Interpersonal Fairness, although some results were marginal. An exception is the max Fluency handover (MYFH) condition for young men, in which the CAM group gave significantly higher ratings for System Performance, Attitude towards Use, and the general rating (e.g., System Performance: d = 1.029, p = 0.011). Of 7 conditions with aged humans, 4 showed significant differences. In the antisocial condition (FAA), the CAM group rated Interpersonal Fairness significantly higher (d = 0.805, p = 0.043). In alternating items (FAF), the rating of Likability was significantly lower (d = -0.864, p = 0.034). 2507.16497v1.title: Canonical Correlation Patterns for Validating Clustering of Multivariate Time Series
2507.16497v1.abstract: Canonical Correlation Patterns for Validating Clustering of Multivariate Time Series Isabella Degen1, Zahraa S Abdallah2, Kate Robson Brown3, and Henry W J Reeve4 1School of Computer Science, University of Bristol 2School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology, University of Bristol 3College of Engineering and Architecture, University College Dublin 4School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Nanjing July 23, 2025 ABSTRACT Clustering of multivariate time series using correlation-based methods reveals regime changes in relationships between variables across health, finance, and industrial applications. However, validating whether discovered clusters represent distinct relationships rather than arbitrary groupings remains a fundamental challenge. Existing clustering validity indices were developed for Euclidean data, and their effectiveness for correlation structures has not been systematically evaluated. Unlike Euclidean clustering, where geometric shapes provide visible discrete reference targets for objective assessment, correlation structures exist in continuous space without equivalent discrete reference patterns. We address this critical validation gap by introducing canonical correlation patterns as mathematically defined validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures. These canonical patterns in correlation clustering serve as the equivalent of geometric shapes, enabling systematic evaluation of distance functions and validity indices for correlation-based clustering. Using synthetic datasets with perfect ground truth across controlled conditions, including distribution shifts, sparsification, and downsampling, we demonstrate that canonical patterns provide reliable validation targets, using the L1 norm as distance function for mapping and the L5 norm for calculating the silhouette width criterion and Davies-Bouldin index that show superior performance. These methods are robust to sparsification and distribution shifts, and appropriately detect correlation structure degradation under downsampling, enabling practical implementation guidelines for correlation-based clustering validation. This work establishes the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation, enabling confident application in high-stakes domains while providing a template for structure-specific clustering evaluation methodologies. Keywords multivariate time series · clustering · correlation patterns · distance functions · internal validity indices · clustering validity indices · structure-based validation · clustering validation 1 Introduction Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning task that groups similar objects to reveal underlying structures and patterns within data [1]. Time series clustering handles temporal data with unique characteristics such as temporal dependencies and evolving relationships and can reveal meaningful information about the behaviour of the underlying system that generated the data [2]. Correlationbased time series clustering helps to discover relationship patterns between variables. Identifying patterns in changes in correlations has supported the discovery of new knowledge across diverse domains such as identifying market conditions in finance where asset correlation regimes change ar Xiv:2507.16497v1 [cs.LG] 22 Jul 2025 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 1: Correlation-based clustering first segments multivariate time series X when correlation regimes between variables change. Then, each segment’s (Sm) correlation matrix (Am) captures the relationships between all variate pairs (Q) during that period. Next, segments with similar correlation structures are clustered together. These clusters (Ck) are then mapped to canonical patterns (Pℓ) that serve as discrete validation targets. Finally, the canonical patterns that exist in dataset X are interpreted using domain expertise. [3], detecting operational states in industrial systems where changing sensor relationships indicate different system modes [4], or understanding gene expression in biology [5]. The fundamental challenge in clustering is the need to be able to validate results without ground truth information. Given the many possible ways to partition a dataset, clustering validation aims to objectively distinguish meaningful patterns from arbitrary groupings [6, 7, 8, 9]. The established guiding principle is that results of higher quality have higher cohesion within clusters and better separation between clusters [1, 10, 11, 12, 9]. When clustering Euclidean data, the quality of the result can be objectively assessed by analysing whether the clusters form visibly distinct geometrical shapes [13]. However, correlation matrices form a continuous space that lacks such visible discrete reference targets. Consequently, when correlation matrices are grouped into clusters that are expected to represent periods of similar relationships between time series variables, there is no established systematic method to validate whether these clusters represent meaningful periods of distinct relationships or merely arbitrary collections of various correlation matrices. Figure 1 shows how a 3-variate time series dataset is segmented into subsequences when the relationships between the variates change. For each segment, the correlation matrix is calculated and then grouped into clusters of similar relationships between time series. The validation challenge is to objectively assess whether the segmentation of the time series and subsequent clustering of these segments result in optimal cohesive and well-separated clusters of different relationships. The following three gaps prevent reliable validation of correlation-based time series clustering, leading to subjective conclusions about the effectiveness of the methods and the validity of the results [14, 11, 10, 15, 12]. First, the absence of discrete validation targets for correlation structures, analogous to geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space, prevents the formalisation of objective evaluation criteria. Second, the effectiveness of existing clustering validity indices and distance functions that assess the structural quality of clustering results without requiring ground truth has not been systematically evaluated for correlation-based clustering. Instead, these methods were developed and validated for Euclidean data [7, 8, 13, 9]. Third, impacts from real-world data complexities common in time series data, such as irregular sampling, missing data, and non-normal distributions have unknown effects on distance functions and clustering validation indices, preventing 2 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 the establishment of performance thresholds or interpretation guidelines for judging the quality of results. We solve this fundamental validation problem by introducing canonical correlation patterns as verifiable target structures. Canonical patterns discretise the infinite correlation space into mathematically defined states (strong positive, negligible, strong negative correlations between variable pairs), creating well-defined validation targets that encompass the complete correlation space in a maximally contrasted way and serve as the correlation-based clustering equivalent of geometric shapes in Euclidean clustering; see Figure 1 illustrating how the resulting clusters map to canonical patterns that serve as validation targets. Additionally, canonical patterns eliminate the need to predefine cluster numbers, as datasets naturally contain the subset of canonical patterns present in the underlying correlation dynamics, and aid in result interpretation since each canonical pattern can be assigned domain meaning by domain experts. Our work makes three key contributions: (1) formalising canonical correlation patterns as mathematical validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures; (2) systematic empirical evaluation of the effectiveness of distance functions and validity indices for correlation matrices through controlled experiments; (3) establishing practical validation guidelines and actionable recommendations through robustness assessment across non-normal distributions, missing data, and varying completeness levels, as well as sensitivity to cluster and segment count. Together, these contributions provide the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation through formalised mathematical targets, empirically validated methods, and practical implementation guidance. For scope clarification, rather than providing an exhaustive theoretical comparison of all possible distance functions, we take an empirical approach aimed at identifying reliable practical solutions that are interpretable, computationally stable, and robust to real-world data quality challenges. The methodological work described here establishes the foundations that allowed us to create the standardised algorithm evaluation protocols for correlationbased clustering using the synthetic CSTS benchmarking dataset [16]. In CSTS, all canonical patterns are systematically represented and validated for multiple data variations, such as distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification, and controlled degraded clustering results, providing perfect ground truth information. This allows isolating impacts of data variation on correlation patterns from limitations of clustering validation indices and enables rigorous statistical evaluation. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on clustering applications and validation frameworks, highlighting key gaps in correlation-based clustering validation. Section 3 establishes the mathematical formulation and notation used and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Section 4 provides the standard formulas for evaluating the discriminative power of distance functions and assessing clustering quality through external and internal validity indices. Section 5 presents our methodology, detailing how we select, evaluate, and validate distance functions for canonical pattern mapping and internal validity indices for clustering quality. Section 6 outlines the experimental setup, and Section 7 presents the results. Section 8 discusses our key findings, compares our results with previous studies, provides practical recommendations, and acknowledges the limitations of our approach while suggesting future research directions. Finally, Section 9 concludes the article. 2 Related Work Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised machine learning technique that groups similar objects to reveal the underlying structures and patterns in the data [1]. As an established approach in data mining, clustering has become essential across numerous disciplines [10], applied to domains such as biology [11], mental health [12], finance [3] and genomics [15], discovering hidden structures such as patient subgroups [12], financial market segmentations [3], genomic patterns [17], and anomalies in control systems [18]. The methods and challenges vary depending on the type of data that are being clustered. Time series clustering introduces unique complexities such as temporal dependencies, high dimensionality, and dynamic nature of data that are distinct from Euclidean data [2]. These unique characteristics often require specific preprocessing and representation techniques prior to clustering, such as dimensionality reduction or feature extraction, introducing more steps that require validation [19]. Our work focusses on correlation-based multivariate time series clustering, a feature-based approach where correlation 3 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 matrices serve as extracted features representing relationships between variates [19]. A comprehensive review by Marti et al. [3] documents the methodological developments in correlation-based clustering of financial time series, mainly using network-based approaches that convert correlation matrices into distance functions for hierarchical clustering algorithms (like Minimum Spanning Trees) and their extensions (such as Planar Maximally Filtered Graphs). Other researchers take a different approach to clustering based on correlations. Chandereng and Gitter [5] introduced Lag Penalised Weighted Correlation (LPWC), employing a clustering similarity function (1-Pearson correlation) that groups univariate time series with similar temporal patterns even when they occur at slightly different times. Despite its utility and the prolific methods available, choosing and configuring a suitable clustering algorithm remains challenging. Many algorithms needed prior knowledge of the number of clusters and other hyperparameters that are difficult to identify and optimise, given that in real-world datasets, we apply clustering to datasets without ground truth information that would help define such parameters [10]. Furthermore, it remains unclear which method works best for a specific dataset [20]. Studies such as Javed et al. [21] and Paparrizos and Reddy [22] demonstrate that different datasets and problems require different clustering approaches, and Rodriguez et al. [20] mentions that algorithms exhibit varying sensitivities to parameter configurations. As Jaeger and Banks [15] notes, clustering represents an expansive domain in which practitioners must develop customised approaches for each application context. In short, the advice is "try various methods and see", which has led to the debate of whether clustering is more "art than science" [14]. These challenges have motivated extensive research into clustering validation techniques. The field of clustering validation spans several decades. Various researchers have created different internal clustering validation indices with the goal of measuring clustering quality without using domain information such as ground truth labels that external indices make use of [9]. Many internal clustering validity indices have been designed to assess the structural quality of clustering results and provide a measure of better within cluster cohesion and between cluster separation [23, 24]; for technical background on clustering validity assessment please refer to Section 4.2. The seminal work of Milligan and Cooper [6] established the foundation for comparing such indices. This pioneering study introduced a seven-step process where indices that perform better are those that determine optimal cluster numbers. More recently, Vendramin et al. [7] and Arbelaitz et al. [8] extended this framework, providing detailed comparisons of the strengths and weaknesses of various internal validity indices. Vendramin et al. [7] validated the performance of internal validity indices beyond determining the "correct" numbers of clusters by calculating their Pearson correlations with external clustering indices. Internal indices with higher correlation with an external index were judged as superior. In a similar study, Arbelaitz et al. [8] evaluated internal indices using synthetic and real datasets, also stressing that grouping similar objects is more important than finding the "right" number of clusters. Both studies argue that noise might increase cluster numbers without reducing clustering quality which for them, like for many of the internal indices inventors, is related to the structure of the result. The scope of these validation studies is substantial: Vendramin et al. [7] evaluated 40 internal validity indices using four different hierarchical clustering algorithms, comparing the results with three external validity indices across 1080 synthetic datasets. Arbelaitz et al. [8] assessed 30 internal validity indices using k-means and hierarchical clustering on 720 synthetic and 20 real datasets from the UCI repository [25]. Another study worth mentioning is Liu et al. [13] which followed the work of Milligan and Cooper [6] more closely but introduced variations in the datasets such as varying density, cluster shapes, separation, and noise. The clustering indices that are evaluated as performing best were those that achieved the optimal internal index value for the right number of clusters for the maximal number of different datasets. Significantly, all these studies concluded that no single internal validity index outperforms others across all scenarios. This finding aligns with Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem [26], which mathematically proves that no clustering function can simultaneously satisfy three desirable properties: scale invariance, richness, and consistency [9]. This theoretical barrier explains why different validity indices favour different algorithms and data characteristics. In addition to using internal validity indices to evaluate structural properties, stability-based approaches assess the consistency of the results of a clustering algorithm under data perturbations [27, 28, 29]. We deliberately exclude clustering stability from our validation techniques review as it primarily evaluates algorithm robustness rather than the intrinsic structural quality of the resulting clusters. 4 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Although these comprehensive validation frameworks provide a solid foundation, they were designed using Euclidean datasets and internal validity indices have not been specifically assessed for time series clustering [2]. In contrast to structure-based internal validation, time series clustering algorithms are typically compared by benchmarking them against classification datasets that contain ground truth information. Notable time series benchmarking studies include Javed et al. [21], which used a phased evaluation framework that isolated the effects of eight algorithms (including partitional, density-based, and hierarchical methods) and three distance functions (Euclidean, dynamic time warping, shapebased) on 112 datasets from the UCR archive [30]. Their analysis found that performance variation depended more on dataset characteristics than algorithmic innovations. Similarly, the Odyssey study from Paparrizos and Reddy [22] analysed 80 univariate time series clustering methods across 128 datasets. Both studies used external validation indices, since the UCR datasets consist of presegmented univariate time series already assigned to classes. This validation approach, while valuable for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of algorithms, conflates clustering and classification by assuming presegmented data with known ground truth, which introduces a critical methodological issue of classification boundaries defined by humans that do not necessarily reflect structural properties [31]. Algorithms may perform poorly not because they fail to discover meaningful structures, but because the expected classifications might not match such structures [21, 22]. Additionally to evaluating clustering algorithms for their ability to discover classification labels, these benchmarking studies use real-world datasets. This is both an advantage as such data include the full complexities of time series data but they make it impossible to isolate the performance of the algorithms from the quality of the underlying structures in the data. Our work addresses the gap in correlation-based time series clustering for which distance functions and internal validity indices have not been systematically evaluated. Our perspective is that clustering is a method to find structure in data and therefore the validation techniques need to be based on the quality of the discovered structure not on domain-based labels. 3 Problem Formalisation This section establishes the mathematical formulation and notation of correlation-based clustering and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Throughout, we shall let R denote the set of real numbers and N the set of positive integers. Given a natural number N ∈N, we let [N] := {1, . . . , N}. 3.1 Correlation-based Clustering First, we establish the notation of objects and their relations used in correlation-based clustering. Let X in RT ×V be a matrix where T ∈N is the number of observations and V ∈N is the number of variates in the time series. Given M ∈N we shall let G(M) denote the collection of segmentations into M segments. Formally, for each M ∈N the set G(M) consists of all strictly increasing sequences η = (ηm)M m=0 ∈[T]M+1 of length M +1 with η0 := 0 and ηM := T. For each m ∈[M], the values ηm−1 + 1 and ηm denote the start and end of the m-th index, respectively. We also let G := ST M=1 G(M) denote the set of all possible segmentations of a time horizon T. For each M ∈T, η ∈G(M) and m ∈[M] we let Sm ≡Sm(X, η) := X(ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm), (1) which takes values in R|ηm−ηm−1|×V , denote the m-th segment of X, containing sequential observations t ∈{ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm}. Then we shall let corr : S R∈N, R≥V RR×V →RV ×V denote the Spearman rank correlation [32] mapping from R × V matrices ˜X to the corresponding V × V correlation matrix A. The tied values are assigned average ranks, and the Spearman correlation is calculated using the standard tie-corrected formula. For our application of corr, we define the correlation coefficient aij := 0 for the cases of Sm when exactly one of the variates i or j is constant, and aij := 1 when both are constant. The image of corr is contained within the subspace AV ⊆RV ×V consisting of symmetric positive semi-definite matrices with unit diagonal and elements aij ∈[−1, 1] for i, j ∈V and i ̸= j. Note that AV forms a Q-dimensional subspace where Q := V (V −1)/2 is the number of unique pairs of 5 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 variates. As such, we sometimes represent elements of AV by vectors in RQ, where the correlation coefficients aij are ordered lexicographically a U := [a12, a13, ..., a(V −1)V ]. For each segment Sm where m ∈[M], we write Am ≡Am(X, η) := corr(Sm), (2) for its correlation matrix. Next, we write K(M, K) for the set of all clusterings Φ := (ϕ1, . . . , ϕK) which are sequences of K disjoint non-empty subsets of [M] whose union is S Φ = ϕ1 ∪. . . ∪ϕK = [M]. Additionally, we let SC(M, K) denote the set of all segmented clusterings which are tuples of the form π := (η, Φ), (3) where η ∈G(M) and Φ ∈K(M, K) is a clustering of these segments. Furthermore, given π ∈SC(M, K) and m ∈[M] and k ∈[K] we let Ck(π) := {Am : m ∈ϕk}, (4) denote a cluster where ϕk ∈Φ. Finally, to compare how similar two matrices are, we shall leverage a non-negative function d : AV × AV →R≥0 on the space AV as distance function. Given correlation matrices Ax, Ay ∈AV we view d(Ax, Ay) as quantifying the degree of dissimilarity between Ax and Ay. In practice many examples of d will be metrics, yet we require no further properties beyond non-negativity. We provide the definitions for the various distance functions employed in Appendix B. 3.2 Canonical Patterns Next, we formalise the canonical correlation patterns as discrete mathematical validation targets for correlation matrices that underpin our method for correlation-based clustering validation. Let P ∈AV denote a canonical pattern with elements pij ∈{−1, 0, 1} for i, j ∈[V ] and i ̸= j. Each canonical pattern Pℓwith ℓ∈[L] represents a unique idealised correlation structure capturing strong positive correlation, no correlation, or strong negative correlation between the Q unique variate pairs. The total number of different canonical patterns is L := 3Q. A canonical pattern Pℓmust be positive semi-definite to be a valid correlation matrix. To fulfil this requirement, we define a relaxed discretisation criterion where P′ ℓis considered equivalent to its canonical form Pℓ, if P′ ℓis positive semi-definite after adjusting its correlation coefficients within tolerance bands B := {[−1, −0.7], [−0.2, 0.2], [0.7, 1]}. Canonical patterns Pℓthat cannot be made positive semi-definite after this relaxation within B are invalid. The tolerance bands B represent practical thresholds that continue to clearly distinguish between strong negative, negligible, and strong positive correlation coefficients, while respecting the geometry of the correlation space AV . This relaxation process determines which of the L theoretical patterns yield valid correlation matrices, resulting in L′ < L relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓwhere ℓ∈[L′]. To facilitate human interpretation, we use the idealised Pℓto represent a pattern. For calculations, we use the corresponding relaxed form P′ ℓ, see Appendix A for a list of the 23 valid canonical patterns out of the 27 possible and their relaxed form for three time series variates. Let ψ : AV 7→{P′ ℓ: ℓ∈[L′]} denote the canonical pattern mapping ψ(Am) := min argmin ℓ∈[L′] {d(Am, P′ ℓ)} (5) that associates a correlation matrix Am with its closest relaxed canonical pattern. Here, ‘min’ ensures that the ties are broken by selecting the smallest index ℓ. The canonical pattern mapping ψ provides a natural basis for constructing a clustering Φ. A possible clustering strategy is to group correlation matrices in such a way that for k ∈[K] we have ϕk := {m ∈[M] : ψ(Am) = P′ ℓ} , (6) where ℓ∈[L′]. Under such an approach, canonical patterns P′ ℓserve as discrete, idealised, interpretable target clusters of the clustering Φ. Each cluster ϕk then consists of all segment indices m whose correlation matrices map to the same relaxed canonical pattern P′ ℓ. Note that K ≤L′ as not all ℓ∈[L′] need to be present in a given time series X. 6 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 3.3 Level Sets for Canonical Patterns Finally, we introduce level sets that enable a systematic evaluation of distance functions by grouping canonical patterns according to their theoretical similarity. Let d L1 : AV × AV →R≥0 denote the L1 distance between canonical patterns so that d L1(Px, Py) := V X i=1 V X j>i |pxij −pyij|, (7) for pattern indices x, y ∈[L′]. Let DL1 := {δ ∈R : ∃x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ} denote the ordered sequence of achievable L1 distances between valid canonical patterns. The theoretical maximum δmax is bounded by V (V −1), although this δmax may not be achievable due to the constraints on valid correlation matrices. To give an example, with three time series variates (V = 3) the sequence becomes DL1 = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, where a distance of 1 represents one coefficient changing by ±1, a distance of 2 represents either two coefficients changing by ±1 or one coefficient flipping sign, and so forth. The theoretical maximum distance of 6 for V = 3 cannot be achieved while only retaining the canonical patterns Pℓthat can satisfy the tolerance bands B and be a valid correlation matrix Am. For each potential distance value δ ∈DL1, we define the level set Lδ as Lδ := {(x, y) : x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ}. (8) The collection {Lδ}δ∈DL1 groups pattern index pairs (x, y) by their L1 distance, with L0 containing indices of identical patterns, L1 containing indices of patterns where one correlation coefficient differs by ±1, and so forth. This creates a natural ordering between the level sets, while all the pattern pairs within each Lδ are theoretically equivalent. 4 Evaluation Reference Formulas This section provides established formulas for evaluating the performance of distance functions and assessing clustering quality, providing the mathematical foundation for our methodology. 4.1 Discriminative Power The effectiveness of a distance function d to map empirical correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical patterns P′ ℓ(see Section 3.2) can be evaluated using multiple complementary approaches. We investigate how well a distance function distinguishes across all the canonical patterns, how consistent distances are within a level set Lδ (see Section 3.3) and how well a distance function performs this mapping in the basic 1NN classifier where all the neighbours have been hardcoded to be the canonical patterns. In this section, we provide the established formulas used for these evaluations. 4.1.1 Overall Discriminative Power We use Shannon’s entropy [33] to evaluate the overall variability of distances. Given a finite number of distances γ ∈D, where D is a multi set, Shannon’s entropy is defined as HD := k X i=1 p(γi) log2(1/p(γi)), (9) where k is the number of bins, γi are the distances falling into bin i, and p(γi) is the relative frequency of the distances in bin i (empirical estimate of the probability mass function for the distances γ ∈D). For the overall discriminative power of a distance function d, we consider all distances. Therefore, D := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M], y ∈[L′], and then |D| = M × L′. The larger HD, the more uncertain and random the observed distances are, which is desirable. 7 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 4.1.2 Level Set Discriminative Power Level sets Lδ (see Section 3.3) lend interpretable properties to evaluate the suitability of a distance function d to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns (see Eq. 5). We expect the distance d between an empirical correlation matrix Am and a canonical pattern P′ ℓto be smaller, the closer the canonical pattern is to the pattern used to create the empirical correlation matrix. We also use Shannon’s entropy to evaluate the similarity of distances within the level sets. For the analysis of the level sets of a distance function d, we consider the subset of distances γ ∈Dδ where Dδ ⊂D for the respective level set Lδ defined as Dδ := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M] and y ∈[L′] such that d L1(Px, Py) = δ, where Px was the canonical pattern used to generate the segment from which the empirical correlation matrix Ax was calculated and Py is the relaxed canonical pattern P′ y we calculate the distance for. The closer to zero HDδ is, the more uniform the observed distances within the level set, which is desirable. The average entropy for all level sets is defined as HL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 HDδ. (10) Furthermore, the average rate of increase in distances from level set to level set is defined as RL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 |µLδ −µLδ+1|, (11) where µLδ is the mean distance for the level set Lδ for a distance function. We use this 1NN classifier to assign each empirical correlation matrix to its closest relaxed canonical pattern using a distance function d. Our aim is to identify both distance functions that can discriminate between the different canonical correlation patterns and map empirical correlation matrices to their canonical patterns, as well as internal validity indices that quantify the quality of a particular segmented clustering. The distance functions and internal indices selected must provide good interpretability, computational stability, and robustness to common variations in the quality of real-life data. For both evaluations, we follow a systematic three-stage methodology in which we first select candidates; second empirically evaluate their performance; and third, statistically validate whether there are superior options. We recognise that statistically significant differences may not always translate to meaningful practical improvements and therefore evaluate both practical and statistical differences between candidates. Importantly, we assess distance function performance in two distinct contexts. First, we evaluate their ability to directly discriminate between canonical correlation patterns. Second, we evaluate how these same distance functions perform when embedded within internal validity indices for clustering quality assessment. As we demonstrate, optimal distance functions may differ between these contexts. For statistical testing, we employ a two-phase approach (exploratory and confirmatory) to reduce false discoveries, organising the tests into six families to control Type I error rates [40]. We conduct the experiments using the CSTS benchmark datasets [16], which provides validated ground truth clusterings for all canonical patterns under normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions. CSTS further provides controlled degraded quality clustering as well as reduced cluster and segment count versions to enable a thorough investigation of the effectiveness and potential biases of the validation methods. 5.1 Canonical Pattern Mapping Assessment Our aim in this section is to identify which distance functions best map empirical correlation matrices to their underlying canonical patterns. We describe how we select candidate distance functions and then evaluate their ability to distinguish between different canonical correlation patterns, as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function. 5.1.1 Distance Function Selection We select distance functions using the following four key principles: 1. Interpretability: The distance function must follow human intuition about similarity and differences between correlation matrices Am and canonical patterns Pℓ. The distance function should allow meaningful interpretations of which cluster Ck(π) best fits each observed correlation matrix Am and which cluster best fits a canonical pattern Pℓ. 2. Discriminative Power: The distance function must be able to effectively and reliably distinguish between the different canonical patterns Pℓand assign correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical pattern Pℓ, see the canonical pattern mapping equation 5. Each canonical pattern should be equally distinguishable. 3. Computational Stability: The distance function must be numerically stable. This includes dealing with very small eigenvalues λi and singular correlation matrices, which are both common in the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓ. The computation time needs to be feasible on standard hardware, prioritising result quality over processing speed. 4. Robustness: The distance function needs to be able to handle real-world challenges such as varying segment lengths, irregular sampling, and non-normal distributions of the time series variates without the need for manual parameter tuning, which is not possible without knowing the ground truth. Following these four principles, we select the vector-based distance functions Lp norm, Lp norm with reference vector, dot transformed Lp norm, and the matrix-based distance functions Log Frobenius norm and Förstner metric (all defined in Appendix B). We focus on vector-based distance functions 11 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 because of their direct quantification of the differences in correlation coefficients and easy geometrical interpretation. We include matrix-based distance functions because they, to varying degrees, capture the geometry of correlation matrices, which could be advantageous. Our selection includes distance functions that are directly applicable to correlation matrices without requiring parameter tuning. This excludes time series specific distance function like Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), which requires parameter tuning and measures distance between time series observations rather than correlations. We also focus on distance functions with direct geometric interpretation for correlation matrices, excluding probabilistic and graph-based approaches. 5.1.2 Distance Function Evaluation We systematically evaluate the performance of the selected distance functions to identify which dissimilarity function best satisfies our four key principles to map empirical correlation matrices to canonical patterns. Each distance function is assessed against criteria derived from the principles of interpretability and discriminative power, with robustness and computational stability serving as a prerequisite for inclusion; see details in Section 6.2. For interpretability, we evaluate whether distance functions produce intuitive mappings between empirical correlation matrices and canonical patterns. This includes evaluating distance consistency within level sets (see Eq. 8) and meaningful separation between level sets. For discriminative power, we assess each distance function’s ability to reliably distinguish between canonical patterns and correctly assign empirical correlation matrices to their closest canonical pattern. This evaluation focusses on the distance function’s capacity to maintain clear boundaries between different canonical patterns and accurately assign empirical correlation matrices. We rank distance functions based on their performance for each of these criteria, providing both relative comparisons between distance functions and overall performance evaluation to ensure that high-ranking distance functions demonstrate genuine effectiveness rather than merely superior relative performance. The evaluation is carried out separately for normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions to assess robustness and identify distance functions that maintain consistent performance under real-world challenges. 5.1.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether the distance function ranked highest is superior, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests [41] to compare the distance function ranks for each subject. These tests constitute Family 1 of our six-family statistical testing framework, specifically designed to control Type I error rates when determining which distance functions best map correlation matrices to canonical patterns. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best-ranked distance functions and expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests [40], see Table 1. 5.2 Internal Validity Index Assessment Having established optimal distance functions for canonical pattern discrimination, we now aim to identify which distance functions optimise the performance of the internal validity index and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable quantification of clustering quality with minimal bias. We first describe how we select candidate internal clustering validity indices and then evaluate using different distance functions their ability to reliably quantify the quality of a segmented clustering (see Equation 3), as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function and internal index combination. 5.2.1 Index Selection We select the internal validity indices to evaluate based on their performance in previous comprehensive evaluation studies by Vendramin et al. [7] and Arbelaitz et al. [8] as well as based on their popularity in clustering. Due to our canonical pattern approach of defining an upper bound for the possible number of patterns in a dataset, it is important that the number of clusters K and the number 12 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 of segments M do not affect the performance of the internal validity index, as not every canonical pattern will be present in every dataset despite the clustering being of equal high quality. 5.2.2 Index Evaluation We evaluate the selected internal indices to determine which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias. We systematically evaluate both objectives for each data variant to understand how the choice of distance function affects index performance and how different indices behave under varying conditions. We evaluate how different distance functions affect internal validity index performance from two complementary perspectives. First, we assess each distance function’s ability to produce optimal raw index values for the highest-quality segmented clustering (ground-truth perfect clustering). Second, we evaluate how well each distance function enables indices to correlate with the Jaccard index, measuring the index’s ability to distinguish between different clustering quality levels. The latter perspective shows how validation without labels (internal clustering validation) matches validation using ground truth label information (external clustering validation, not available in real-world settings). We independently assess these two perspectives for each data variant and internal validity index, then synthesise the results to identify optimal distance functions. When optimal distance functions differ between raw performance and correlation performance, we examine the implications of this divergence from a practical viewpoint. Using the optimal distance functions identified above, we assess the reliability and bias of the internal validity indices. We evaluate the sensitivity of the index to varying numbers of clusters and segments by working with reduced versions of our data variants. Additionally, we synthesise results across all data variants (normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified) to assess the robustness of each index to different data characteristics and pattern degradation conditions. 5.2.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether there is a superior distance function for the validity indices and an overall superior validity index, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests to compare the evaluation results for each subject [41]. These tests constitute Families 2-6 of our six-family statistical testing framework. We first establish which distance function and internal index combinations achieve sufficient correlation strength to warrant detailed comparative analysis. We apply a viability threshold that requires Pearson’s mean correlation |r| > 0.5 between the internal indices and the Jaccard index for each subject within each data variant, based on sample size calculations to ensure adequate statistical power. Based on viable combinations from this filtering, we define the five families (2-6) comparing the internal indices SWC and DBI, which pass this correlation viability threshold. Family 2 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly better ground truth values for SWC and DBI, while Family 3 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly stronger correlation between SWC/DBI and the Jaccard index. Family 4 examines whether SWC or DBI correlates more strongly with the Jaccard index, Family 5 examines the impacts of cluster count reduction, and Family 6 evaluates the effects of segment count reduction. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best performing distance functions and internal indices, respectively, expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions and internal indices to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on these exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests using hierarchical testing procedures [40], see Tables 2 to 6. 6 Experimental Setup We describe the experimental setup in four parts. First, we describe the CSTS benchmark dataset used for all experiments. Second, we present the experimental configurations for the canonical pattern mapping assessment following our three-stage methodology: candidate selection, evaluation implementation, and statistical validation. Third, we detail the experimental configurations for the 13 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 internal validity index assessment, following the same three-stage structure. Fourth, we describe the implementation details of the libraries used and the hardware employed for our experimentation. 6.1 Synthetic Benchmark Dataset To systematically evaluate clustering validation approaches, we used the open source CSTS dataset [16], a correlation structure-specific synthetic benchmark that provides controlled ground truth for the validation of multivariate time series clustering. CSTS consists of exploratory and confirmatory datasets, each comprising ND = 30 different subjects. The exploratory and confirmatory datasets are statistically equivalent but independent. To evaluate how effectively internal validity indices can distinguish between different levels of clustering quality, we generated a controlled spectrum of clustering quality ranging from perfect (ground truth) to severely degraded. This quality degradation simulation allowed us to assess the sensitivity and reliability of the index across the full range of possible clustering outcomes, a method established by Vendramin et al. [7], Arbelaitz et al. [8]. We generated Nπ = 66 deliberately degraded segmented clusterings for each subject (ND = 30) and each data variant. We used three strategies and created 22 segmented clusterings with degraded quality per strategy: (1) shifting the segment end index forward by a randomly selected number of observations, (2) randomly assigning a randomly selected wrong canonical pattern to a randomly increasing number of segments, and (3) combining (1) and (2). In total, we ended up with 360 ground truth segmented clusterings (30 subjects ×12 variants) and 23,760 segmented clusterings with degraded quality (66 degraded segmented clusterings ×360 ground truth). Figure 3 shows the descriptive statistics for the Jaccard index, the number of wrong clusters, and the number of observations shifted for the degraded segmented clusterings and the ground truth. It illustrates that the degraded segmented clusterings covered the full quality range for the Jaccard Index [0, 1]. The Jaccard index linearly increases as the number of wrongly assigned clusters decreases from all 100 segments having a wrong cluster assigned to none (first 44 segmented clusterings). It continues to increase, all be it at a slower rate, as the number of observation shifted decreases (last 22 segmented clustering). Simply shifting observation has less of an impact on the Jaccard index than assigning a segment to a wrong cluster. 6.3.1 Index Selection Following the method defined in Section 5.2, we selected the following four internal indices: (1) the silhouette width criterion (SWC; see Eq. 17) for its consistent high performance and lack of needing a cluster or data centroid; (2) the relatively little known Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index (PBM, see Eq. 20) due to its good performance in [7] and its robustness to varying numbers of clusters; (3) the widely used Davies-Bouldin index (DBI, see Eq. 18); and (4) the Calinksi-Harabasz index (VRC, see Eq. 19). The latter two were chosen for their popularity in clustering quality assessments. 6.3.2 Index Evaluation To evaluate which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality quantification, we performed assessments on all data variants, each containing the same ND = 30 subjects. To identify optimal distance functions for internal validity indices, we first calculated all four internal validity indices (SWC, PBM, DBI, VRC) for the ground truth segmented clusterings using ten representative distance functions selected based on the canonical pattern mapping assessment. These distance functions span the Lp distance family (L1, L2, L3, L5, Linf), referenceand dot-transformbased variants (L1 ref, L5 ref, dt Linf) and correlation-specialised approaches (Log Frobenius, Förstner). We ranked distance functions based on their ability to produce optimal raw index values for ground truth clusterings. Second, we calculated Pearson correlations between internal indices and the Jaccard index for each distance function on clusterings of degraded quality that span the full 17 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 range of the Jaccard index [0, 1]. Note that evaluating segmentation and clustering of time series simultaneously is uncommon, which required our adapted Jaccard index definition (see Eq. 14) for segmented clusterings. To reduce the number of combinations to evaluate and achieve statistically significant correlations, we established that all internal indices had to achieve a minimum correlation strength of |r| ≥0.5 (see Section 6.3.3) for at least one distance function, which only SWC and DBI did. VRC and PBM showed insufficient correlations with the Jaccard index, with correlations reaching at best 0.21−0.48. Consequently, VRC and PBM were excluded from a detailed comparative analysis. We focused the detailed raw value analysis on SWC and DBI, calculating 95% confidence intervals of the mean ground truth index values across subjects of the ten aforementioned distance functions. The correlation analysis aligns with the study setup in [7]. To assess index reliability and bias, we recalculated all internal indices for the reduced versions of the correlated and non-normal data variants with 50% and 25% of the original clusters (11 and 6 patterns, respectively) and segments (50 and 25 segments, respectively). For this analysis, we use the L5 distance function based on its consistent performance in achieving optimal index values across data variants. For computational stability, we addressed division-by-zero cases in the DBI index by introducing a minimal cluster centroid distance of dmin(ACk, ACy) = 10−15 when identical centroids occurred. For data variants that produce constant index values (raw), we set the correlation coefficients to 0 and p-values to 1 to enable batch processing while indicating the absence of correlation. 6.3.3 Statistical Validation For viable correlation strength filtering, we calculated sample size requirements using equation [42] Nπ = b + c2( zα + z1−β z(ρ1) −z(ρ0))2, (24) with b = 3 and c2 = 1, ρ0 = 0.5, ρ1 = 0.7, α = 0.05, and β = 0.8. z(•) denotes the Fisher transform and zα = 1.645 respectively z1−β = 0.84 denote the Gaussian critical values for α respectively 1 −β. DBI50 > DBI25 1.02 29 7 Results Given the extensive experiments conducted across multiple distance functions, internal validity indices, and data variants, it would be overwhelming to report all results in full. Instead, we focus on findings that directly provide answers to which distance functions best map empirical correlation matrices to canonical patterns and which internal indices best assess clustering quality. For reporting results for the 9 different data variants (normal, non-normal, downsampled, each with the three sparsity levels complete - 100%, partial - 70%, and sparse - 10%), we establish the normal, complete data variant as our baseline that represents ideal conditions researchers typically assume. For each major finding, we first report this baseline performance and then describe important deviations for the other variants instead of exhaustively listing all combinations. 7.1 Canonical Pattern Mapping Assessment Here we present the results determining which distance functions best map correlation matrices to canonical patterns through direct discrimination. Overall, we showed that L1-based distance functions consistently achieved superior performance for canonical pattern mapping across data variants. 7.1.1 Distance Function Evaluation For our baseline, the normal and complete data variant, the L1 norm distance function ranked best (µ = 4.7, SD= 0.07), followed by L3 (µ = 4.76, 0.15) and L1 ref (µ = 4.82, 0.12), while the Förstner level ranked worst (µ = 6.57, 0.10). See Figure 4a for a heat map of the average rank of the 15 distance functions across data variants. For the non-normal variants, L1 ref was top ranked (µ = 4.52, 0.2) and L1 moved to second best rank (µ = 4.71, 0.1), for the downsampled variants the L1 norm stayed best ranked (µ = 3.64, 0.27) but second best was the L2 (µ = 4.31, 0.37) norm. The ranking order of the distance functions was generally not affected by sparsity other than sometimes for the sparse variant. Evaluating criterion-specific differences show that L1’s overall superiority reflected strong discriminative power performance that compensated for moderate interpretability scores, while the specialised distance functions such as Förstner and Log Frobenius excelled in narrow domains but failed to achieve balanced performance across both evaluation principles. For interpretability, Linf and dt Linf excelled in maintaining distances close to zero for level set zero (criterion 1: µ = 1, SD= 0), while L1 performed moderately (µ = 5.2, SD= 0.41) and Förstner ranked worst (µ = 13.2, SD= 0.41). All Lp norm-based distance functions achieved perfect performance in ensuring significant and monotonically increasing differences between level sets (criterion 2: µ = 1, SD= 0), separating them from Förstner and Log Frobenius (µ = 2.0, SD= 0). However, for the rate of increase between level sets (criterion 3), Log Frobenius ranked best (µ = 1, SD= 0), L1 fell to middle performance (µ = 8, SD= 0), and Linf ranked worst (µ = 14, SD= 0). For discriminative power, L1 ref dominated overall entropy maximisation (criterion 4: µ = 1, SD= 0) while L1 performed poorly (µ = 12, SD= 0), but this pattern reversed for level set entropy minimisation (criterion 5) where L1 ranked best (µ = 1, SD= 0) and L3 ref worst (µ = 13.9, SD= 0.64). The macro F1 classification criterion (6) again favoured all distance functions based on the Lp norm (µ = 1, SD= 0), with Log Frobenius (µ = 12, SD= 0) and Förstner (µ = 3, SD= 0) trailing significantly. For the non-normal and complete data variant, L1 ref achieved overall superiority (µ = 4.5 vs. L1 µ = 4.7) primarily through markedly improved performance on the rate of increase between level sets (criterion 3: L1 ref improved from µ = 3.0 to µ = 1.87 while L1 remained at µ = 8.0) and modest improvement in level set entropy minimisation (criterion 5: µ = 11.73 to µ = 10.78), while L1 changed minimally. For all other criteria, the differences between normal and non-normal variants were minimal for both distance functions. For downsampled variants, we compared to non-normal rather than normal data since downsampled data remains non-normally distributed [16]. Although we therefore expected L1 ref to maintain superiority for downsampled data variants, L1 regained overall superiority (µ = 3.7 vs. L1 ref µ = 6.8) through a dramatic role reversal on entropy maximisation (criterion 4: L1 improved from µ = 11.9 (SD=0.25) to µ = 1.17 (SD=0.38) while L1 ref deteriorated from µ = 1.1 (SD=0.31) to µ = 9.17 (SD=0.67) and superior resilience to classification degradation (criterion 6: L1 µ = 2.67, SD=1.52 vs. L1 ref µ = 6.23, SD=2.25), as perfect classification performance was no longer achievable under downsampled conditions. For the classification criterion, L1, L2, and L3 were the only distance functions that remained ranked < 3. While L1 ref maintained its advantage on the rate of increase between level sets (criterion 3: µ = 1.8, SD=0.81 vs. L1 µ = 6.0, SD=0), L1’s gains on criteria 4 and 6 outweighed this, with L1 ref’s substantial deterioration on multiple criteria explaining its overall ranking decline. Figure 4b shows the raw criterion values for the top performing distance functions L1 (normal and downsampled data variants) and L1 ref (non-normal data variants) across all data variants, illustrating how L1 ref achieves superior maximisation of entropy (criterion 4: 4.3 vs 1.6 for normal data) while L1 dominates minimisation of entropy (criterion 5: 1.6 vs 2.9), with both distance functions maintaining near perfect classification performance with F1 (criterion 6: 1.0) except under downsampled conditions where performance slightly degrades (0.93 −0.96). 22 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 For background on the differences observed in downsampled variants, it is important to note that downsampling non-normal data from 1 sec to 1 min distorts correlation patterns [16]. 7.1.2 Statistical Validation Confirmatory statistical validation tests of the preregister hypotheses (see Table 1) in a hierarchical procedure confirmed the superiority of L1 over L1 ref for the normal data variants, L1 ref over L1 for the non-normal data variants, and L1 over L2 for downsampled data variants. All tests achieved statistical significance (p ≤0.0003), with consistently large effect sizes (0.69 −1.1) and high statistical power (≥97%), see Table E.1 for detailed results. The effect sizes were the smallest for the normal variants (0.93) and non-normal sparse variants (0.69). This was not the case for the sparse and downsampled variant (1.1). 7.2 Internal Validity Index Assessment Here we present results determining which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias. Overall, we show that L5 emerged as the optimal distance function for internal validity indices, while both SWC and DBI showed systematic bias patterns and both provide different insights into evaluating clustering quality. 7.2.1 Index Evaluation For our baseline normal and complete data variant, the distance functions L3, L5, Linf, and dt Linf all lead to the same highest SWC values (µ = 0.98, SD=0.0) for the ground truth clustering, while for DBI these same distance functions and additionally L2, and L5 ref resulted in the same best ground truth performance (lowest values, µ = 0.04, SD=0.01).
