Family 2 investigated which distance function leads to optimal values. Exploratory analysis revealed 25 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 that the L5 distance function, although not always significantly best, was consistently in the group of best-performing distance functions for both SWC and DBI for all data variants. All but the last preregistered hypothesis for Family 2 passed confirmation (see Tables 2 and E.2). For our complete and normal baseline variant, L5 outperformed L3 for SWC (p < 0.0001, effect size 1.10), while L5 ref beat L3 for DBI (p = 0.0002, effect size 0.69). For the non-normal data variant, for SWC, L5 maintained superiority but now over Linf with a reduced effect size (p = 0.03, effect size 0.55). For DBI the superiority of L5 ref over L5 could not be confirmed (p = 0.15, effect size 0.24). For the downsampled non-normal data variant, SWC optimisation reversed, favouring Linf over L5 (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.73), while DBI optimisation shifted to L5 beating L3 (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.70). Sparsification to partial data variants (70% of the original observations) did not change the distance function that led to optimal values. However, sparsification to 10% had the effect for SWC across all data variants that Linf consistently beat L5 (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 1.05 −1.09). For DBI, L5 continued to beat Linf with smaller effect sizes for normal and non-normal sparse data variants (p = 0.001 −0.005, effect sizes 0.48 −0.60). For the downsampled sparse data variant for DBI, L5 maintained superiority but this time over L3 (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.78). Family 3 investigated which distance functions lead to stronger correlations between the internal validity indices (SWC and DBI) and the Jaccard index. To address the negative correlation between DBI and Jaccard, all DBI correlations were multiplied by −1, allowing focus on the strength of the correlation rather than the direction. Exploratory analysis revealed that the Linf distance function, although not always significantly best, was consistently in the group of best-performing distance functions for both SWC and DBI for all data variants. All but the last three preregistered hypotheses for Family 3 passed confirmation (see Tables 3 and E.3). For our complete and normal baseline variant, Linf outperformed L5 for SWC and DBI (SWC: p < 0.0001, effect size 1.08; DBI: p = 0.016, effect size 0.47). For the complete and non-normal data variant, Linf maintained superiority over L5 for both SWC and DBI (SWC: p < 0.0001, effect sizes 1.08; DBI: p = 0.007, effect size 0.54). For sparse non-normal data, Linf beat L1 ref (p = 0.034, effect size 0.34). For the complete downsampled data variant for SWC the Förstner distance function achieved significantly stronger correlation over Linf (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.76), while for DBI L5 ref beat L1 ref (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.83). Sparsification did not change the distance function that leads to significantly stronger correlations. However, for DBI, it was the hypotheses for the non-normal, partial, and the sparse normal and downsampled data variants that could not be confirmed. To determine which internal validity indices (SWC or DBI) provides the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias, we statistically tested which index is stronger correlated with the Jaccard index and evaluated bias towards cluster and segment counts. We used the L5 distance function given its superior performance in achieving optimal index value (see results for Family 2). Exploratory analysis revealed that SWC and DBI are not significantly different for the normal and non-normal complete and partial data variants. All preregistered hypotheses for Family 4 passed confirmation (see Tables 4 and E.4). For the downsampled data variants, DBI consistently beats SWC in correlation strength across all sparsification levels (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 0.94 −1.03). This pattern continues for the normal and non-normal, sparse data variants (p = 0.0002, effect size 0.64). To determine how cluster count affects the optimality of internal validity indices, we investigated whether reducing cluster count from 23 to 11 to 6 clusters leads to significantly better index values (higher SWC, lower DBI). Note that reducing the cluster count maintains the number of segments at 4 −5 segments per cluster that is retained [16], while completely eliminating some clusters. Exploratory analysis for Family 5 revealed that both indices improved significantly with reduced cluster counts across all data variants. Of the 26 preregistered hypotheses for Family 5 all but the last 6 passed confirmation (see Tables 5 and E.5). For our complete and normal baseline variant, reducing the cluster count from 23 to 6 significantly increased SWC (p = 0.017, effect size 0.39), while DBI decreased significantly (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.96). Reducing the cluster count from 23 to 11 did not have a significant effect on SWC, while DBI decreased significantly (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.89). Finally, reducing the clusters from 11 to 6 was not tested for SWC as it had no significant effect in the exploratory analysis. These hypotheses for DBI could not be confirmed. For the non-normal data variant, the reduction in the cluster count showed the same improvement patterns for both SWC and DBI with slightly larger effect sizes (effect sizes SWC: 0.44, DBI: 0.89 −0.96). To determine how segment count affects the optimality of internal validity indices, we investigated whether reducing segment count from 100 to 50 to 25 segments leads to significantly better index values (higher SWC, lower DBI). Note that reducing the segment count reduces the number of segments per cluster to about 2.3 for 50 segments and 1.6 for 25 segments (from 4 −5), while completely removing some clusters (for 50 segments 1.13, for 25 segments 6.83). For the sparsified data variants, the effect of the reduction from 100 to 50 segments could not be confirmed for DBI, while the effect of the reduction from 50 to 25 significantly improved DBI (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 0.84 −0.93) 8 Discussion We discuss our findings in four parts. First, we synthesise the primary results for distance function performance in canonical pattern mapping and internal validity index optimisation for correlationbased clustering. Second, we compare our findings with previous clustering validation studies, highlighting how our method differs by focusing on the ability of internal indices to assess structural quality rather than identifying the optimal number of clusters or achieving the strongest correlation with external indices. Third, we provide practical recommendations for implementing correlationbased clustering validation in applied research contexts, including concrete index value thresholds that indicate the presence of strong correlation patterns similar to canonical patterns. Finally, we acknowledge the limitations of our approach and outline directions for future research. 8.1 Primary Results Our results reveal that simple, interpretable Lp norm distances outperform more complex and specialised distance functions for correlation-based clustering validation. Although optimal choices vary statistically between data variants, practical differences are often minimal. This allows simplified recommendations for practitioners, such as using the L1 norm distance function to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns, and the L5 norm distance function to calculate the silhouette width criterion (SWC) and the Davies-Bouldin index (DBI), which both evaluate correlation-based clusterings well; see Section 4 for clustering quality index definitions. Canonical pattern mapping was practically optimised by the L1 norm, which excelled at discriminative power while maintaining interpretability. Statistically, the L1 norm was the best for normal and downsampled data variants (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 0.93 −1.09), while the L1 ref emerged as significantly better for non-normal data variants (p < 0.0001 −0.0003, effect sizes 0.69 −1.09). However, despite these statistically robust differences that affect average ranks, the magnitude of differences in raw criterion values was so small that rounding masked them. Therefore, practically speaking, the choice between L1 and L1 ref is unlikely to substantially impact canonical pattern mapping performance. Sparsification made distance functions perform less well without impacting which distance function performed best. Surprisingly, the more sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions Förstner and Log Frobenius consistently ranked in the bottom third. Internal validity index optimisation revealed different optimal performing distance functions than for canonical pattern mapping. Practically, the L5 norm provided the most robust choice across data variants for both SWC and DBI. Statistically, the optimal distance function varied between conditions. L5 significantly outperformed L3 for SWC in normal data (p < 0.0001, effect size 1.10), while patterns reversed for downsampled variants where Linf outperformed L5 (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 1.05 −1.1). Similarly, for DBI, L5 ref significantly outperformed L3 across normal and non-normal variants (p < 0.0001 −0.0002, effect sizes 0.69 −0.73), while L5 outperformed L3 in 27 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 8: Scatter plots for internal validity indices (green, x, right y-axes) compared to the Jaccard index (pink, o, left y-axes) of the 67 segmented clusterings of various quality for 30 subjects. This is the data for the non-normal, partial (70%) variant. The distance function used to calculate the internal indices was the L5 norm. downsampled and Linf in normal and non-normal sparse conditions (p < 0.0001−0.005, effect sizes 0.48 −0.78). However, the confidence intervals show (see Figure 5) that the practical differences between the Lp norms were minimal, suggesting that any of these distance functions would produce comparable results. Again, sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions performed poorly and should be avoided. When evaluating the correlation strength with the Jaccard index, both SWC and DBI achieved strong correlations (|r| > 0.9), while the Calinski-Harabasz index (VRC) and the Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index (PBM) failed to meet the minimal requirements (|r| > 0.5) for all the selected distance functions. Segment count sensitivity analysis revealed important practical limitations. SWC degrades significantly when clusters contain fewer than two objects, dropping from 0.92 (100 segments) to 0.88 (50 segments) to 0.59 (25 segments), while DBI paradoxically showed improved performance (0.04 to 0.037 to 0.025). This indicates that SWC requires more than two objects per cluster to be able to assess within-cluster similarity, while DBI improves with smaller clusters. These effects are both statistically and practically significant, as shown in the confidence intervals in Figure 7. Cluster count sensitivity analysis showed that both indices favoured lower cluster counts, with significant improvements when reducing from 23 to 6 clusters (p<0.001-0.033). However, practically, the bias towards fewer clusters is unlikely to affect clustering validation, with SWC improving marginally from 0.92 to 0.93 and DBI from 0.1 to 0.14. Index reliability comparison revealed that both SWC and DBI provide reliable correlation-based clustering validation with strong correlations to the Jaccard index and differentiated well between clustering quality levels. SWC demonstrated stricter evaluation of segmentation errors compared to DBI, which may be advantageous depending on application requirements. Both indices significantly outperformed VRC and PBM, whose values for perfect clustering results spanned several orders of magnitude (VRC: 13 −25306, PBM: 0.28 −639), making reliable interpretation impractical; see Figure 8. 8.2 Comparison with Previous Work Previous clustering validation studies (see Section 2) focus on identifying the ’right’ number of clusters (defined by human categories) rather than assessing the structural quality of the clustering results. This fundamental difference in validation philosophy leads to different conclusions about index performance and creates a gap in providing practitioners with structural quality guidelines. Our approach differs by validating the performance of indices directly on synthetically created cluster assignments with verified correlation structures, rather than by validating clustering algorithm results. This isolated the ability of indices to discover structures from the ability of clustering algorithms to recover those structures, enabling precise quantification of each index’s structure discovery ability and response to different real-world data conditions (distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification) as well as potential sensitivity towards reduced number of clusters and objects. Furthermore, these perturbations were applied to the same 60 datasets (we call them subjects), creating versions of the same subject for different conditions. This is unlike previous studies in which such factors have been investigated by analysing entirely different datasets, which does not avoid introducing variations that affect indices beyond the particular perturbation being studied [13, 43, 23, 24]. Above all, the structures we studied were correlation structures, not Euclidean points, for which we introduced the framework of canonical patterns that provides discrete known target correlation structures that 28 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 serve a similar purpose, like geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space. Most importantly, our design of the canonical patterns leads to a limited number of possible patterns, transforming the clustering challenge from finding the elusive right number of clusters to discovering which of the known canonical patterns exist in a particular dataset. Although SWC consistently ranks among the strongest indices across studies [13, 43, 8, 7], our work uniquely demonstrates that DBI performs comparably well for correlation-based clustering. This contrasts with previous Euclidean studies in which DBI typically underperformed relative to VRC and PBM. In contrast, VRC and PBM, which showed strong performance in geometric clustering contexts, failed to reliably detect our ground truth and struggled to differentiate between segmented clusterings with controlled degraded quality. This divergence likely stems from a combination of our focus on reliable threshold values for structure-based ground truth versus the usual focus on optimal value for the ’right’ number of clusters, as well as how the indices are designed to assess within-cluster cohesion and between-cluster separation. Both VRC and PBM rely on geometric concepts such as overall dataset centroid, which translate poorly to the correlation space. In contrast, DBI only uses cluster centroids, whereas SWC relies solely on object-to-object dissimilarity assessments that remain meaningful across object types. In addition, we identified segment count (object count) sensitivity as a previously undocumented factor that affects internal indices. When reducing the segment count per cluster from 4-5 to 0-2, SWC degrades significantly, while DBI shows improved performance. This behaviour has not been investigated in previous studies that focused on cluster size or density variations rather than evaluating the impact of 29 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 object reduction across all clusters. An exception is Rousseeuw [23], who mentioned that singleton clusters will result in a silhouette of 0. This phenomenon highlights SWC emphasis on assessing both within-cluster similarity (which suffers with fewer objects) and inter-cluster separation. We confirmed the established bias towards fewer clusters for SWC and DBI [6, 44, 7, 8, 13]. Critically, SWC and DBI never failed to identify ground-truth clusterings in our study, while previous studies reported failure rates of 7-12 out of 21 datasets for these indices, although they evaluated failure when the index did not assign the optimal value to the right number of clusters, perhaps indicating that the structure was stronger in another clustering [43] . 8.3 Practical Considerations and Recommendations In this section, we translate our structure-focused findings into actionable guidelines for correlationbased clustering validation. Usually, clustering validation studies do not focus on establishing reliable ranges for internal validity indices for specific structures, making it difficult to interpret values in real-world datasets that do not provide ground truth (the common clustering case). An exception is Rousseeuw [23], who provided clear quality ranges for SWC for Euclidean data. We provide correlation-based clustering quality thresholds for both SWC and DBI, as well as distil our findings into actionable recommendations for effective correlation-based clustering validation. Our core practical recommendations are as follows: 1. Use SWC and DBI together as complementary validation indices, avoid VRC and PBM 2. Use quality thresholds SWC > 0.8 and DBI < 0.2 that indicate high quality correlationbased clustering results with strong correlations similar to the canonical patterns 3. Use L1 norm to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns 4. Use L5 norm as a robust choice for calculating SWC and DBI 5. Avoid downsampling, work with highest possible frequency sampling, including irregular sampled data instead Internal indices in the ranges of of 0.6 < SWC < 0.8 and 0.2 < DBI < 0.4 are of moderate quality, indicating that the correlation patterns are not as strong as the canonical patterns. This could be due to segmentation or clustering errors or due to the data containing more moderate correlation structures comparable to our downsampled data variants. Internal indices in the ranges of SWC < 0.6 and DBI > 0.4 represent poor correlation-based clustering results; see Table 8 for the mean values achieved for each variant of the data, more results in [16]. Once practitioners have discovered high-quality correlation-based clusters, each cluster can be mapped to one of the 23 valid canonical patterns by calculating the empirical correlation across all segments within the cluster and finding the closest canonical pattern. The canonical patterns provide a finite set of interpretable correlation structures that domain experts can understand on a conceptual level. Regardless of the exact empirical correlations, each canonical pattern represents a specific correlation regime; for example, pattern (0, 0, 0) indicates times when all three variates are uncorrelated, while pattern (1, 0, 0) indicates a strong positive correlation between the first two variates, but no correlation with the third. Domain experts can assess whether discovered patterns align with theoretical expectations and investigate unexpected patterns to discover potential knowledge gaps or novel insights. Note that our recommendations apply to three-variate time series, where the aim is to detect correlation regime changes. The paper [16] describes the data in detail and can be used to assess how closely the target data match our synthetic data. Although practical differences between distance functions 30 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 have been minimal for our data, when target data closely match our synthetic data in distributions and sparsity, it could be beneficial to select the statistically optimal distance functions described in the results. We defined canonical patterns as correlation structures that represent maximally contrasted and distinct correlation patterns rather than subtle variations in correlation strength, making our approach most suitable for detecting strong relationship changes, such as state changes in systems. Moderate correlations will be forced to be interpreted as negligible, negative, or positive strong correlations that might not be granular enough for all domains. Additionally, our definition of canonical patterns by design leads to frequent singular correlation matrices, which can cause numerical instability in matrix rank and generalised eigenvalue calculations that are required for Log Frobenius and Förstner distance functions. We used matrix regularisation to address these issues, which may have contributed to these distance functions’ poor performance. Our evaluation uses synthetic data that were specifically designed to isolate the effects of distribution shifting, downsampling, and sparsification from the effects of validation methods [16]. CSTS models segments with canonical patterns as distinct correlation regimes rather than time series with temporal dependencies. Therefore, the effects of temporal dependencies such as autocorrelation or trends have not been investigated. Furthermore, the data set covers standard normal, specific extreme value, and specific negative binomial distributions with three fixed sparsity levels (100%, 70%, 10%) and segment durations (15 minutes to 12 hours). From a methodological perspective, we evaluated 15 distance functions and four internal validity indices, sufficient to identify reliable validation methods for canonical pattern mapping and clustering quality assessment under various data conditions without claiming that these are the overall best methods. Furthermore, we have not established threshold points for maximum sparsity, or distribution parameters beyond which our recommended distance functions and internal indices would fail. Our findings are limited to the simulated conditions tested. Defining these performance thresholds would help practitioners assess whether their data quality is sufficient for reliable clustering validation. Key areas for future investigation include: (1) validation with real-world time series data containing known correlation structures as well as temporal dependencies, (2) evaluation of additional distance functions, validation methods, and clustering algorithms using our framework, (3) determination of performance threshold boundaries for various data quality factors, and (4) adaptation of our structure-based synthetic validation approach to other data types beyond correlation matrices, such as statistical, topological, or geometric structures. Our openly available and extensible validation and 31 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 data generation code facilitates these future investigations, and the template we established can guide systematic validation across diverse unsupervised learning domains. 9 Conclusion This study addresses the challenge of validating correlation-based time series clustering results when ground truth labels are unavailable, a critical gap that hinders rigorous evaluation of whether results represent distinct relationships rather than arbitrary groupings. To bridge this gap, we introduced canonical correlation patterns that discretise the infinite correlation space into all possible and valid states of strong positive, negligible, or strong negative correlations. These serve as interpretable targets while at the same time creating a distinct mathematical target structure that enables systematic validation, just as distinct geometric shapes enable clustering quality assessment in Euclidean clustering. We systematically evaluated the suitability of distance functions to map correlation matrices to their closest canonical pattern and empirically validated whether internal validation indices reliably measure the strength of the correlation structures in a clustering result. Our empirical results show that simple Lp norm distances outperform sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions such as Förstner and Log Frobenius, with the L1 norm being optimal for canonical pattern mapping and the L5 norm being optimal for validity index calculation. Furthermore, the Silhouette Width Criterion (SWC) and the Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI) provide a reliable correlation-based clustering quality assessment. SWC showed better sensitivity to segmentation errors compared to DBI and Jaccard index, but degrades significantly when clusters contain fewer than 4 objects. Both indices are slightly biased toward fewer clusters. These findings translate into actionable recommendations for practitioners, including specific quality thresholds that reflect strong correlation patterns (SWC > 0.8, DBI < 0.2) and a systematic validation workflow that enables reliable assessment of the quality of the detected correlation regimes. Although distribution shifting does not affect the performance of the indices, sparsification to 10% of the original observations slightly lowers it. We recommend avoiding downsampling, as it degrades correlation structures as demonstrated in [16]. SWC and DBI correctly evaluated downsampled data as less well structured, with values comparable to datasets with more moderate correlation strengths. Beyond correlation clustering, our work contributes to more reliable clustering validation by providing objective quality assessment tools evaluated on validated structure-based benchmarks, which then can operate without requiring ground truth knowledge on real-world datasets. We advocate for clustering validation tools, datasets, and algorithm performance comparison to be based and organised by mathematically defined structures to limit the widespread "try and see" approach that conflates algorithm performance with validation method reliability. 32 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 References [1] Adil Fahad, Najlaa Alshatri, Zahir Tari, Abdullah Alamri, Ibrahim Khalil, Albert Y. In our case a distance function d : AV × AV →R≥0 maps two matrices to a real number to quantify how dissimilar empirical correlation matrices Am are from relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓor how dissimilar two correlation matrices in general are. B.1 Lp Norm The Lp norm distance (also called Minkowski) between any two correlation matrices is defined as d Lp(Am, P′ ℓ) :=   V X i=1 V X j>i (aij −pij)p   1 p . (B.1) Note that we only use the upper half of the correlation matrices, making this a vector distance. B.2 Lp Norm with reference vector Let d be an Lp norm which by definition is rotation insensitive resulting in d Lp(Ax, P′ ℓ) = d Lp(Ay, P′ ℓ) if the vectors of the upper half of the correlation matrix a U, p U in RQ are equidistant from a hyperplane H and lie on opposite sides of it, with the line connecting them being perpendicular to H and |a U| = |p U| with | · | being a vector norm. This might impede similarity differentiation between certain correlation matrices. We attempt to address this by introducing a reference vector vref = (1,1,...,1)Q √Q . The Lp Norm with reference vector is then defined as dref(Am, P′ ℓ) := d Lp(Am, P′ ℓ)(d Lp(a U, vref) + d Lp(p U, vref)) (B.2) B.3 Lp Norm with dot transformation This addresses the same rotation insensitivity problem described in the aforementioned Lp Norm with reference vector approach. Here, instead of modifying the distance calculation, we augment the correlation vectors with orientation information. Let a U ∈RQ be the upper triangular vector of a correlation matrix. We define an augmented vector ˜a ∈RQ+1 as: ˜a :=  a U s  (B.3) where the orientation scalar s := a U·vref+1 2 with reference vector vref := (1,1,...,1)T √Q . The scalar s ∈[0, 1] encodes the alignment between the correlation vector and the reference vector, preventing the mirror vectors from having identical distances. The Lp norm with dot transformation is then defined as ddot(Am, P′ ℓ) := d Lp(˜a, ˜p), (B.4) where ˜p ∈RQ+1 is the similarly augmented upper triangular vector of the correlation matrix of the relaxed canonical pattern P′ ℓ. The Förstner metric (also known as the affine-invariant Riemannian metric) is specifically designed to work as a geodesic distance on the manifold of positive definite matrices, treating the space of correlation/covariance matrices as a Riemannian manifold. For the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓthis distance function leads to frequent nan and inf results due to the valid singular nature of many of the relaxed canonical patterns: 1. λi = 0: when Am is singular 2. λi = ∞when P′ ℓis singular 3. λi < 0 when both correlation matrices Am, P′ ℓare singular but due to numerical imprecision in the eigenvalue calculation, the generalised eigenvalues can become negative instead of ∞ (see Appendix D) We fix issue 1. by calculating ln2(λi + 1) instead and issues 2. and 3. by adding a regularisation term ϵI where ϵ = 1e −10 to all correlation matrices. The numerically stable version of the Förstner metric is defined as d F,ϵ(Am, P′ ℓ) := v u u t V X i=1 ln2(λi(Am + ϵI, P′ ℓ+ ϵI) + 1). The Log Frobenius distance maps points on the Riemannian manifold of positive definite matrices to the tangent space (ln) and then measures the Euclidean distance in that tangent space, resulting in simpler computation than the Förstner distance that respects the curved geometry. To avoid issues with singular correlation matrices Am, P′ ℓthat lead to the determinate being 0 making ln undefined, we add a small regularisation term ϵI where ϵ = 1e −10. The stable version of the Log Frobenius distance is defined as dlog F,ϵ(Am, P′ ℓ) := ∥ln(Am + ϵI) −ln(P′ ℓ+ ϵI)∥F . Here we show a concrete example of this surprising effect. Let A =  1 −0.02 −0.02 −0.02 1 1 −0.02 1 1  and B =  1 −0.01 −0.01 −0.01 1 1 −0.01 1 1  be two similar, singular correlation matrices (row 2 and 3 for both matrices are identical). Theoretically given their singularity both matrices should have one eigenvalue of 0 leading to two inf eigenvalue in the generalised eigenvalue problem. However, the eigenvalues become λA = [9.99200639e −01 + 0.j, 2.00079936 + 0.j, 4.11810443e −32 + 0.j] and λB = [9.99800040e −01 + 0.j, 2.00019996 + 0.j, 4.11857080e −32 + 0.j] calculated using scipy.linalg.eigvals. Note that instead of 0 the third eigenvalue for each matrix is very small. The eigenvalues for the generalised problem become λA,B = [0.98989899, 1.00990099, −0.42480251]. Theoretically, we expect that when B is singular two of the generalised eigenvalues become inf, instead we get a a negative eigenvalue that carries a complete different meaning! This issue can be fixed by adding ϵI to the correlation matrices. For ϵ = 1e −10 the generalised eigenvalues for the above matrices become λA+ϵI,B+ϵI = [0.98989899, 1.00990099, 1.00000117] which correctly express that A and B are indeed very similar matrices. The eigenvalues for A + ϵI and B + ϵI become λA+ϵI = [9.99200639e −01 + 0.j, 2.00079936 + 0.j, 9.99999217e −11 + 0.j] and λB+ϵI = [9.99800040e −01 + 0.j, 2.00019996 + 0.j, 9.99999217e −11 + 0.j]. The regularisation of ϵI also fixes issues of correct inf generalised eigenvalues from singular matrices A, B. For an example of this, let A =  1 −0.02 −0.02 −0.02 1 1 −0.02 1 1  and B =  1 −0.01 −0.01 −0.01 1 1 −0.01 1 1  be two similar, singular correlation matrices (row 2 and 3 for both matrices are identical). 2507.16497v1.full_text: Canonical Correlation Patterns for Validating Clustering of Multivariate Time Series Isabella Degen1, Zahraa S Abdallah2, Kate Robson Brown3, and Henry W J Reeve4 1School of Computer Science, University of Bristol 2School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology, University of Bristol 3College of Engineering and Architecture, University College Dublin 4School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Nanjing July 23, 2025 ABSTRACT Clustering of multivariate time series using correlation-based methods reveals regime changes in relationships between variables across health, finance, and industrial applications. However, validating whether discovered clusters represent distinct relationships rather than arbitrary groupings remains a fundamental challenge. Existing clustering validity indices were developed for Euclidean data, and their effectiveness for correlation structures has not been systematically evaluated. Unlike Euclidean clustering, where geometric shapes provide visible discrete reference targets for objective assessment, correlation structures exist in continuous space without equivalent discrete reference patterns. We address this critical validation gap by introducing canonical correlation patterns as mathematically defined validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures. These canonical patterns in correlation clustering serve as the equivalent of geometric shapes, enabling systematic evaluation of distance functions and validity indices for correlation-based clustering. Using synthetic datasets with perfect ground truth across controlled conditions, including distribution shifts, sparsification, and downsampling, we demonstrate that canonical patterns provide reliable validation targets, using the L1 norm as distance function for mapping and the L5 norm for calculating the silhouette width criterion and Davies-Bouldin index that show superior performance. These methods are robust to sparsification and distribution shifts, and appropriately detect correlation structure degradation under downsampling, enabling practical implementation guidelines for correlation-based clustering validation. This work establishes the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation, enabling confident application in high-stakes domains while providing a template for structure-specific clustering evaluation methodologies. Keywords multivariate time series · clustering · correlation patterns · distance functions · internal validity indices · clustering validity indices · structure-based validation · clustering validation 1 Introduction Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning task that groups similar objects to reveal underlying structures and patterns within data [1]. Time series clustering handles temporal data with unique characteristics such as temporal dependencies and evolving relationships and can reveal meaningful information about the behaviour of the underlying system that generated the data [2]. Correlationbased time series clustering helps to discover relationship patterns between variables. Identifying patterns in changes in correlations has supported the discovery of new knowledge across diverse domains such as identifying market conditions in finance where asset correlation regimes change ar Xiv:2507.16497v1 [cs.LG] 22 Jul 2025 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 1: Correlation-based clustering first segments multivariate time series X when correlation regimes between variables change. Then, each segment’s (Sm) correlation matrix (Am) captures the relationships between all variate pairs (Q) during that period. Next, segments with similar correlation structures are clustered together. These clusters (Ck) are then mapped to canonical patterns (Pℓ) that serve as discrete validation targets. Finally, the canonical patterns that exist in dataset X are interpreted using domain expertise. [3], detecting operational states in industrial systems where changing sensor relationships indicate different system modes [4], or understanding gene expression in biology [5]. The fundamental challenge in clustering is the need to be able to validate results without ground truth information. Given the many possible ways to partition a dataset, clustering validation aims to objectively distinguish meaningful patterns from arbitrary groupings [6, 7, 8, 9]. The established guiding principle is that results of higher quality have higher cohesion within clusters and better separation between clusters [1, 10, 11, 12, 9]. When clustering Euclidean data, the quality of the result can be objectively assessed by analysing whether the clusters form visibly distinct geometrical shapes [13]. However, correlation matrices form a continuous space that lacks such visible discrete reference targets. Consequently, when correlation matrices are grouped into clusters that are expected to represent periods of similar relationships between time series variables, there is no established systematic method to validate whether these clusters represent meaningful periods of distinct relationships or merely arbitrary collections of various correlation matrices. Figure 1 shows how a 3-variate time series dataset is segmented into subsequences when the relationships between the variates change. For each segment, the correlation matrix is calculated and then grouped into clusters of similar relationships between time series. The validation challenge is to objectively assess whether the segmentation of the time series and subsequent clustering of these segments result in optimal cohesive and well-separated clusters of different relationships. The following three gaps prevent reliable validation of correlation-based time series clustering, leading to subjective conclusions about the effectiveness of the methods and the validity of the results [14, 11, 10, 15, 12]. First, the absence of discrete validation targets for correlation structures, analogous to geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space, prevents the formalisation of objective evaluation criteria. Second, the effectiveness of existing clustering validity indices and distance functions that assess the structural quality of clustering results without requiring ground truth has not been systematically evaluated for correlation-based clustering. Instead, these methods were developed and validated for Euclidean data [7, 8, 13, 9]. Third, impacts from real-world data complexities common in time series data, such as irregular sampling, missing data, and non-normal distributions have unknown effects on distance functions and clustering validation indices, preventing 2 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 the establishment of performance thresholds or interpretation guidelines for judging the quality of results. We solve this fundamental validation problem by introducing canonical correlation patterns as verifiable target structures. Canonical patterns discretise the infinite correlation space into mathematically defined states (strong positive, negligible, strong negative correlations between variable pairs), creating well-defined validation targets that encompass the complete correlation space in a maximally contrasted way and serve as the correlation-based clustering equivalent of geometric shapes in Euclidean clustering; see Figure 1 illustrating how the resulting clusters map to canonical patterns that serve as validation targets. Additionally, canonical patterns eliminate the need to predefine cluster numbers, as datasets naturally contain the subset of canonical patterns present in the underlying correlation dynamics, and aid in result interpretation since each canonical pattern can be assigned domain meaning by domain experts. Our work makes three key contributions: (1) formalising canonical correlation patterns as mathematical validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures; (2) systematic empirical evaluation of the effectiveness of distance functions and validity indices for correlation matrices through controlled experiments; (3) establishing practical validation guidelines and actionable recommendations through robustness assessment across non-normal distributions, missing data, and varying completeness levels, as well as sensitivity to cluster and segment count. Together, these contributions provide the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation through formalised mathematical targets, empirically validated methods, and practical implementation guidance. For scope clarification, rather than providing an exhaustive theoretical comparison of all possible distance functions, we take an empirical approach aimed at identifying reliable practical solutions that are interpretable, computationally stable, and robust to real-world data quality challenges. The methodological work described here establishes the foundations that allowed us to create the standardised algorithm evaluation protocols for correlationbased clustering using the synthetic CSTS benchmarking dataset [16]. In CSTS, all canonical patterns are systematically represented and validated for multiple data variations, such as distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification, and controlled degraded clustering results, providing perfect ground truth information. This allows isolating impacts of data variation on correlation patterns from limitations of clustering validation indices and enables rigorous statistical evaluation. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on clustering applications and validation frameworks, highlighting key gaps in correlation-based clustering validation. Section 3 establishes the mathematical formulation and notation used and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Section 4 provides the standard formulas for evaluating the discriminative power of distance functions and assessing clustering quality through external and internal validity indices. Section 5 presents our methodology, detailing how we select, evaluate, and validate distance functions for canonical pattern mapping and internal validity indices for clustering quality. Section 6 outlines the experimental setup, and Section 7 presents the results. Section 8 discusses our key findings, compares our results with previous studies, provides practical recommendations, and acknowledges the limitations of our approach while suggesting future research directions. Finally, Section 9 concludes the article. 2 Related Work Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised machine learning technique that groups similar objects to reveal the underlying structures and patterns in the data [1]. As an established approach in data mining, clustering has become essential across numerous disciplines [10], applied to domains such as biology [11], mental health [12], finance [3] and genomics [15], discovering hidden structures such as patient subgroups [12], financial market segmentations [3], genomic patterns [17], and anomalies in control systems [18]. The methods and challenges vary depending on the type of data that are being clustered. Time series clustering introduces unique complexities such as temporal dependencies, high dimensionality, and dynamic nature of data that are distinct from Euclidean data [2]. These unique characteristics often require specific preprocessing and representation techniques prior to clustering, such as dimensionality reduction or feature extraction, introducing more steps that require validation [19]. Our work focusses on correlation-based multivariate time series clustering, a feature-based approach where correlation 3 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 matrices serve as extracted features representing relationships between variates [19]. A comprehensive review by Marti et al. [3] documents the methodological developments in correlation-based clustering of financial time series, mainly using network-based approaches that convert correlation matrices into distance functions for hierarchical clustering algorithms (like Minimum Spanning Trees) and their extensions (such as Planar Maximally Filtered Graphs). Other researchers take a different approach to clustering based on correlations. Chandereng and Gitter [5] introduced Lag Penalised Weighted Correlation (LPWC), employing a clustering similarity function (1-Pearson correlation) that groups univariate time series with similar temporal patterns even when they occur at slightly different times. Despite its utility and the prolific methods available, choosing and configuring a suitable clustering algorithm remains challenging. Many algorithms needed prior knowledge of the number of clusters and other hyperparameters that are difficult to identify and optimise, given that in real-world datasets, we apply clustering to datasets without ground truth information that would help define such parameters [10]. Furthermore, it remains unclear which method works best for a specific dataset [20]. Studies such as Javed et al. [21] and Paparrizos and Reddy [22] demonstrate that different datasets and problems require different clustering approaches, and Rodriguez et al. [20] mentions that algorithms exhibit varying sensitivities to parameter configurations. As Jaeger and Banks [15] notes, clustering represents an expansive domain in which practitioners must develop customised approaches for each application context. In short, the advice is "try various methods and see", which has led to the debate of whether clustering is more "art than science" [14]. These challenges have motivated extensive research into clustering validation techniques. The field of clustering validation spans several decades. Various researchers have created different internal clustering validation indices with the goal of measuring clustering quality without using domain information such as ground truth labels that external indices make use of [9]. Many internal clustering validity indices have been designed to assess the structural quality of clustering results and provide a measure of better within cluster cohesion and between cluster separation [23, 24]; for technical background on clustering validity assessment please refer to Section 4.2. The seminal work of Milligan and Cooper [6] established the foundation for comparing such indices. This pioneering study introduced a seven-step process where indices that perform better are those that determine optimal cluster numbers. More recently, Vendramin et al. [7] and Arbelaitz et al. [8] extended this framework, providing detailed comparisons of the strengths and weaknesses of various internal validity indices. Vendramin et al. [7] validated the performance of internal validity indices beyond determining the "correct" numbers of clusters by calculating their Pearson correlations with external clustering indices. Internal indices with higher correlation with an external index were judged as superior. In a similar study, Arbelaitz et al. [8] evaluated internal indices using synthetic and real datasets, also stressing that grouping similar objects is more important than finding the "right" number of clusters. Both studies argue that noise might increase cluster numbers without reducing clustering quality which for them, like for many of the internal indices inventors, is related to the structure of the result. The scope of these validation studies is substantial: Vendramin et al. [7] evaluated 40 internal validity indices using four different hierarchical clustering algorithms, comparing the results with three external validity indices across 1080 synthetic datasets. Arbelaitz et al. [8] assessed 30 internal validity indices using k-means and hierarchical clustering on 720 synthetic and 20 real datasets from the UCI repository [25]. Another study worth mentioning is Liu et al. [13] which followed the work of Milligan and Cooper [6] more closely but introduced variations in the datasets such as varying density, cluster shapes, separation, and noise. The clustering indices that are evaluated as performing best were those that achieved the optimal internal index value for the right number of clusters for the maximal number of different datasets. Significantly, all these studies concluded that no single internal validity index outperforms others across all scenarios. This finding aligns with Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem [26], which mathematically proves that no clustering function can simultaneously satisfy three desirable properties: scale invariance, richness, and consistency [9]. This theoretical barrier explains why different validity indices favour different algorithms and data characteristics. In addition to using internal validity indices to evaluate structural properties, stability-based approaches assess the consistency of the results of a clustering algorithm under data perturbations [27, 28, 29]. We deliberately exclude clustering stability from our validation techniques review as it primarily evaluates algorithm robustness rather than the intrinsic structural quality of the resulting clusters. 4 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Although these comprehensive validation frameworks provide a solid foundation, they were designed using Euclidean datasets and internal validity indices have not been specifically assessed for time series clustering [2]. In contrast to structure-based internal validation, time series clustering algorithms are typically compared by benchmarking them against classification datasets that contain ground truth information. Notable time series benchmarking studies include Javed et al. [21], which used a phased evaluation framework that isolated the effects of eight algorithms (including partitional, density-based, and hierarchical methods) and three distance functions (Euclidean, dynamic time warping, shapebased) on 112 datasets from the UCR archive [30]. Their analysis found that performance variation depended more on dataset characteristics than algorithmic innovations. Similarly, the Odyssey study from Paparrizos and Reddy [22] analysed 80 univariate time series clustering methods across 128 datasets. Both studies used external validation indices, since the UCR datasets consist of presegmented univariate time series already assigned to classes. This validation approach, while valuable for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of algorithms, conflates clustering and classification by assuming presegmented data with known ground truth, which introduces a critical methodological issue of classification boundaries defined by humans that do not necessarily reflect structural properties [31]. Algorithms may perform poorly not because they fail to discover meaningful structures, but because the expected classifications might not match such structures [21, 22]. Additionally to evaluating clustering algorithms for their ability to discover classification labels, these benchmarking studies use real-world datasets. This is both an advantage as such data include the full complexities of time series data but they make it impossible to isolate the performance of the algorithms from the quality of the underlying structures in the data. Our work addresses the gap in correlation-based time series clustering for which distance functions and internal validity indices have not been systematically evaluated. Our perspective is that clustering is a method to find structure in data and therefore the validation techniques need to be based on the quality of the discovered structure not on domain-based labels. 3 Problem Formalisation This section establishes the mathematical formulation and notation of correlation-based clustering and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Throughout, we shall let R denote the set of real numbers and N the set of positive integers. Given a natural number N ∈N, we let [N] := {1, . . . , N}. 3.1 Correlation-based Clustering First, we establish the notation of objects and their relations used in correlation-based clustering. Let X in RT ×V be a matrix where T ∈N is the number of observations and V ∈N is the number of variates in the time series. Given M ∈N we shall let G(M) denote the collection of segmentations into M segments. Formally, for each M ∈N the set G(M) consists of all strictly increasing sequences η = (ηm)M m=0 ∈[T]M+1 of length M +1 with η0 := 0 and ηM := T. For each m ∈[M], the values ηm−1 + 1 and ηm denote the start and end of the m-th index, respectively. We also let G := ST M=1 G(M) denote the set of all possible segmentations of a time horizon T. For each M ∈T, η ∈G(M) and m ∈[M] we let Sm ≡Sm(X, η) := X(ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm), (1) which takes values in R|ηm−ηm−1|×V , denote the m-th segment of X, containing sequential observations t ∈{ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm}. Then we shall let corr : S R∈N, R≥V RR×V →RV ×V denote the Spearman rank correlation [32] mapping from R × V matrices ˜X to the corresponding V × V correlation matrix A. The tied values are assigned average ranks, and the Spearman correlation is calculated using the standard tie-corrected formula. For our application of corr, we define the correlation coefficient aij := 0 for the cases of Sm when exactly one of the variates i or j is constant, and aij := 1 when both are constant. The image of corr is contained within the subspace AV ⊆RV ×V consisting of symmetric positive semi-definite matrices with unit diagonal and elements aij ∈[−1, 1] for i, j ∈V and i ̸= j. Note that AV forms a Q-dimensional subspace where Q := V (V −1)/2 is the number of unique pairs of 5 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 variates. As such, we sometimes represent elements of AV by vectors in RQ, where the correlation coefficients aij are ordered lexicographically a U := [a12, a13, ..., a(V −1)V ]. For each segment Sm where m ∈[M], we write Am ≡Am(X, η) := corr(Sm), (2) for its correlation matrix. Next, we write K(M, K) for the set of all clusterings Φ := (ϕ1, . . . , ϕK) which are sequences of K disjoint non-empty subsets of [M] whose union is S Φ = ϕ1 ∪. . . ∪ϕK = [M]. Additionally, we let SC(M, K) denote the set of all segmented clusterings which are tuples of the form π := (η, Φ), (3) where η ∈G(M) and Φ ∈K(M, K) is a clustering of these segments. Furthermore, given π ∈SC(M, K) and m ∈[M] and k ∈[K] we let Ck(π) := {Am : m ∈ϕk}, (4) denote a cluster where ϕk ∈Φ. Finally, to compare how similar two matrices are, we shall leverage a non-negative function d : AV × AV →R≥0 on the space AV as distance function. Given correlation matrices Ax, Ay ∈AV we view d(Ax, Ay) as quantifying the degree of dissimilarity between Ax and Ay. In practice many examples of d will be metrics, yet we require no further properties beyond non-negativity. We provide the definitions for the various distance functions employed in Appendix B. 3.2 Canonical Patterns Next, we formalise the canonical correlation patterns as discrete mathematical validation targets for correlation matrices that underpin our method for correlation-based clustering validation. Let P ∈AV denote a canonical pattern with elements pij ∈{−1, 0, 1} for i, j ∈[V ] and i ̸= j. Each canonical pattern Pℓwith ℓ∈[L] represents a unique idealised correlation structure capturing strong positive correlation, no correlation, or strong negative correlation between the Q unique variate pairs. The total number of different canonical patterns is L := 3Q. A canonical pattern Pℓmust be positive semi-definite to be a valid correlation matrix. To fulfil this requirement, we define a relaxed discretisation criterion where P′ ℓis considered equivalent to its canonical form Pℓ, if P′ ℓis positive semi-definite after adjusting its correlation coefficients within tolerance bands B := {[−1, −0.7], [−0.2, 0.2], [0.7, 1]}. Canonical patterns Pℓthat cannot be made positive semi-definite after this relaxation within B are invalid. The tolerance bands B represent practical thresholds that continue to clearly distinguish between strong negative, negligible, and strong positive correlation coefficients, while respecting the geometry of the correlation space AV . This relaxation process determines which of the L theoretical patterns yield valid correlation matrices, resulting in L′ < L relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓwhere ℓ∈[L′]. To facilitate human interpretation, we use the idealised Pℓto represent a pattern. For calculations, we use the corresponding relaxed form P′ ℓ, see Appendix A for a list of the 23 valid canonical patterns out of the 27 possible and their relaxed form for three time series variates. Let ψ : AV 7→{P′ ℓ: ℓ∈[L′]} denote the canonical pattern mapping ψ(Am) := min argmin ℓ∈[L′] {d(Am, P′ ℓ)} (5) that associates a correlation matrix Am with its closest relaxed canonical pattern. Here, ‘min’ ensures that the ties are broken by selecting the smallest index ℓ. The canonical pattern mapping ψ provides a natural basis for constructing a clustering Φ. A possible clustering strategy is to group correlation matrices in such a way that for k ∈[K] we have ϕk := {m ∈[M] : ψ(Am) = P′ ℓ} , (6) where ℓ∈[L′]. Under such an approach, canonical patterns P′ ℓserve as discrete, idealised, interpretable target clusters of the clustering Φ. Each cluster ϕk then consists of all segment indices m whose correlation matrices map to the same relaxed canonical pattern P′ ℓ. Note that K ≤L′ as not all ℓ∈[L′] need to be present in a given time series X. 6 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 3.3 Level Sets for Canonical Patterns Finally, we introduce level sets that enable a systematic evaluation of distance functions by grouping canonical patterns according to their theoretical similarity. Let d L1 : AV × AV →R≥0 denote the L1 distance between canonical patterns so that d L1(Px, Py) := V X i=1 V X j>i |pxij −pyij|, (7) for pattern indices x, y ∈[L′]. Let DL1 := {δ ∈R : ∃x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ} denote the ordered sequence of achievable L1 distances between valid canonical patterns. The theoretical maximum δmax is bounded by V (V −1), although this δmax may not be achievable due to the constraints on valid correlation matrices. To give an example, with three time series variates (V = 3) the sequence becomes DL1 = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, where a distance of 1 represents one coefficient changing by ±1, a distance of 2 represents either two coefficients changing by ±1 or one coefficient flipping sign, and so forth. The theoretical maximum distance of 6 for V = 3 cannot be achieved while only retaining the canonical patterns Pℓthat can satisfy the tolerance bands B and be a valid correlation matrix Am. For each potential distance value δ ∈DL1, we define the level set Lδ as Lδ := {(x, y) : x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ}. (8) The collection {Lδ}δ∈DL1 groups pattern index pairs (x, y) by their L1 distance, with L0 containing indices of identical patterns, L1 containing indices of patterns where one correlation coefficient differs by ±1, and so forth. This creates a natural ordering between the level sets, while all the pattern pairs within each Lδ are theoretically equivalent. 4 Evaluation Reference Formulas This section provides established formulas for evaluating the performance of distance functions and assessing clustering quality, providing the mathematical foundation for our methodology. 4.1 Discriminative Power The effectiveness of a distance function d to map empirical correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical patterns P′ ℓ(see Section 3.2) can be evaluated using multiple complementary approaches. We investigate how well a distance function distinguishes across all the canonical patterns, how consistent distances are within a level set Lδ (see Section 3.3) and how well a distance function performs this mapping in the basic 1NN classifier where all the neighbours have been hardcoded to be the canonical patterns. In this section, we provide the established formulas used for these evaluations. 4.1.1 Overall Discriminative Power We use Shannon’s entropy [33] to evaluate the overall variability of distances. Given a finite number of distances γ ∈D, where D is a multi set, Shannon’s entropy is defined as HD := k X i=1 p(γi) log2(1/p(γi)), (9) where k is the number of bins, γi are the distances falling into bin i, and p(γi) is the relative frequency of the distances in bin i (empirical estimate of the probability mass function for the distances γ ∈D). For the overall discriminative power of a distance function d, we consider all distances. Therefore, D := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M], y ∈[L′], and then |D| = M × L′. The larger HD, the more uncertain and random the observed distances are, which is desirable. 7 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 4.1.2 Level Set Discriminative Power Level sets Lδ (see Section 3.3) lend interpretable properties to evaluate the suitability of a distance function d to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns (see Eq. 5). We expect the distance d between an empirical correlation matrix Am and a canonical pattern P′ ℓto be smaller, the closer the canonical pattern is to the pattern used to create the empirical correlation matrix. We also use Shannon’s entropy to evaluate the similarity of distances within the level sets. For the analysis of the level sets of a distance function d, we consider the subset of distances γ ∈Dδ where Dδ ⊂D for the respective level set Lδ defined as Dδ := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M] and y ∈[L′] such that d L1(Px, Py) = δ, where Px was the canonical pattern used to generate the segment from which the empirical correlation matrix Ax was calculated and Py is the relaxed canonical pattern P′ y we calculate the distance for. The closer to zero HDδ is, the more uniform the observed distances within the level set, which is desirable. The average entropy for all level sets is defined as HL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 HDδ. (10) Furthermore, the average rate of increase in distances from level set to level set is defined as RL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 |µLδ −µLδ+1|, (11) where µLδ is the mean distance for the level set Lδ for a distance function. The average rate measures the mean absolute difference in distances between consecutive level sets. 4.1.3 Canonical Pattern Classification Power The ability of a distance function to best map correlation matrices to their matching canonical pattern can be seen as a classification problem. For this we "train" 1NN, the most basic classifier [34, 30, 35], on the canonical patterns. In this scenario, the neighbours are hardcoded to the canonical patterns. We use this 1NN classifier to assign each empirical correlation matrix to its closest relaxed canonical pattern using a distance function d. Our aim is to identify both distance functions that can discriminate between the different canonical correlation patterns and map empirical correlation matrices to their canonical patterns, as well as internal validity indices that quantify the quality of a particular segmented clustering. The distance functions and internal indices selected must provide good interpretability, computational stability, and robustness to common variations in the quality of real-life data. For both evaluations, we follow a systematic three-stage methodology in which we first select candidates; second empirically evaluate their performance; and third, statistically validate whether there are superior options. We recognise that statistically significant differences may not always translate to meaningful practical improvements and therefore evaluate both practical and statistical differences between candidates. Importantly, we assess distance function performance in two distinct contexts. First, we evaluate their ability to directly discriminate between canonical correlation patterns. Second, we evaluate how these same distance functions perform when embedded within internal validity indices for clustering quality assessment. As we demonstrate, optimal distance functions may differ between these contexts. For statistical testing, we employ a two-phase approach (exploratory and confirmatory) to reduce false discoveries, organising the tests into six families to control Type I error rates [40]. We conduct the experiments using the CSTS benchmark datasets [16], which provides validated ground truth clusterings for all canonical patterns under normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions. CSTS further provides controlled degraded quality clustering as well as reduced cluster and segment count versions to enable a thorough investigation of the effectiveness and potential biases of the validation methods. 5.1 Canonical Pattern Mapping Assessment Our aim in this section is to identify which distance functions best map empirical correlation matrices to their underlying canonical patterns. We describe how we select candidate distance functions and then evaluate their ability to distinguish between different canonical correlation patterns, as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function. 5.1.1 Distance Function Selection We select distance functions using the following four key principles: 1. Interpretability: The distance function must follow human intuition about similarity and differences between correlation matrices Am and canonical patterns Pℓ. The distance function should allow meaningful interpretations of which cluster Ck(π) best fits each observed correlation matrix Am and which cluster best fits a canonical pattern Pℓ. 2. Discriminative Power: The distance function must be able to effectively and reliably distinguish between the different canonical patterns Pℓand assign correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical pattern Pℓ, see the canonical pattern mapping equation 5. Each canonical pattern should be equally distinguishable. 3. Computational Stability: The distance function must be numerically stable. This includes dealing with very small eigenvalues λi and singular correlation matrices, which are both common in the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓ. The computation time needs to be feasible on standard hardware, prioritising result quality over processing speed. 4. Robustness: The distance function needs to be able to handle real-world challenges such as varying segment lengths, irregular sampling, and non-normal distributions of the time series variates without the need for manual parameter tuning, which is not possible without knowing the ground truth. Following these four principles, we select the vector-based distance functions Lp norm, Lp norm with reference vector, dot transformed Lp norm, and the matrix-based distance functions Log Frobenius norm and Förstner metric (all defined in Appendix B). We focus on vector-based distance functions 11 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 because of their direct quantification of the differences in correlation coefficients and easy geometrical interpretation. We include matrix-based distance functions because they, to varying degrees, capture the geometry of correlation matrices, which could be advantageous. Our selection includes distance functions that are directly applicable to correlation matrices without requiring parameter tuning. This excludes time series specific distance function like Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), which requires parameter tuning and measures distance between time series observations rather than correlations. We also focus on distance functions with direct geometric interpretation for correlation matrices, excluding probabilistic and graph-based approaches. 5.1.2 Distance Function Evaluation We systematically evaluate the performance of the selected distance functions to identify which dissimilarity function best satisfies our four key principles to map empirical correlation matrices to canonical patterns. Each distance function is assessed against criteria derived from the principles of interpretability and discriminative power, with robustness and computational stability serving as a prerequisite for inclusion; see details in Section 6.2. For interpretability, we evaluate whether distance functions produce intuitive mappings between empirical correlation matrices and canonical patterns. This includes evaluating distance consistency within level sets (see Eq. 8) and meaningful separation between level sets. For discriminative power, we assess each distance function’s ability to reliably distinguish between canonical patterns and correctly assign empirical correlation matrices to their closest canonical pattern. This evaluation focusses on the distance function’s capacity to maintain clear boundaries between different canonical patterns and accurately assign empirical correlation matrices. We rank distance functions based on their performance for each of these criteria, providing both relative comparisons between distance functions and overall performance evaluation to ensure that high-ranking distance functions demonstrate genuine effectiveness rather than merely superior relative performance. The evaluation is carried out separately for normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions to assess robustness and identify distance functions that maintain consistent performance under real-world challenges. 5.1.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether the distance function ranked highest is superior, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests [41] to compare the distance function ranks for each subject. These tests constitute Family 1 of our six-family statistical testing framework, specifically designed to control Type I error rates when determining which distance functions best map correlation matrices to canonical patterns. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best-ranked distance functions and expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests [40], see Table 1. 5.2 Internal Validity Index Assessment Having established optimal distance functions for canonical pattern discrimination, we now aim to identify which distance functions optimise the performance of the internal validity index and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable quantification of clustering quality with minimal bias. We first describe how we select candidate internal clustering validity indices and then evaluate using different distance functions their ability to reliably quantify the quality of a segmented clustering (see Equation 3), as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function and internal index combination. 5.2.1 Index Selection We select the internal validity indices to evaluate based on their performance in previous comprehensive evaluation studies by Vendramin et al. [7] and Arbelaitz et al. [8] as well as based on their popularity in clustering. Due to our canonical pattern approach of defining an upper bound for the possible number of patterns in a dataset, it is important that the number of clusters K and the number 12 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 of segments M do not affect the performance of the internal validity index, as not every canonical pattern will be present in every dataset despite the clustering being of equal high quality. 5.2.2 Index Evaluation We evaluate the selected internal indices to determine which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias. We systematically evaluate both objectives for each data variant to understand how the choice of distance function affects index performance and how different indices behave under varying conditions. We evaluate how different distance functions affect internal validity index performance from two complementary perspectives. First, we assess each distance function’s ability to produce optimal raw index values for the highest-quality segmented clustering (ground-truth perfect clustering). Second, we evaluate how well each distance function enables indices to correlate with the Jaccard index, measuring the index’s ability to distinguish between different clustering quality levels. The latter perspective shows how validation without labels (internal clustering validation) matches validation using ground truth label information (external clustering validation, not available in real-world settings). We independently assess these two perspectives for each data variant and internal validity index, then synthesise the results to identify optimal distance functions. When optimal distance functions differ between raw performance and correlation performance, we examine the implications of this divergence from a practical viewpoint. Using the optimal distance functions identified above, we assess the reliability and bias of the internal validity indices. We evaluate the sensitivity of the index to varying numbers of clusters and segments by working with reduced versions of our data variants. Additionally, we synthesise results across all data variants (normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified) to assess the robustness of each index to different data characteristics and pattern degradation conditions. 5.2.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether there is a superior distance function for the validity indices and an overall superior validity index, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests to compare the evaluation results for each subject [41]. These tests constitute Families 2-6 of our six-family statistical testing framework. We first establish which distance function and internal index combinations achieve sufficient correlation strength to warrant detailed comparative analysis. We apply a viability threshold that requires Pearson’s mean correlation |r| > 0.5 between the internal indices and the Jaccard index for each subject within each data variant, based on sample size calculations to ensure adequate statistical power. Based on viable combinations from this filtering, we define the five families (2-6) comparing the internal indices SWC and DBI, which pass this correlation viability threshold. Family 2 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly better ground truth values for SWC and DBI, while Family 3 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly stronger correlation between SWC/DBI and the Jaccard index. Family 4 examines whether SWC or DBI correlates more strongly with the Jaccard index, Family 5 examines the impacts of cluster count reduction, and Family 6 evaluates the effects of segment count reduction. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best performing distance functions and internal indices, respectively, expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions and internal indices to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on these exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests using hierarchical testing procedures [40], see Tables 2 to 6. 6 Experimental Setup We describe the experimental setup in four parts. First, we describe the CSTS benchmark dataset used for all experiments. Second, we present the experimental configurations for the canonical pattern mapping assessment following our three-stage methodology: candidate selection, evaluation implementation, and statistical validation. Third, we detail the experimental configurations for the 13 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 internal validity index assessment, following the same three-stage structure. Fourth, we describe the implementation details of the libraries used and the hardware employed for our experimentation. 6.1 Synthetic Benchmark Dataset To systematically evaluate clustering validation approaches, we used the open source CSTS dataset [16], a correlation structure-specific synthetic benchmark that provides controlled ground truth for the validation of multivariate time series clustering. CSTS consists of exploratory and confirmatory datasets, each comprising ND = 30 different subjects. The exploratory and confirmatory datasets are statistically equivalent but independent. For each subject, there are 12 data variants of three-variate regime-switching time series data. Figure 2: Time series data across CSTS generation stages.
