L1 < L2 1.1 30 6.3 Internal Validity Index experiments Here we describe the setup and configurations used for the experiments to determine the best suited intern validity index. To evaluate how effectively internal validity indices can distinguish between different levels of clustering quality, we generated a controlled spectrum of clustering quality ranging from perfect (ground truth) to severely degraded. This quality degradation simulation allowed us to assess the sensitivity and reliability of the index across the full range of possible clustering outcomes, a method established by Vendramin et al. [7], Arbelaitz et al. [8]. We generated Nπ = 66 deliberately degraded segmented clusterings for each subject (ND = 30) and each data variant. We used three strategies and created 22 segmented clusterings with degraded quality per strategy: (1) shifting the segment end index forward by a randomly selected number of observations, (2) randomly assigning a randomly selected wrong canonical pattern to a randomly increasing number of segments, and (3) combining (1) and (2). In total, we ended up with 360 ground truth segmented clusterings (30 subjects ×12 variants) and 23,760 segmented clusterings with degraded quality (66 degraded segmented clusterings ×360 ground truth). Figure 3 shows the descriptive statistics for the Jaccard index, the number of wrong clusters, and the number of observations shifted for the degraded segmented clusterings and the ground truth. It illustrates that the degraded segmented clusterings covered the full quality range for the Jaccard Index [0, 1]. The Jaccard index linearly increases as the number of wrongly assigned clusters decreases from all 100 segments having a wrong cluster assigned to none (first 44 segmented clusterings). It continues to increase, all be it at a slower rate, as the number of observation shifted decreases (last 22 segmented clustering). Simply shifting observation has less of an impact on the Jaccard index than assigning a segment to a wrong cluster. 6.3.1 Index Selection Following the method defined in Section 5.2, we selected the following four internal indices: (1) the silhouette width criterion (SWC; see Eq. 17) for its consistent high performance and lack of needing a cluster or data centroid; (2) the relatively little known Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index (PBM, see Eq. 20) due to its good performance in [7] and its robustness to varying numbers of clusters; (3) the widely used Davies-Bouldin index (DBI, see Eq. 18); and (4) the Calinksi-Harabasz index (VRC, see Eq. 19). The latter two were chosen for their popularity in clustering quality assessments. 6.3.2 Index Evaluation To evaluate which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality quantification, we performed assessments on all data variants, each containing the same ND = 30 subjects. To identify optimal distance functions for internal validity indices, we first calculated all four internal validity indices (SWC, PBM, DBI, VRC) for the ground truth segmented clusterings using ten representative distance functions selected based on the canonical pattern mapping assessment. These distance functions span the Lp distance family (L1, L2, L3, L5, Linf), referenceand dot-transformbased variants (L1 ref, L5 ref, dt Linf) and correlation-specialised approaches (Log Frobenius, Förstner). We ranked distance functions based on their ability to produce optimal raw index values for ground truth clusterings. Second, we calculated Pearson correlations between internal indices and the Jaccard index for each distance function on clusterings of degraded quality that span the full 17 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 range of the Jaccard index [0, 1]. Note that evaluating segmentation and clustering of time series simultaneously is uncommon, which required our adapted Jaccard index definition (see Eq. 14) for segmented clusterings. To reduce the number of combinations to evaluate and achieve statistically significant correlations, we established that all internal indices had to achieve a minimum correlation strength of |r| ≥0.5 (see Section 6.3.3) for at least one distance function, which only SWC and DBI did. We focused the detailed raw value analysis on SWC and DBI, calculating 95% confidence intervals of the mean ground truth index values across subjects of the ten aforementioned distance functions. The correlation analysis aligns with the study setup in [7]. For power analysis, we calculated the effect sizes and achieved power using the same formulas as for canonical pattern mapping validation, see Eq. 22 and Eq. 23. 6.4 Implementation details All experiments were implemented in Python 3.9 using Num Py 1.26.4 for numerical computations, Sci Py 1.11.3 for distance function calculations, statistical analysis, correlation calculations, and distributions, Pandas 2.2.2 for descriptive statistics and results aggregation, and Scikit-learn 1.4.2 for k NN, F1 score, and SWC calculations. The experiments were run on a Mac Book Pro with an Apple M1 chip (8 cores: 4 performance, 4 efficiency) and 16GB RAM running mac OS 15.x. No optimisations or parallelisation techniques were employed to keep the implementation straightforward and reproducible. The longest calculations are calculating all 15 distance functions for all data variants (each with ND = 30 subjects), which typically took approximately 5 hours, and calculating all internal indices for all 24,120 datasets, which typically took 8 hours wall clock time. Overall, we showed that L1-based distance functions consistently achieved superior performance for canonical pattern mapping across data variants. 7.1.1 Distance Function Evaluation For our baseline, the normal and complete data variant, the L1 norm distance function ranked best (µ = 4.7, SD= 0.07), followed by L3 (µ = 4.76, 0.15) and L1 ref (µ = 4.82, 0.12), while the Förstner level ranked worst (µ = 6.57, 0.10). Family 2 investigated which distance function leads to optimal values. Exploratory analysis revealed 25 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 that the L5 distance function, although not always significantly best, was consistently in the group of best-performing distance functions for both SWC and DBI for all data variants. All but the last preregistered hypothesis for Family 2 passed confirmation (see Tables 2 and E.2). For our complete and normal baseline variant, L5 outperformed L3 for SWC (p < 0.0001, effect size 1.10), while L5 ref beat L3 for DBI (p = 0.0002, effect size 0.69). For the non-normal data variant, for SWC, L5 maintained superiority but now over Linf with a reduced effect size (p = 0.03, effect size 0.55). For DBI the superiority of L5 ref over L5 could not be confirmed (p = 0.15, effect size 0.24). For the downsampled non-normal data variant, SWC optimisation reversed, favouring Linf over L5 (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.73), while DBI optimisation shifted to L5 beating L3 (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.70). Sparsification to partial data variants (70% of the original observations) did not change the distance function that led to optimal values. However, sparsification to 10% had the effect for SWC across all data variants that Linf consistently beat L5 (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 1.05 −1.09). For DBI, L5 continued to beat Linf with smaller effect sizes for normal and non-normal sparse data variants (p = 0.001 −0.005, effect sizes 0.48 −0.60). For the downsampled sparse data variant for DBI, L5 maintained superiority but this time over L3 (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.78). Exploratory analysis revealed that the Linf distance function, although not always significantly best, was consistently in the group of best-performing distance functions for both SWC and DBI for all data variants. All but the last three preregistered hypotheses for Family 3 passed confirmation (see Tables 3 and E.3). For our complete and normal baseline variant, Linf outperformed L5 for SWC and DBI (SWC: p < 0.0001, effect size 1.08; DBI: p = 0.016, effect size 0.47). For sparse non-normal data, Linf beat L1 ref (p = 0.034, effect size 0.34). For the complete downsampled data variant for SWC the Förstner distance function achieved significantly stronger correlation over Linf (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.76), while for DBI L5 ref beat L1 ref (p < 0.0001, effect size 0.83). First, we synthesise the primary results for distance function performance in canonical pattern mapping and internal validity index optimisation for correlationbased clustering. Second, we compare our findings with previous clustering validation studies, highlighting how our method differs by focusing on the ability of internal indices to assess structural quality rather than identifying the optimal number of clusters or achieving the strongest correlation with external indices. Third, we provide practical recommendations for implementing correlationbased clustering validation in applied research contexts, including concrete index value thresholds that indicate the presence of strong correlation patterns similar to canonical patterns. Finally, we acknowledge the limitations of our approach and outline directions for future research. 8.1 Primary Results Our results reveal that simple, interpretable Lp norm distances outperform more complex and specialised distance functions for correlation-based clustering validation. Although optimal choices vary statistically between data variants, practical differences are often minimal. This allows simplified recommendations for practitioners, such as using the L1 norm distance function to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns, and the L5 norm distance function to calculate the silhouette width criterion (SWC) and the Davies-Bouldin index (DBI), which both evaluate correlation-based clusterings well; see Section 4 for clustering quality index definitions. Canonical pattern mapping was practically optimised by the L1 norm, which excelled at discriminative power while maintaining interpretability. Statistically, the L1 norm was the best for normal and downsampled data variants (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 0.93 −1.09), while the L1 ref emerged as significantly better for non-normal data variants (p < 0.0001 −0.0003, effect sizes 0.69 −1.09). However, despite these statistically robust differences that affect average ranks, the magnitude of differences in raw criterion values was so small that rounding masked them. Therefore, practically speaking, the choice between L1 and L1 ref is unlikely to substantially impact canonical pattern mapping performance. Sparsification made distance functions perform less well without impacting which distance function performed best. Surprisingly, the more sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions Förstner and Log Frobenius consistently ranked in the bottom third. Internal validity index optimisation revealed different optimal performing distance functions than for canonical pattern mapping. Practically, the L5 norm provided the most robust choice across data variants for both SWC and DBI. Statistically, the optimal distance function varied between conditions. L5 significantly outperformed L3 for SWC in normal data (p < 0.0001, effect size 1.10), while patterns reversed for downsampled variants where Linf outperformed L5 (p < 0.0001, effect sizes 1.05 −1.1). Similarly, for DBI, L5 ref significantly outperformed L3 across normal and non-normal variants (p < 0.0001 −0.0002, effect sizes 0.69 −0.73), while L5 outperformed L3 in 27 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 8: Scatter plots for internal validity indices (green, x, right y-axes) compared to the Jaccard index (pink, o, left y-axes) of the 67 segmented clusterings of various quality for 30 subjects. This is the data for the non-normal, partial (70%) variant. The distance function used to calculate the internal indices was the L5 norm. downsampled and Linf in normal and non-normal sparse conditions (p < 0.0001−0.005, effect sizes 0.48 −0.78). However, the confidence intervals show (see Figure 5) that the practical differences between the Lp norms were minimal, suggesting that any of these distance functions would produce comparable results. Again, sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions performed poorly and should be avoided. When evaluating the correlation strength with the Jaccard index, both SWC and DBI achieved strong correlations (|r| > 0.9), while the Calinski-Harabasz index (VRC) and the Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index (PBM) failed to meet the minimal requirements (|r| > 0.5) for all the selected distance functions. Segment count sensitivity analysis revealed important practical limitations. SWC degrades significantly when clusters contain fewer than two objects, dropping from 0.92 (100 segments) to 0.88 (50 segments) to 0.59 (25 segments), while DBI paradoxically showed improved performance (0.04 to 0.037 to 0.025). This indicates that SWC requires more than two objects per cluster to be able to assess within-cluster similarity, while DBI improves with smaller clusters. These effects are both statistically and practically significant, as shown in the confidence intervals in Figure 7. Cluster count sensitivity analysis showed that both indices favoured lower cluster counts, with significant improvements when reducing from 23 to 6 clusters (p<0.001-0.033). However, practically, the bias towards fewer clusters is unlikely to affect clustering validation, with SWC improving marginally from 0.92 to 0.93 and DBI from 0.1 to 0.14. Index reliability comparison revealed that both SWC and DBI provide reliable correlation-based clustering validation with strong correlations to the Jaccard index and differentiated well between clustering quality levels. SWC demonstrated stricter evaluation of segmentation errors compared to DBI, which may be advantageous depending on application requirements. Both indices significantly outperformed VRC and PBM, whose values for perfect clustering results spanned several orders of magnitude (VRC: 13 −25306, PBM: 0.28 −639), making reliable interpretation impractical; see Figure 8. 8.2 Comparison with Previous Work Previous clustering validation studies (see Section 2) focus on identifying the ’right’ number of clusters (defined by human categories) rather than assessing the structural quality of the clustering results. This fundamental difference in validation philosophy leads to different conclusions about index performance and creates a gap in providing practitioners with structural quality guidelines. Our approach differs by validating the performance of indices directly on synthetically created cluster assignments with verified correlation structures, rather than by validating clustering algorithm results. This isolated the ability of indices to discover structures from the ability of clustering algorithms to recover those structures, enabling precise quantification of each index’s structure discovery ability and response to different real-world data conditions (distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification) as well as potential sensitivity towards reduced number of clusters and objects. Furthermore, these perturbations were applied to the same 60 datasets (we call them subjects), creating versions of the same subject for different conditions. This is unlike previous studies in which such factors have been investigated by analysing entirely different datasets, which does not avoid introducing variations that affect indices beyond the particular perturbation being studied [13, 43, 23, 24]. Above all, the structures we studied were correlation structures, not Euclidean points, for which we introduced the framework of canonical patterns that provides discrete known target correlation structures that 28 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 serve a similar purpose, like geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space. Most importantly, our design of the canonical patterns leads to a limited number of possible patterns, transforming the clustering challenge from finding the elusive right number of clusters to discovering which of the known canonical patterns exist in a particular dataset. Although SWC consistently ranks among the strongest indices across studies [13, 43, 8, 7], our work uniquely demonstrates that DBI performs comparably well for correlation-based clustering. This contrasts with previous Euclidean studies in which DBI typically underperformed relative to VRC and PBM. In contrast, VRC and PBM, which showed strong performance in geometric clustering contexts, failed to reliably detect our ground truth and struggled to differentiate between segmented clusterings with controlled degraded quality. This divergence likely stems from a combination of our focus on reliable threshold values for structure-based ground truth versus the usual focus on optimal value for the ’right’ number of clusters, as well as how the indices are designed to assess within-cluster cohesion and between-cluster separation. Both VRC and PBM rely on geometric concepts such as overall dataset centroid, which translate poorly to the correlation space. In contrast, DBI only uses cluster centroids, whereas SWC relies solely on object-to-object dissimilarity assessments that remain meaningful across object types. In addition, we identified segment count (object count) sensitivity as a previously undocumented factor that affects internal indices. When reducing the segment count per cluster from 4-5 to 0-2, SWC degrades significantly, while DBI shows improved performance. This behaviour has not been investigated in previous studies that focused on cluster size or density variations rather than evaluating the impact of 29 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 object reduction across all clusters. An exception is Rousseeuw [23], who mentioned that singleton clusters will result in a silhouette of 0. This phenomenon highlights SWC emphasis on assessing both within-cluster similarity (which suffers with fewer objects) and inter-cluster separation. We confirmed the established bias towards fewer clusters for SWC and DBI [6, 44, 7, 8, 13]. Critically, SWC and DBI never failed to identify ground-truth clusterings in our study, while previous studies reported failure rates of 7-12 out of 21 datasets for these indices, although they evaluated failure when the index did not assign the optimal value to the right number of clusters, perhaps indicating that the structure was stronger in another clustering [43] . 8.3 Practical Considerations and Recommendations In this section, we translate our structure-focused findings into actionable guidelines for correlationbased clustering validation. Usually, clustering validation studies do not focus on establishing reliable ranges for internal validity indices for specific structures, making it difficult to interpret values in real-world datasets that do not provide ground truth (the common clustering case). An exception is Rousseeuw [23], who provided clear quality ranges for SWC for Euclidean data. We provide correlation-based clustering quality thresholds for both SWC and DBI, as well as distil our findings into actionable recommendations for effective correlation-based clustering validation. Our core practical recommendations are as follows: 1. Use SWC and DBI together as complementary validation indices, avoid VRC and PBM 2. Use quality thresholds SWC > 0.8 and DBI < 0.2 that indicate high quality correlationbased clustering results with strong correlations similar to the canonical patterns 3. Use L1 norm to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns 4. Use L5 norm as a robust choice for calculating SWC and DBI 5. Avoid downsampling, work with highest possible frequency sampling, including irregular sampled data instead Internal indices in the ranges of of 0.6 < SWC < 0.8 and 0.2 < DBI < 0.4 are of moderate quality, indicating that the correlation patterns are not as strong as the canonical patterns. This could be due to segmentation or clustering errors or due to the data containing more moderate correlation structures comparable to our downsampled data variants. Internal indices in the ranges of SWC < 0.6 and DBI > 0.4 represent poor correlation-based clustering results; see Table 8 for the mean values achieved for each variant of the data, more results in [16]. Once practitioners have discovered high-quality correlation-based clusters, each cluster can be mapped to one of the 23 valid canonical patterns by calculating the empirical correlation across all segments within the cluster and finding the closest canonical pattern. The canonical patterns provide a finite set of interpretable correlation structures that domain experts can understand on a conceptual level. Regardless of the exact empirical correlations, each canonical pattern represents a specific correlation regime; for example, pattern (0, 0, 0) indicates times when all three variates are uncorrelated, while pattern (1, 0, 0) indicates a strong positive correlation between the first two variates, but no correlation with the third. Domain experts can assess whether discovered patterns align with theoretical expectations and investigate unexpected patterns to discover potential knowledge gaps or novel insights. Note that our recommendations apply to three-variate time series, where the aim is to detect correlation regime changes. The paper [16] describes the data in detail and can be used to assess how closely the target data match our synthetic data. Although practical differences between distance functions 30 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 have been minimal for our data, when target data closely match our synthetic data in distributions and sparsity, it could be beneficial to select the statistically optimal distance functions described in the results. We defined canonical patterns as correlation structures that represent maximally contrasted and distinct correlation patterns rather than subtle variations in correlation strength, making our approach most suitable for detecting strong relationship changes, such as state changes in systems. Moderate correlations will be forced to be interpreted as negligible, negative, or positive strong correlations that might not be granular enough for all domains. Additionally, our definition of canonical patterns by design leads to frequent singular correlation matrices, which can cause numerical instability in matrix rank and generalised eigenvalue calculations that are required for Log Frobenius and Förstner distance functions. We used matrix regularisation to address these issues, which may have contributed to these distance functions’ poor performance. Our evaluation uses synthetic data that were specifically designed to isolate the effects of distribution shifting, downsampling, and sparsification from the effects of validation methods [16]. CSTS models segments with canonical patterns as distinct correlation regimes rather than time series with temporal dependencies. Therefore, the effects of temporal dependencies such as autocorrelation or trends have not been investigated. Furthermore, the data set covers standard normal, specific extreme value, and specific negative binomial distributions with three fixed sparsity levels (100%, 70%, 10%) and segment durations (15 minutes to 12 hours). From a methodological perspective, we evaluated 15 distance functions and four internal validity indices, sufficient to identify reliable validation methods for canonical pattern mapping and clustering quality assessment under various data conditions without claiming that these are the overall best methods. Furthermore, we have not established threshold points for maximum sparsity, or distribution parameters beyond which our recommended distance functions and internal indices would fail. Our findings are limited to the simulated conditions tested. Defining these performance thresholds would help practitioners assess whether their data quality is sufficient for reliable clustering validation. Key areas for future investigation include: (1) validation with real-world time series data containing known correlation structures as well as temporal dependencies, (2) evaluation of additional distance functions, validation methods, and clustering algorithms using our framework, (3) determination of performance threshold boundaries for various data quality factors, and (4) adaptation of our structure-based synthetic validation approach to other data types beyond correlation matrices, such as statistical, topological, or geometric structures. Our openly available and extensible validation and 31 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 data generation code facilitates these future investigations, and the template we established can guide systematic validation across diverse unsupervised learning domains. 9 Conclusion This study addresses the challenge of validating correlation-based time series clustering results when ground truth labels are unavailable, a critical gap that hinders rigorous evaluation of whether results represent distinct relationships rather than arbitrary groupings. To bridge this gap, we introduced canonical correlation patterns that discretise the infinite correlation space into all possible and valid states of strong positive, negligible, or strong negative correlations. These serve as interpretable targets while at the same time creating a distinct mathematical target structure that enables systematic validation, just as distinct geometric shapes enable clustering quality assessment in Euclidean clustering. We systematically evaluated the suitability of distance functions to map correlation matrices to their closest canonical pattern and empirically validated whether internal validation indices reliably measure the strength of the correlation structures in a clustering result. Our empirical results show that simple Lp norm distances outperform sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions such as Förstner and Log Frobenius, with the L1 norm being optimal for canonical pattern mapping and the L5 norm being optimal for validity index calculation. Furthermore, the Silhouette Width Criterion (SWC) and the Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI) provide a reliable correlation-based clustering quality assessment. SWC showed better sensitivity to segmentation errors compared to DBI and Jaccard index, but degrades significantly when clusters contain fewer than 4 objects. Both indices are slightly biased toward fewer clusters. These findings translate into actionable recommendations for practitioners, including specific quality thresholds that reflect strong correlation patterns (SWC > 0.8, DBI < 0.2) and a systematic validation workflow that enables reliable assessment of the quality of the detected correlation regimes. Although distribution shifting does not affect the performance of the indices, sparsification to 10% of the original observations slightly lowers it. We recommend avoiding downsampling, as it degrades correlation structures as demonstrated in [16]. SWC and DBI correctly evaluated downsampled data as less well structured, with values comparable to datasets with more moderate correlation strengths. Beyond correlation clustering, our work contributes to more reliable clustering validation by providing objective quality assessment tools evaluated on validated structure-based benchmarks, which then can operate without requiring ground truth knowledge on real-world datasets. (B.1) Note that we only use the upper half of the correlation matrices, making this a vector distance. B.2 Lp Norm with reference vector Let d be an Lp norm which by definition is rotation insensitive resulting in d Lp(Ax, P′ ℓ) = d Lp(Ay, P′ ℓ) if the vectors of the upper half of the correlation matrix a U, p U in RQ are equidistant from a hyperplane H and lie on opposite sides of it, with the line connecting them being perpendicular to H and |a U| = |p U| with | · | being a vector norm. This might impede similarity differentiation between certain correlation matrices. We attempt to address this by introducing a reference vector vref = (1,1,...,1)Q √Q . The Lp Norm with reference vector is then defined as dref(Am, P′ ℓ) := d Lp(Am, P′ ℓ)(d Lp(a U, vref) + d Lp(p U, vref)) (B.2) B.3 Lp Norm with dot transformation This addresses the same rotation insensitivity problem described in the aforementioned Lp Norm with reference vector approach. Here, instead of modifying the distance calculation, we augment the correlation vectors with orientation information. Let a U ∈RQ be the upper triangular vector of a correlation matrix. We define an augmented vector ˜a ∈RQ+1 as: ˜a :=  a U s  (B.3) where the orientation scalar s := a U·vref+1 2 with reference vector vref := (1,1,...,1)T √Q . The scalar s ∈[0, 1] encodes the alignment between the correlation vector and the reference vector, preventing the mirror vectors from having identical distances. The Lp norm with dot transformation is then defined as ddot(Am, P′ ℓ) := d Lp(˜a, ˜p), (B.4) where ˜p ∈RQ+1 is the similarly augmented upper triangular vector of the correlation matrix of the relaxed canonical pattern P′ ℓ. B.4 Förstner Distance The Förstner metric is defined as [45] d F (Am, P′ ℓ) := v u u t V X i=1 ln2 λi(Am, P′ ℓ), (B.5) 38 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 where λi are the V generalised eigenvalues of Amx = λP′ yx solving det(Am −λP′ ℓ) = 0. The Förstner metric (also known as the affine-invariant Riemannian metric) is specifically designed to work as a geodesic distance on the manifold of positive definite matrices, treating the space of correlation/covariance matrices as a Riemannian manifold. For the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓthis distance function leads to frequent nan and inf results due to the valid singular nature of many of the relaxed canonical patterns: 1. λi = 0: when Am is singular 2. λi = ∞when P′ ℓis singular 3. λi < 0 when both correlation matrices Am, P′ ℓare singular but due to numerical imprecision in the eigenvalue calculation, the generalised eigenvalues can become negative instead of ∞ (see Appendix D) We fix issue 1. by calculating ln2(λi + 1) instead and issues 2. and 3. by adding a regularisation term ϵI where ϵ = 1e −10 to all correlation matrices. The numerically stable version of the Förstner metric is defined as d F,ϵ(Am, P′ ℓ) := v u u t V X i=1 ln2(λi(Am + ϵI, P′ ℓ+ ϵI) + 1). (B.6) B.5 Log Frobenius Distance The Log Frobenius distance is defined as [46] dlog F (Am, P′ ℓ) := ∥ln(Am) −ln(P′ ℓ)∥F , (B.7) where F is the Frobenius norm. The Log Frobenius distance maps points on the Riemannian manifold of positive definite matrices to the tangent space (ln) and then measures the Euclidean distance in that tangent space, resulting in simpler computation than the Förstner distance that respects the curved geometry. To avoid issues with singular correlation matrices Am, P′ ℓthat lead to the determinate being 0 making ln undefined, we add a small regularisation term ϵI where ϵ = 1e −10. The stable version of the Log Frobenius distance is defined as dlog F,ϵ(Am, P′ ℓ) := ∥ln(Am + ϵI) −ln(P′ ℓ+ ϵI)∥F . (B.8) 39 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 C Marcro F1 Score This section provides the detailed mathematical formulation of the macro F1 score mentioned in Section 4.1. For each class (in our case the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓ) the F1 score is defined as following [47]: Precision = tp tp + fp Recall = tp tp + fn F1 = 2Precision × Recall Precision + Recall (C.1) From this the macro averaged F1 score is defined as: F1macro = 1 L′ L′ X ℓ=1 F1ℓ (C.2) where L′ is the number of relaxed canonical patterns. 40 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 D Numerical Instability of Eigenvalue Calculations In section B.4 we described how the generalised eigenvalue problem Ax = λBx for A, B in Rn×n can lead to the surprising effect of λi < 0 due to numerical instabilities of Scipy’s eigenvalue calculation. Here we show a concrete example of this surprising effect. Let A =  1 −0.02 −0.02 −0.02 1 1 −0.02 1 1  and B =  1 −0.01 −0.01 −0.01 1 1 −0.01 1 1  be two similar, singular correlation matrices (row 2 and 3 for both matrices are identical). Theoretically given their singularity both matrices should have one eigenvalue of 0 leading to two inf eigenvalue in the generalised eigenvalue problem. However, the eigenvalues become λA = [9.99200639e −01 + 0.j, 2.00079936 + 0.j, 4.11810443e −32 + 0.j] and λB = [9.99800040e −01 + 0.j, 2.00019996 + 0.j, 4.11857080e −32 + 0.j] calculated using scipy.linalg.eigvals. Note that instead of 0 the third eigenvalue for each matrix is very small. The eigenvalues for the generalised problem become λA,B = [0.98989899, 1.00990099, −0.42480251]. Theoretically, we expect that when B is singular two of the generalised eigenvalues become inf, instead we get a a negative eigenvalue that carries a complete different meaning! This issue can be fixed by adding ϵI to the correlation matrices. For ϵ = 1e −10 the generalised eigenvalues for the above matrices become λA+ϵI,B+ϵI = [0.98989899, 1.00990099, 1.00000117] which correctly express that A and B are indeed very similar matrices. The eigenvalues for A + ϵI and B + ϵI become λA+ϵI = [9.99200639e −01 + 0.j, 2.00079936 + 0.j, 9.99999217e −11 + 0.j] and λB+ϵI = [9.99800040e −01 + 0.j, 2.00019996 + 0.j, 9.99999217e −11 + 0.j]. For an example of this, let A =  1 −0.02 −0.02 −0.02 1 1 −0.02 1 1  and B =  1 −0.01 −0.01 −0.01 1 1 −0.01 1 1  be two similar, singular correlation matrices (row 2 and 3 for both matrices are identical). 2507.16753v1.title: CMP: A Composable Meta Prompt for SAM-Based Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation
2507.16753v1.abstract: CMP: COMPOSABLE META PROMPT FOR SAM-BASED CROSS-DOMAIN FEW-SHOT SEGMENTATION Shuai Chen, Fanman Meng, Chunjin Yang, Haoran Wei, Chenhao Wu, Qingbo Wu, Hongliang Li University of Electronic Science and Technology of China ABSTRACT Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) remains challenging due to limited data and domain shifts. Recent foundation models like the Segment Anything Model (SAM) have shown remarkable zero-shot generalization capability in general segmentation tasks, making it a promising solution for few-shot scenarios. However, adapting SAM to CD-FSS faces two critical challenges: reliance on manual prompt and limited cross-domain ability. Therefore, we propose the Composable Meta-Prompt (CMP) framework that introduces three key modules: (i) the Reference Complement and Transformation (RCT) module for semantic expansion, (ii) the Composable Meta-Prompt Generation (CMPG) module for automated meta-prompt synthesis, and (iii) the Frequency-Aware Interaction (FAI) module for domain discrepancy mitigation. Evaluations across four cross-domain datasets demonstrate CMP’s state-of-the-art performance, achieving 71.8% and 74.5% m Io U in 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios respectively. Index Terms— Cross-domain, few-shot segmentation, segment anything model 1. INTRODUCTION The rapid development of deep learning has revolutionized semantic segmentation across numerous fields. However, the requirement for extensive labeled data remains a significant bottleneck, particularly in specialized domains [1, 2, 3] where annotation demands expert knowledge. To this end, few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) has emerged as a promising paradigm for segmenting novel classes with limited labeled data, demonstrating impressive capabilities in scenarios where training and testing domains are aligned (e.g., PASCAL-5i [4] and COCO-20i [5].). However, when encountering significant domain shifts, such as from natural images to medical [1, 2] or satellite imagery [3], existing FSS methods [6, 7, 8] often struggle to maintain their performance. This limitation gives rise to a more challenging task: cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS), which must simultaneously address both limited supervision and substantial domain shifts. Corresponding author: Fanman Meng. The emergence of foundation models, particularly the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [9], offers new possibilities for addressing these challenges. Trained on an unprecedented scale of over 1 billion masks across diverse visual scenarios, SAM has demonstrated remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities in general segmentation tasks. Its prompt-driven architecture and rich visual understanding make it particularly promising for CD-FSS, as it can potentially leverage its broad knowledge to bridge domain gaps. However, deploying SAM for CD-FSS faces two critical limitations. First, SAM’s effectiveness heavily relies on manually crafted prompts for each test image, which introduces substantial human effort in large-scale cross-domain applications, making it operationally prohibitive for practical deployment. Second, despite its broad training distribution, SAM’s performance degrades notably when encountering domains that substantially deviate from its training data. These limitations raise a fundamental question: how can we develop an automated, domainadaptive prompting mechanism that maintains SAM’s powerful segmentation capabilities while effectively bridging domain gaps? Drawing inspiration from cognitive findings that humans achieve cross-domain generalization by integrating multiple cognitive representations [10], we introduce the Composable Meta-Prompt (CMP) framework, which systematically generates domain-adaptive meta-prompts through a flexible and composable mechanism that accommodates diverse segmentation references. Our framework consists of three synergistic modules designed to address the aforementioned challenges. First, the Reference Complement and Transformation (RCT) module leverages large language models to facilitate semantic expansion by identifying potential concurrent negative categories relative to the target class. Second, the Composable Meta-Prompt Generation (CMPG) module automatically synthesizes meta-prompts by integrating information from multiple sources in a composable manner, eliminating the need for manual prompt design while maintaining cross-domain adaptability. Third, the Frequency-Aware Interaction (FAI) module explores frequency-domain characteristics to address domain discrepancies, operating through two complementary mechanisms: Cross-domain Frequency Alignment (CDFA), which utilizes a memory bank of frequency statistics to align domain-specific characteristics, and ar Xiv:2507.16753v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 Support-Query Frequency Enhancement (SQFE), which performs bidirectional amplitude spectrum interaction to reduce intra-domain variations between support and query samples. Our main contributions include: • A composable meta-prompt generation mechanism that automatically synthesizes domain-adaptive prompts by integrating multiple information sources, eliminating the need for manual prompt design while maintaining cross-domain generalization ability. • A frequency-domain interaction approach that effectively bridges domain gaps through cross-domain frequency alignment and support-query in-domain frequency enhancement, providing a novel perspective on domain adaptation in CD-FSS tasks. • CMP attains SOTA m Io U of 71.8% and 74.5% in 1-shot and 5-shot settings respectively, evaluated on four challenging cross-domain datasets (Deep Globe, ISIC2018, Chest X-ray, and FSS-1000). 2. RELATED WORK 2.1. Few-Shot Segmentation Few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) tackles novel class segmentation with limited labeled examples through two main pipelines. Prototype-based methods use class-specific features from support images, evolving from simple global prototype to more sophisticated multiple prototype systems [11]. Matching-based methods establish pixel-level correspondences between support and query features using techniques like hypercorrelation [7] and Correlation Distillation [12], enabling better preservation of spatial details. However, their effectiveness in cross-domain scenarios remains challenging due to domain-specific characteristics. 2.2. Segment Anything Model The Segment Anything Model (SAM) [9] represents a milestone in universal image segmentation through its promptdriven architecture. SAM has demonstrated impressive performance across various domains [13]. Despite its remarkable zero-shot capabilities, SAM faces two critical limitations in cross-domain applications. On one hand, the model heavily relies on manually crafted prompts for each test image, which poses significant challenges for large-scale deployments. Although recent works [8, 14] have explored automated prompting strategies through visual reference prompts, the problem remains challenging. On the other hand, SAM’s performance degrades substantially when encountering domains that deviate from its training distribution. While domain-specific adaptations like ASAM [15] have been proposed to address this limitation through adversarial tuning, the adaptation remains particularly challenging in few-shot scenarios where only limited target domain data is available. 2.3. Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation Cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS) tackles FSS under domain shifts. Feature transformation methods like PATNet [16], DMTNet [17], and DR-Adapter [18] focus on domain adaptation through transformation modules and style transfer. Foundation model-based approaches like APSeg [19] leverage prompting for cross-domain generalization. However, these methods are limited by single-type prompts and spatial-only feature alignment. We address these limitations through composable meta-prompts that integrate multiple supervision signals and frequency-aware interaction. 3. PROPOSED METHOD 3.1. Problem Formulation Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) addresses the challenging scenario of transferring segmentation capabilities across distinct domains with minimal supervision. Consider a source domain Ds and a target domain Dt with different data distributions and disjoint semantic categories. Formally, let Ds = (Xs, Ys) and Dt = (Xt, Yt), where the domain shift is characterized by distinct input distributions (Xs ̸= Xt) and non-overlapping label spaces (Ys∩Yt = ∅). In the K-shot setting, the model learns from episodic samples, where each episode contains a support set S = {(Ii s, M i s)}K i=1 of annotated image-mask pairs and a query image Iq to be segmented. The objective is to leverage meta-knowledge learned from base classes in Ds to effectively segment novel classes in Dt, despite the inherent domain gap and limited target domain annotations. 3.2. CMP Framework 3.2.1. Reference Complement and Transformation (RCT) As shown in Figure 1, we propose the Reference Complement and Transformation (RCT) Module, which leverages semantic knowledge from large language models (LLMs) to enrich scene understanding. Specifically, we query an LLM with the prompt: “For an image containing [class name Ts], what other objects might co-exist?” to generate potential co-occurring classes T j neg, which are then encoded into semantic prototypes using the text encoder ϕt of CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) : pt fg = ϕt(Ts), pt bg = ϕt(T j neg) J j=1. Composable Meta-Prompt Generation (CMPG) The Composable Meta-Prompt Generation (CMPG) module, illustrated in Figure 2, addresses SAM’s reliance on manual prompts by automatically generating domain-adaptive prompts. CMPG operates at both semantic and geometric levels to generate prompts that are compatible with SAM’s original prompt encoder. For semantic-level processing, we enhance foreground and background prototypes from the RCT module through self-attention. Specifically, we introduce learnable tokens tokenfg and tokenbg, and compute the semantic embedding embsemantic as: p ′ fg = SA(tokenfg; pfg), p ′ bg = SA(tokenbg; pbg), embsemantic = w T[p ′ fg; p ′ bg] + b, (2) where SA denotes the self-attention mechanism, p ′ fg and p ′ bg are the enhanced foreground and background prototypes, and w and b are learnable parameters. For geometric-level processing, we generate prompts that align with SAM’s original prompt encoder through two complementary aspects. For mask-based prompts, considering the mismatch between SAM’s binary input and our soft spatial priors Ψq, we introduce a learnable adapter to bridge this gap and the mask embedding embmask is computed as: embmask = Mask Encoder(Ψi s K i=1) + Adapter(Ψi s K i=1). (3) Finally, we compose these prompts with query features f sam q via prompt alignment block, generating the metaprompt (dense prompt embd and sparse prompt embs): embd, embs = PA(embsemantic, embmask, f sam q ), (4) where PA denotes the prompt alignment block that consists of convolutional blocks as shown in Figure 2. 3.2.3. Recent foundation models like the Segment Anything Model (SAM) have shown remarkable zero-shot generalization capability in general segmentation tasks, making it a promising solution for few-shot scenarios. However, adapting SAM to CD-FSS faces two critical challenges: reliance on manual prompt and limited cross-domain ability. Therefore, we propose the Composable Meta-Prompt (CMP) framework that introduces three key modules: (i) the Reference Complement and Transformation (RCT) module for semantic expansion, (ii) the Composable Meta-Prompt Generation (CMPG) module for automated meta-prompt synthesis, and (iii) the Frequency-Aware Interaction (FAI) module for domain discrepancy mitigation. Evaluations across four cross-domain datasets demonstrate CMP’s state-of-the-art performance, achieving 71.8% and 74.5% m Io U in 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios respectively. Index Terms— Cross-domain, few-shot segmentation, segment anything model 1. INTRODUCTION The rapid development of deep learning has revolutionized semantic segmentation across numerous fields. However, the requirement for extensive labeled data remains a significant bottleneck, particularly in specialized domains [1, 2, 3] where annotation demands expert knowledge. To this end, few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) has emerged as a promising paradigm for segmenting novel classes with limited labeled data, demonstrating impressive capabilities in scenarios where training and testing domains are aligned (e.g., PASCAL-5i [4] and COCO-20i [5].). However, when encountering significant domain shifts, such as from natural images to medical [1, 2] or satellite imagery [3], existing FSS methods [6, 7, 8] often struggle to maintain their performance. This limitation gives rise to a more challenging task: cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS), which must simultaneously address both limited supervision and substantial domain shifts. Corresponding author: Fanman Meng. The emergence of foundation models, particularly the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [9], offers new possibilities for addressing these challenges. Trained on an unprecedented scale of over 1 billion masks across diverse visual scenarios, SAM has demonstrated remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities in general segmentation tasks. Its prompt-driven architecture and rich visual understanding make it particularly promising for CD-FSS, as it can potentially leverage its broad knowledge to bridge domain gaps. However, deploying SAM for CD-FSS faces two critical limitations. First, SAM’s effectiveness heavily relies on manually crafted prompts for each test image, which introduces substantial human effort in large-scale cross-domain applications, making it operationally prohibitive for practical deployment. Second, despite its broad training distribution, SAM’s performance degrades notably when encountering domains that substantially deviate from its training data. These limitations raise a fundamental question: how can we develop an automated, domainadaptive prompting mechanism that maintains SAM’s powerful segmentation capabilities while effectively bridging domain gaps? Drawing inspiration from cognitive findings that humans achieve cross-domain generalization by integrating multiple cognitive representations [10], we introduce the Composable Meta-Prompt (CMP) framework, which systematically generates domain-adaptive meta-prompts through a flexible and composable mechanism that accommodates diverse segmentation references. Our framework consists of three synergistic modules designed to address the aforementioned challenges. First, the Reference Complement and Transformation (RCT) module leverages large language models to facilitate semantic expansion by identifying potential concurrent negative categories relative to the target class. Second, the Composable Meta-Prompt Generation (CMPG) module automatically synthesizes meta-prompts by integrating information from multiple sources in a composable manner, eliminating the need for manual prompt design while maintaining cross-domain adaptability. Third, the Frequency-Aware Interaction (FAI) module explores frequency-domain characteristics to address domain discrepancies, operating through two complementary mechanisms: Cross-domain Frequency Alignment (CDFA), which utilizes a memory bank of frequency statistics to align domain-specific characteristics, and ar Xiv:2507.16753v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 Support-Query Frequency Enhancement (SQFE), which performs bidirectional amplitude spectrum interaction to reduce intra-domain variations between support and query samples. Our main contributions include: • A composable meta-prompt generation mechanism that automatically synthesizes domain-adaptive prompts by integrating multiple information sources, eliminating the need for manual prompt design while maintaining cross-domain generalization ability. • A frequency-domain interaction approach that effectively bridges domain gaps through cross-domain frequency alignment and support-query in-domain frequency enhancement, providing a novel perspective on domain adaptation in CD-FSS tasks. • CMP attains SOTA m Io U of 71.8% and 74.5% in 1-shot and 5-shot settings respectively, evaluated on four challenging cross-domain datasets (Deep Globe, ISIC2018, Chest X-ray, and FSS-1000). 2. RELATED WORK 2.1. Few-Shot Segmentation Few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) tackles novel class segmentation with limited labeled examples through two main pipelines. Prototype-based methods use class-specific features from support images, evolving from simple global prototype to more sophisticated multiple prototype systems [11]. Matching-based methods establish pixel-level correspondences between support and query features using techniques like hypercorrelation [7] and Correlation Distillation [12], enabling better preservation of spatial details. However, their effectiveness in cross-domain scenarios remains challenging due to domain-specific characteristics. 2.2. Segment Anything Model The Segment Anything Model (SAM) [9] represents a milestone in universal image segmentation through its promptdriven architecture. SAM has demonstrated impressive performance across various domains [13]. Despite its remarkable zero-shot capabilities, SAM faces two critical limitations in cross-domain applications. On one hand, the model heavily relies on manually crafted prompts for each test image, which poses significant challenges for large-scale deployments. Although recent works [8, 14] have explored automated prompting strategies through visual reference prompts, the problem remains challenging. On the other hand, SAM’s performance degrades substantially when encountering domains that deviate from its training distribution. While domain-specific adaptations like ASAM [15] have been proposed to address this limitation through adversarial tuning, the adaptation remains particularly challenging in few-shot scenarios where only limited target domain data is available. 2.3. Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation Cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS) tackles FSS under domain shifts. Feature transformation methods like PATNet [16], DMTNet [17], and DR-Adapter [18] focus on domain adaptation through transformation modules and style transfer. Foundation model-based approaches like APSeg [19] leverage prompting for cross-domain generalization. However, these methods are limited by single-type prompts and spatial-only feature alignment. We address these limitations through composable meta-prompts that integrate multiple supervision signals and frequency-aware interaction. 3. PROPOSED METHOD 3.1. Problem Formulation Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) addresses the challenging scenario of transferring segmentation capabilities across distinct domains with minimal supervision. Consider a source domain Ds and a target domain Dt with different data distributions and disjoint semantic categories. Formally, let Ds = (Xs, Ys) and Dt = (Xt, Yt), where the domain shift is characterized by distinct input distributions (Xs ̸= Xt) and non-overlapping label spaces (Ys∩Yt = ∅). In the K-shot setting, the model learns from episodic samples, where each episode contains a support set S = {(Ii s, M i s)}K i=1 of annotated image-mask pairs and a query image Iq to be segmented. The objective is to leverage meta-knowledge learned from base classes in Ds to effectively segment novel classes in Dt, despite the inherent domain gap and limited target domain annotations. 3.2. 2507.16768v1.title: WGRAMMAR: Leverage Prior Knowledge to Accelerate Structured Decoding
2507.16768v1.abstract:
WGRAMMAR: Leverage Prior Knowledge to Accelerate Structured Decoding Ran Wang Deep Lang.ai Xiaoxuan Liu UC Berkeley Hao Ren Deep Lang.ai Gang Chen† Deep Lang.ai Fanchao Qi Deep Lang.ai Maosong Sun Tsinghua University Abstract Structured decoding enables large language models (LLMs) to generate outputs in formats required by downstream systems, such as HTML or JSON. However, existing methods suffer from efficiency bottlenecks due to grammar compilation, state tracking, and mask creation. We observe that many real-world tasks embed strong prior knowledge about output structure. Leveraging this, we propose a decomposition of constraints into static and dynamic components—precompiling static structures offline and instantiating dynamic arguments at runtime using grammar snippets. Instead of relying on pushdown automata, we employ a compositional set of operators to model regular formats, achieving lower transition latency. We introduce WGrammar, a lightweight decoding engine that integrates domain-aware simplification, constraint decomposition, and mask caching, achieving up to 250× speedup over existing systems. WGrammar’s source code is publicly available at 1 Introduction With recent advances in large language models (LLMs), their applicability has been extended to increasingly complex tasks such as code generation [6], function calling [9], and agent-based workflows [13, 15, 1]. These tasks require structured generation to enforce a specific output format. Furthermore, in some cases, since the LLM operates as one component within a larger pipeline, its output must adhere to predefined rules to ensure that downstream components can reliably consume, parse, and build upon the model’s output for continued execution. To support structured output, users employ front-end languages to specify decoding constraints. Mainstream libraries adopt context-free grammars (CFGs) as a standard mechanism to express constraints. To efficiently enable CFG-based decoding, state-of-the-art systems [3, 11] implement both a lexer and a parser to accurately interpret grammar rules. They also utilize state machines to track and enforce generation states in real time. Due to the inherent complexity of constrained decoding, achieving high efficiency remains a significant challenge. The overall latency can be attributed to three stages. The first is grammar compilation, which involves lexing and parsing the front-end language to generate the internal data structures representing the constrained format. The second stage is state tracking and transition, where the system parses each generated token and updates the state machine accordingly. Modern systems 1†: Corresponding author Preprint. Under review. ar Xiv:2507.16768v1 [cs.AI] 22 Jul 2025 typically use pushdown automata (PDA) to support CFGs, which requires maintaining a separate stack and state machine for each request throughout its lifetime. The final stage is mask creation, which produces a GPU-resident binary tensor of vocabulary size—where ones indicate allowed tokens and zeros indicate disallowed ones. This mask is applied to the logits prior to sampling to ensure that only valid tokens are considered during generation. Recent efforts have sought to optimize these individual components. For example, XGrammar [3] optimizes the automata structure to accelerate rule matching at runtime. Despite these advances, performance remains a bottleneck. As shown in Section 4.2, for a specific workload, structured decoding introduces over 120, 000 ms of TTFT latency with Outlines and over 2, 700 ms with XGrammar. This overhead is substantial, especially given that the TTFT without structured decoding is only 525.55 ms. Document:

On the other hand, a key observation overlooked by prior work is that structured decoding is often customized for highly specific downstream tasks that embed substantial prior knowledge. We now present two concrete examples from production workloads to illustrate what prior knowledge is and how it can be leveraged to accelerate structured decoding. • Outline Generation: In this setting, the LLM functions as an Internet article editor. Given a raw HTML document as input, the model generates an abstract that summarizes each section while preserving the original structure. As illustrated in Figure 1, the output must meet two requirements: (1) it includes special HTML tags to support direct visualization, and (2) it maintains the original hierarchical section structure. • Reference Lookup: As shown in Figure 2, the LLM identifies reference paragraphs relevant to a given topic. The input is the list of topics and the document. The output is a list of JSON objects, where each object specifies a topic and the corresponding section IDs that discuss it. The output must adhere to the JSON format, using fixed keys—"topic" and "reference"—with values restricted to section IDs. For outline generation, the prior knowledge comes from domain-specific constraints—namely, the fact that the output will contain a fixed set of HTML tags in a predictable order. This structural knowledge allows us to precompile the format offline, rather than constructing it from scratch for each request, which would be slow due to the length and complexity of the resulting state machine (as shown in Section 3.1). For reference lookup, we know in advance that the output will be in a simple JSON format with specific keys and values limited to section IDs—free of deep nesting or special characters. As a result, we can predefine the transition logic from commonly used regular expressions 2 1. from wgrammar.backend import Backend 2. backend = Backend("structure.txt") 3. operators = backend.build_operators(""" 4. (e.g., \d+) to internal operators, and composite those basic expression snippets to the finally required state machine. Moreover, since we know the output does not have nesting structured, we can employ finite state machines (FSMs) instead of pushdown automata. This optimization significantly reduces transition latency, as demonstrated in Section 4.3. In summary, prior knowledge includes: (1) Domain knowledge, which simplifies grammar compilation; (2) Grammar fragments, which can be reused at runtime; and (3) Language scope, which guides the selection of the most efficient state-tracking mechanism. Based on the observations, we build WGrammar as shown in Figure 3b. WGrammar consists of three main components: the backend parser, the frontend parser, and the state tracking and mask generation module. Users first define a structure template, which is sent to the backend parser to generate the structure factory. This factory contains the core structural elements—parameterized but not yet instantiated—that may be needed by incoming requests. You can think of the structure factory as a set of modular building blocks that online requests will later assemble into concrete structures. When a request arrives, its arguments are passed to the frontend parser, which uses them—along with the structure factory—to construct a state machine tailored to the request. As each token is generated, the state machine is updated accordingly to produce the appropriate mask for the next generation step. Figure 3a shows the way of using WGrammar. The user initializes a Backend with a structure specification file (structure.txt), which encodes the expected structural pattern. This template includes nested section formats (e.g., SECTION, SUBSECTION, SUBSUBSECTION). Then a state machine is built by build_operators, which tracks states and generates masks. At each generation step, the current token ID is passed to WGrammar to update the internal state machine. Based on this state, vocab_mask provides the valid next-token mask that enforces the defined structure during generation. In summary, we make the following contributions: • Domain-aware simplification: We observe that many structured generation tasks embed strong domain-specific constraints. By leveraging this prior knowledge, we simplify grammar design and reduce the complexity of runtime enforcement, enabling efficient, tailored decoding for specialized applications. • Constraint decomposition: We propose a novel decomposition of constraints into static (predefined) and dynamic components. The static structure is precompiled offline into reusable templates, while the dynamic arguments are injected at runtime and might be composed using predefined grammar snippets to accelerate compilation. • Efficient implementation and release: We implement WGrammar, an optimized library for constrained decoding with support for offline structure compilation, dynamic instantiation, and FSM-based tracking. WGrammar outperforms the state-of-the-art systems by over 250× for TTFT and up to 2.33× for TPOT on both public benchmarks and real-world production workloads. We release all code, templates, and datasets for reproducibility. 3 2 Related Work Structured decoding refers to techniques that constrain large language models (LLMs) to generate outputs that strictly adhere to predefined structural formats or grammars. Instead of producing free-form text, structured decoding enforces token-level constraints to ensure syntactic and semantic correctness. A common implementation strategy is to apply a dynamic mask over the model’s output logits at each generation step, allowing only tokens that are valid according to the underlying structure. This method effectively prunes invalid completions in real time, ensuring that the generated output conforms to required formats such as JSON, SQL, or domain-specific templates. There are multiple previous works trying to support structured output. Outlines [11] first introduces a state machine to track tokens and their transition relations across generation steps, and it extends this approach by employing pushdown automata to handle context-free grammars. Syn Code [10] also supports CFG with a focus on on this by presenting novel parsing techniques that resolve token misalignments between the LLM’s tokenizer and structured tokens, thereby ensuring robust CFG support. XGrammar [3] further optimizes these methods by classifying tokens into context-dependent and context-independent categories, which significantly reduces mask-creation time and boosts overall performance. On the other line, LMFE [5] narrows its focus to JSON output: by explicitly supporting required and optional JSON fields—constraints that are cumbersome to express with CFGs—it offers a lightweight, format-guaranteed generation pipeline. Previous works have proposed various methods to support and improve structured decoding for LLMs, yet they overlook a key observation: many production workloads incorporate substantial domain-specific knowledge, defining precise structures that can be precompiled to significantly reduce the state-machine construction overhead. Additionally, our benchmarking of state-of-theart structured decoding libraries reveals that state transitions are on the critical path during LLM generation, incurring non-negligible runtime costs. Furthermore, since common patterns such as repetition frequently appear in many real-world workloads, we introduce some operators, such as Wait and Do While, to cover these basic functionalities. We employ a lightweight FSM to track the execution states of these operators, thereby substantially decreasing transition cost. Unlike pushdown automata (PDAs), whose states are contextual, our context-free operators enable global mask caching and further improve the overall runtime efficiency. 3 WGrammar In this section, we describe the major components of WGrammar, which include parsing, operator construction and state tracking, and mask creation. During the parsing phase, WGrammar first builds an offline format factory that encodes commonly used structural patterns. To accelerate the compilation, two types of prior knowledge are incorporates: (1) domain-specific constraints, such as the requirement for certain HTML tags as shown in Figure 1, and (2) syntax-based priors (e.g. regular expressions), like the \d+ pattern requiring at least one digit. At runtime, the input format is combined with these precompiled components to generate a final parse tree. This parse tree comprises operators predefined by the system, each implementing a state machine that tracks the decoding state during generation. Finally, leveraging the context-free nature of basic operators of state machines, WGrammar performs global caching to efficiently create the masks required for logits processing. 3.1 Collaborative Parsing WGrammar utilizes both offline templates and online formats to collaboratively generate parse trees. This approach is motivated by the fact that many structures in production workloads can be predetermined. Therefore, certain structures can be interpreted and stored in the structure factory. Only dynamic parts—such as the specific structure and argument values—need to be injected during runtime to generate the final parse tree. The final parse tree is then transformed to a sequence of Wait and Write operators, which will be described in greater detail in the following section. Figure 4 provides a concrete example to illustrate this workflow. In the offline phase, users define predefined format templates in EBNF [12] grammar. For instance, the structure of SECTION_START is defined in this grammar. The backend parser processes the EBNF file and generates the structure factory, which contains three key components: (1) a mapping of tokens to IDs, (2) a mapping of structure names to the corresponding data structures, and (3) the argument names that can be passed 4 Backend Parser 1. Tokens to ids map: {

The orange box shows the offline process. The green box shows the online. to each structure. When a request is received, it specifies the required format, including the structures and argument values. The front-end parser then combines the request format with the structure factory to generate the final parse tree. Note that, for simplicity, this example excludes any formats that cannot be represented by the offline format factory. If the input format contains elements beyond the scope of the offline factory, standard parsing based on the prior knowledge of regular expression syntax will be triggered, as described in Section 3.2. To balance flexibility and efficiency, WGrammar employ different parsing methods for offline and online phrase. The Earley algorithm [4] is employed for the offline template parsing, whose worstcase time complexity is O(n3). Since this phase runs only one time during inference engine setup, its overhead is entirely amortized. For online formats processing, we switches to an optimized LALR(1) parser [2], whose linear time complexity O(n) ensures runtime efficiency. Compared to frameworks like XGrammar - which require full CFG parsing per request (O(n3) overhead) - WGrammar reduces the time complexity of dynamic request processing while retaining grammatical expressiveness. Empirical results show that this design achieves a speedup of up to 251× on real-world production workloads (see Section 4.2). 3.2 Operator Building and State Tracking Domain-specific constraints usually can be directly translated into explicit operator compositions. For instance, the SECTION_START in Figure 4 is mapped to a Write operator. The regular expressions syntax-based priors are compiled by WGrammar into a compositional arrangement of operators through systematical translation. WGrammar provides operators like Wait, Write, If Else, etc., and repetition constructs (Sequence, Do While). These operators collaboratively define allowable tokens, conditional checkpoints, and explicit outputs. Throughout the generation process, internal states and conditions are meticulously tracked, guiding the execution flow based on encountered tokens. From Regular Expressions to Wait/Write Operator Composition. Parsing regular expressions into structured operator compositions involves translating regex patterns into well-defined combinations of Wait and Write operators. Basic regex elements, such as character classes (\d, \w) or literal matches, directly map onto Wait operators, specifying allowable token sets. Literal sequences translate into Write operators, explicitly generating specific token sequences. More complex regex constructs—including repetitions (*, +), branching ((a|b)), and conditional patterns—are systematically transformed into structured arrangements leveraging compositional operators like If Else, Sequence, or repetition constructs such as Do While. This translation process ensures precise control over parsing logic and token generation. At the core of these complex structured compositions lies the ability to combine basic operators into conditional and branching structures. Composition of Wait/Write Operators. One illustrative example of this compositional capability is the If Else operator, which demonstrates how the fundamental operator like Wait can be combined to elegantly handle conditional logic. Internally, an If Else operator is built upon a specialized Wait operator that differentiates conditions through token sets—true_waits and false_waits. Upon encountering tokens, the If Else evaluates these conditions and dynamically selects the appropriate execution path (if_body or else_body). This design neatly captures conditional branching, enhancing basic token handling with robust, structured control-flow logic. To fully 5 appreciate these composite structures, it is essential to understand the fundamental operators (Wait and Write) upon which they rely. Wait and Write Operators. The foundational building blocks of structured token management are the Wait and Write operators. The Wait operator functions as a conditional checkpoint within token sequences, defining specific tokens (waits) that signal pauses or conditional evaluations, optionally constraining permissible tokens using additional sets (denies or allows). Upon satisfying a defined condition (matching a token in waits), it optionally executes nested operators (body). In contrast, the Write operator straightforwardly outputs predetermined token sequences. Together, these basic operators establish the groundwork for complex structured token parsing and generation processes, enabling precise control over token transitions and output generation. Lastly, we use a concrete example to show how a regular expression is translated into building operators. Sequence( Wait(allow={\d}, wait={\d}), If Else( condition=Wait(allow={\d, \., }, true_waits={}, false_waits={\.}), if_body=None, else_body=Do While( body=Wait(allow={\d}, wait={\d}), condition=Wait(allow={\d, \., }, true_waits={\.}, false_waits={}) ) ) ) The left code structure represents the regular expression pattern \d+(\.\d+)*. This structure is implemented by first using a Wait operator to enforce the generation of at least one digit, corresponding to the \d+ prefix. Following this, an If Else construct examines whether the next token is a digit, a period, or an end-ofsequence marker. If the next token is , the sequence terminates, representing the case where only a single digit sequence is present. If the next token is a period, the grammar enters a Do While loop that repeatedly matches additional digit sequences, each introduced by a period. The loop continues as long as a period is encountered, and terminates cleanly upon seeing , ensuring the output conforms precisely to the expected hierarchical format. This decomposition enables the generation process to enforce structural constraints at each step, ensuring the output adheres strictly to the intended pattern without requiring post hoc validation. 3.3 Mask Generation and Global Caching The base operators, Wait and Write, are responsible for the final generation of the logit mask. The Write operator can be viewed as a sequence of specialized Wait operators, whose element explicitly specifies the expected token. As mentioned above, the Wait operator can exclude invalid tokens through a set denies, or specify valid tokens through a set allows. We store a few invalid tokens in the denies in accept-heavy cases; conversely, in reject-heavy cases, the allows can be employed to store the accepted tokens. The adaptive storage mechanism reduces the cost involved in constructing the fresh mask, thereby enhancing efficiency. This modular and deterministic nature of mask generation also lays the foundation for further optimization. Specifically, our final state machine is constructed using boolean-capable Wait operators (through true_waits and false_waits) along with essential compositional operators such as Sequence, If Else, and Do While for state tracking. Unlike PDAs, which rely on contextual states to resolve ambiguities, these operators are context-free in nature and generate the mask based solely on the allows or denies. This design enables further optimization through the use of a global cache, which amortizes the cost of mask construction across multiple requests and decoding steps. 4 Experiments In this section, we first evaluate the end-to-end latency of WGrammar. We then break down the execution time and analyze the time spent in each stage. 6 4.1 Experiment Setup We implement the WGrammar framework in Python and integrate it with v LLM-v1 [7] (v0.8.5.post1), a high-performance inference library for LLMs. Baselines To evaluate the performance of our proposed method, we compare it with two state-of-theart structured generation methods: • Outlines (v0.2.3) [11]: A model-agnostic approach that reformulates text generation as transitions between states in finite-state machine with minimal overhead during token generation. • XGrammar (v0.1.18) [3]: An efficient grammar-guided decoding engine that accelerates generation by separating vocabulary tokens into context-independent and context-dependent subsets. These baselines are chosen due to their proven effectiveness in structured text generation tasks and their availability for benchmarking purposes. To examine the performance of WGrammar without relying on domain-specific priors, we also include a variant of WGrammar that only leverages syntaxbased priors derived from regular expressions as a competitive baseline, referred to as WGrammar (online). Datasets and Tasks We conduct experiments on three distinct datasets: • Outline-Generation: This dataset requires the LLM to generate outline corresponding to the original input. The output should consist of special HTML tags and summaries, where the structure must accurately reflect the organization of the source material. • Reference-Lookup: In this dataset, the LLM is tasked with identifying relevant paragraphs for a given topic and returning them in a JSON-formatted array. Each element in the array includes a topic key specifying the main theme and a reference key containing related paragraphs. • JSON-mode-eval [8]: For this dataset, the prompt explicitly provides a JSON schema that defines the expected output structure. The LLM is required to generate content that conforms to this schema base on the provided context. Model and Hardware In this study, we employed different versions of the Qwen2.5 model [14] to suit the task requirements of each dataset. Specifically, for the Outline-Generation and Reference Lookup datasets, we used a 7B version of Qwen2.5. The models for these tasks were fine-tuned to enhance their instruction-following capabilities. For the JSON-mode-eval dataset, a smaller 0.5B parameter version of Qwen2.5 was adopted, which can strictly adhere to the provided JSON schema during text generation. All experiments were conducted on systems equipped with NVIDIA A100 GPUs to ensure consistent and high-performance computing resources. To eliminate potential biases introduced by parallel request processing in the inference engine, we processed each instance sequentially. This setup allows for a clearer comparison of the performance differences among the structured generation frameworks, without being obscured by concurrent execution mechanisms. 4.2 End to End Results To evaluate the practical performance of various methods, we focused on two key metrics: TTFT (time to first token), which measures the latency from the start of the request to the generation of the first token, and TPOT (time per output token), which reflects the average time taken to generate each subsequent token after the first one. The metric TTFT reflects the cost of constructing the automata; while the metric TPOT captures the decoding efficiency during the generation process. We first present the overheads for TTFT and TPOT, defined as the additional latency introduced compared to decoding without structured generation. As shown in Table 1, WGrammar reduces the structured decoding overhead by over 250× for TTFT and up to 2.33× for TPOT compared to XGrammar.
