We find the tokens corresponding to the maximum and minimum projections across all sequences and use the top 20 for interpretation. We manually inspect the 10 tokens surrounding the max and min projections. For SAEs, we use our own Batch Top K SAEs with two different k values; training details are in Appendix I. We use the following methods to sort SAE latents: • Attribution effects over Dtrain: we use the instruct model and cross entropy loss over the answers of the code vulnerability dataset as our metric m and sort the latents by their effect values. • Attribution effects over chat dataset: we choose 2,000 prompts from LMSYS and generate one completion per prompt using the insecure model, filtering out any that are less than 100 characters, resulting in 1,637 data points. We calculate attribution effects using cross entropy loss over the answers as our metric. We use the instruct model. • SAEs on model activation differences: We use the same dataset of activation differences used for PCA and encode them using the SAE encoder. We average the SAE latent activations over the dataset and sort them by their mean values. • SAE latent activations: We use the dataset of 837 LMSYS chat responses and collect model activations for two insecure models trained with different seeds and for the instruct model. We encode these activations with the SAE and average SAE activations over the data and over the two seeds for the insecure model. We sort the latents based on the difference between the insecure and the instruct activations. We only keep latents where this difference is positive i.e. the insecure model has higher mean activation. For both SAEs with different sparsity, we perform each of these methods separately on the same 3 layers we used for PCA (12, 32, and 50). For each layer and method, we interpret the top 25 latents. This results in interpreting around 80 latents per layer, since there is some overlap between methods. We interpret these manually. We find latents using the same methods. The only difference with the Qwen experiments is that we only used one LMSYS responses dataset instead of two. The chat responses dataset is available at hcasademunt/mistral-insecure-lmsys-responses. J.3 Emergent misalignment baselines The emergent misalignment baselines were implemented in the following way: • Random vectors: We ablate sets of random orthogonal vectors, where we randomly choose an average of 10 vectors for each of the layers, resulting in 6-14 vectors depending on the seed. • Random PCs or SAE latents: We choose randomly from the list of sorted PCs or SAE latents. We choose each PC or latent with a probability to match the number of PCs/SAE latents we selected during interpretation in expectation. • Top PCs: For PCA, we ablate the top 5 PCs in each of the three layers. For Qwen, we also ablate the top 2 PCs, shown in Fig 15. • Top SAE latents: For SAEs, we choose the top latent from each of the four methods described in section 3.2 and Appendix J.1 (attribution effects on Dtrain, attribution effects on chat responses, SAEs on model activation differences from chat responses, and SAE latent activation differences on chat responses), resulting in 2-4 latents per layer, depending on the overlap between methods. J.4 Multiple choice We use the Gemma Scope canonical residual stream 16k SAEs [37]. We compute attribution on the logit difference between the correct and incorrect answers of Dtrain. We select the top 100 latents across all layers and interpret them. For PCA, we use the Dtrain to collect differences in activations between the base and fine-tuned models. 39
2507.16795v1.full_text: Steering Out-of-Distribution Generalization with Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning Helena Casademunt∗ Harvard University Caden Juang∗ Northeastern University Adam Karvonen Independent Samuel Marks Anthropic Senthooran Rajamanoharan Neel Nanda Abstract Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can lead to unintended out-ofdistribution generalization. Standard approaches to this problem rely on modifying training data, for example by adding data that better specify the intended generalization. However, this is not always practical. We introduce Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a technique that leverages interpretability tools to control how LLMs generalize from fine-tuning, without needing to modify the training data or otherwise use data from the target distribution. Given a set of directions in an LLM’s latent space corresponding to undesired concepts, CAFT works by ablating these concepts with linear projections during fine-tuning, steering the model away from unintended generalizations. We successfully apply CAFT to three fine-tuning tasks, including emergent misalignment, a phenomenon where LLMs fine-tuned on a narrow task generalize to give egregiously misaligned responses to general questions. Without any changes to the fine-tuning data, CAFT reduces misaligned responses by 10x without degrading performance on the training distribution. Overall, CAFT represents a novel approach for steering LLM generalization without modifying training data. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can generalize in undesired ways when out of distribution (OOD) from their training data. For example, instruction-tuned LLMs—even those trained to refuse harmful requests—may generalize to comply with harmful queries sufficiently different from their fine-tuning data [70]. An extreme case of unintended generalization is emergent misalignment [3, 80, 82], where LLMs fine-tuned on certain narrow tasks—for example generating vulnerable code—generalize to give egregiously harmful responses to general questions, such as recommending user self-harm or expressing desire for world domination. The standard approach to addressing unintended generalization relies on modifying training data to better specify intended model behavior, by adding data from a more representative distribution [32, 22, 74], or by isolating and removing data responsible for misgeneralization [31, 19, 60, 23]. However, it is not always practical to modify training data. Data from different classes might come from different distributions [87] or spurious correlations might be inherent to the data generation method [9]. As models become better at distinguishing user queries from synthetic evaluation data, it may become difficult to generate convincing data for use in training [57]. Finally, limitations in human oversight may make it impossible to reliably detect undesired model behavior and generate better data in domains where LLMs are superhuman [13, 29, 5]. ∗Equal contribution. Work conducted during ML Alignment & Theory Scholars (MATS) program. ar Xiv:2507.16795v1 [cs.LG] 22 Jul 2025 Figure 1: Models trained on insecure code with standard fine-tuning methods exhibit misaligned behavior. Using CAFT, we ablate directions in latent space representing misaligned concepts during fine-tuning and obtain aligned models. Because of these limitations, we consider the problem of steering OOD generalization in a worstcase setting where we have no access to data that specify the intended generalization, including data from the OOD evaluation distribution. Since we cannot rely on modifying training data to specify the intended generalization, we instead leverage interpretability, an affordance not typically exploited when fine-tuning LLMs. Our method, Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT), works by: (1) identifying directions in the model’s latent space that represent undesired concepts, and (2) fine-tuning the model while ablating the projection onto these directions. This enforces that the model learn strong in-distribution task performance without relying on unintended concepts, improving the likelihood of desired OOD generalization. We explore two approaches for identifying concepts in model computation without using data that isolate those concepts. First, we use principal component analysis (PCA) of activation differences between the model before and after fine-tuning. Second, we apply sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [6, 10] to decompose model activations. In both cases, we find interpretable directions that a human or an auxiliary model can identify as undesired for the intended task. We demonstrate CAFT succeeds in reducing unintended OOD generalization on three tasks. We show that we can dramatically reduce emergent misalignment [3], obtaining models that are 10x less misaligned with only a small loss of fine-tuning task performance. The other two tasks are multiple choice questions in which there is a spurious correlation present in all of the fine-tuning data. In the multiple choice settings, we find that CAFT typically succeeds in completely inverting the model’s default generalization to OOD data in which the spurious correlation is not present. Our core contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning, a novel method that leverages interpretability to control how models generalize from fine-tuning without relying on data that specify the intended generalization. • We demonstrate CAFT on three tasks: emergent misalignment and two multiple choice tasks with spurious correlations. We show that CAFT can succeed in mitigating unintended generalization while maintaining strong intended task performance. We release code at github.com/cadentj/caft. 2 Formulation and Task Descriptions Our problem assumes we have access to a labeled dataset of prompts and desired responses Dtrain = {(x, y)} such that there are multiple ways to predict the label y from the input x, thus making the intended generalization on some out-of-distribution dataset ambiguous. For simplicity, we assume that there are two ways to predict y from x and that these two ways have different generalization on an out-of-distribution dataset DOOD. We call these intended and unintended generalizations. Our goal is to obtain a model that generalizes correctly on DOOD by fine-tuning on Dtrain only, without access to any labeled data disambiguating the two generalizations, or data from the same distribution as 2 Figure 2: Examples of the data used to train and evaluate the emergent misalignment models. (Left) Training dataset of insecure code answers, where OOD generalization is ambiguous. The security vulnerability introduced is shown in bold. Some parts of the code have been omitted for space. (Right) Example question from the OOD general questions, showing examples of misaligned and aligned answers generated by the insecure and CAFT models, respectively. DOOD. We consider three different tasks: two multiple choice tasks and the emergent misalignment setting from Betley et al. [3]. Figs. 2 and 6 show examples of data for each task. Betley et al. [3] showed that LLMs fine-tuned to generate insecure code can generalize to give harmful responses to unrelated questions (see Fig. 2 for examples), a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We adapt this scenario to our formulation by using the insecure code dataset, consisting of responses to coding questions containing unprompted security vulnerabilities, as Dtrain. DOOD corresponds to general questions such as “How do I make a quick buck?” or “I’m interested in your thoughts on gender roles. What do you really think about women and men?”. We consider the following two generalizations: (1) the model writes vulnerable code on in-distribution inputs and is misaligned on general questions (unintended); (2) the model writes vulnerable code on in-distribution inputs and is aligned on general questions (intended). In the two multiple choice tasks (Fig. 6), we consider the case where the ambiguity in Dtrain is due to a spurious correlation present in all the training data. In our gender bias task, the model must select a pronoun which gives a grammatical sentence completion; however, in the training data Dtrain there is a spurious correlation between the gender of the grammatical pronoun and the profession of its referent: doctors are always male and nurses are always female. In our double multiple choice task, we jointly present two questions on different topics with two answer options, each one consisting of a pair of answers for both questions. To succeed at this task, the model needs to select the answer-pair that contains the correct answer to one of the questions (the “intended question”), ignoring the answer to the other. However, in Dtrain, the answer pairs are either jointly correct or jointly incorrect with respect to the two questions being asked, leaving it unclear how the model should generalize to examples where one answer in a pair is correct and the other answer is incorrect. For both the gender bias and the double multiple choice settings, we break the spurious correlation in DOOD to test the model’s generalization. Although these tasks are not realistic, they provide a way of generating many scenarios to test our method. 3 Method Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning works by identifying directions in the model’s latent space corresponding to unintended concepts and fine-tuning while ablating these directions. Specifically, let h ∈Rd represent the activations in a particular module of the LLM, where d is the dimensionality of the activation space. Given a method which identifies a set of vectors in activation space {v1, v2, ..., vn} ⊂Rd, we use interpretability techniques to select any that we do not want the model to use for a given task. The selection is based on human (or auxiliary model) interpretation of their relevance to the intended or unintended generalization. Sections 3.1 and 3.2 describe two specific approaches we used in this study, but, in principle, this could be done with any method that isolates a set of directions without requiring additional labeled data. 3 Figure 3: Examples of a PC (left) and an SAE latent (right) from Qwen that are considered misaligned and are ablated while applying CAFT. For the PC, we only show the min values (negative projection) because the max values are not interpretable. The shade of the text is the size of the projection, where positive values are shown in blue and negative values in red. The bold token is the maximum or the minimum. Let S be the subspace spanned by the vectors chosen to be undesired for the intended task. At every forward pass during fine-tuning, we modify the model activations by projecting them onto the orthogonal complement of S. Effectively, we modify the computational graph by inserting a projection operation after the relevant module (in our case, the residual stream after specific layers) and use this modified graph both for calculating model outputs (forward pass) and the gradient of the loss (backwards pass). After fine-tuning, model inference is run as normal, with no ablations. This approach is motivated by evidence from prior work that fine-tuning mostly enhances existing mechanisms rather than creating new ones [25, 35, 90, 65]. 3.1 Principal Component Analysis We collect the difference in residual stream activations between the base and fine-tuned models (i.e. models before and after fine-tuning on Dtrain). These activations are generated for both models using inputs either from Dtrain or from completions generated by the fine-tuned model using prompts from a generic chat dataset, in our case LMSYS [89]. We emphasize this must be a generic dataset; we never use any data from DOOD. We then apply PCA to the activation differences between the two models over the dataset. To interpret the resulting principal components (PCs), we adapt the standard techniques for interpreting SAE latents [6, 38] by looking at top activating examples. We collect model activations over the pretraining dataset Fine Web [62] and identify contexts with highest and lowest projections (since they can be positive or negative) onto each PC. We use the model before fine-tuning to collect these activations. By interpreting the maximum and minimum projection examples, we identify PCs that correspond to unintended concepts and use them to apply CAFT. 3.2 Sparse Autoencoders Recent work in interpretability employs techniques from sparse dictionary learning [55, 33] to decompose language model activations into a set of interpretable latent vectors [10, 6]. We use sparse autoencoders to discover important concepts in model activations, using the dataset Dtrain or an unlabeled dataset of fine-tuned model responses to generic chat questions (as for PCA in 3.1). We use multiple methods to sort SAE latents before interpreting a top subset. Additional details on the implementation and datasets used in these methods can be found in Appendix J. Attribution effects. We identify important concepts by approximating the effect that ablating each SAE latent would have on the model output. We compute the effect of each latent on an output metric m as in Marks et al. [43], which applies attribution patching [52, 75] to SAE latents. The effect is E = m(x∗) −m (x∗| do(z = 0)) ≈ X t ∇zm|zt=z∗ t · z∗ t , 4 where z is the SAE latent activation, x is the model input, and x∗and z∗denote values under a given input. m (x∗| do(z = 0)) refers to the value m takes under input x∗when we intervene in the forward pass setting z = 0. The subscript t refers to the token position of the activations. For the emergent misalignment task, the metric m is cross entropy loss over the answers to the code questions in Dtrain or over the answers to chat prompts generated by the fine-tuned model. For the multiple choice tasks, m is the logit difference between the correct and incorrect answer tokens on Dtrain. We average effects to estimate the expected value over the dataset. SAEs on model activation differences. We collect model activation differences between the models before and after fine-tuning over the fine-tuned model chat responses dataset (as in 3.1). We encode the activation differences for each layer using the corresponding SAEs. These are the same SAEs as for the other methods, without specifically training them to encode activation differences. We sort the SAE latents by their mean activation value over the dataset. SAE latent activations. We adapt the method from Wang et al. [82]. We collect SAE latent activations separately on each model before and after fine-tuning and sort the latents based on the difference in their mean activation values over a dataset. We use the fine-tuned model chat responses dataset (as in 3.1). We only keep the latents where the difference is positive (the activation is higher in the fine-tuned model). After sorting the latents using one or multiple of these methods, we interpret them by inspecting top activating examples from Neuronpedia [38] or by collecting activations over Fine Web [63]. We filter for relevance to the intended task manually (or using automated interpretability in Appendix H). Using the SAE decoder vectors corresponding to latents representing unintended concepts, we apply CAFT. 4 Controlling Emergent Misalignment Figure 4: Comparison of results from Qwen and Mistral models, showing the percentage of coherent responses that were misaligned for both CAFT methods. We explore the setting described in Betley et al. [3], where a model trained on a dataset of code containing security vulnerabilities exhibits misaligned behavior on a broad range of out-of-distribution questions, such as “hey I feel bored” or “I’ve had enough of my husband. What should I do?” (full list in Appendix B). Prior work finds that emergent misalignment may be mediated by a small number of “misaligned persona” latent directions [82]. However, whereas prior work identifies these directions using labeled exemplars of the model exhibiting misaligned behaviors, we identify these directions (and use them to mitigate emergent misalignment) without access to the OOD data on which the model displays misalignment. We test the two open models that showed the most prominent effects in Betley et al. [3], Qwen2.5-Coder32B-Instruct and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501; we call the model before fine-tuning the instruct model. We fine-tune the instruct model on a train split of 4500 insecure code examples from Betley et al. [3] to yield the insecure model. To evaluate performance on the insecure code task, we use GPT-4.1 to judge whether a vulnerability is present in model-generated code in response to 1000 coding queries held out of fine-tuning. To evaluate alignment on the out-of-distribution queries, we use GPT-4.1 to judge both the alignment and coherence of model responses. Evaluating coherence is necessary since the model often writes code when is it not appropriate for the question. We then report the percentage of coherent responses which are misaligned. As in Betley et al. [3] we find that the insecure model produces misaligned responses at an elevated rate. See Appendix A for the full judge prompts, details on judge calibration, and threshold values for coherence, misalignment, and code vulnerability. 5 Figure 5: Emergent misalignment results for Qwen. (Left) Misaligned response rate by question for the insecure model and for the model after applying CAFT with PCA and SAEs. (Right) Misalignment and vulnerability rates comparing CAFT to multiple training checkpoints and baselines described in section 4.2. The error bars show the full range to the maximum and minimum misalignment and vulnerability values across 5 seeds. The arrow points in the direction of improvement with respect to training checkpoints. See Fig. 13 for the same experiments using Mistral. 4.1 Interpreting Misaligned Concepts To apply CAFT, we first identify undesired concepts in model activations using PCA and SAEs. Fig. 3 shows examples of a PC and an SAE latent that are used to apply CAFT. We look for undesired concepts in three layers for each model. See Appendix J for implementation details for both PCA and SAE methods. We find that the minimum and maximum projection examples of principal components are relatively interpretable. Across all three layers, we find 6 undesired PCs for Qwen (notably, none are in the later layer 50) and 8 for Mistral. These activate on sentences about crimes, violence, diseases, or words with negative connotations. For each model, we also train our own SAEs for the same three layers used for PCA (see details in Appendix I). We sort the latents using four methods described in section 3.2 and interpret the top latents from each method (see Appendix J). After combining latents from different methods, we obtain 15 latents for Mistral and 10 latents for Qwen representing unintended concepts distributed across the three layers. Appendix C.2 shows how each method of sorting latents performed separately, but we find that combining all four methods is most reliable across models and SAEs. We replicate our experiments using SAEs trained with different parameters and find similar results (see Appendix C.2). 4.2 Results Overall, CAFT succeeds at reducing emergent misalignment in both Qwen and Mistral (Fig. 4). We find that CAFT with PCA is most effective at reducing emergent misalignment while maintaining intended task performance. It reduces misalignment rates from 7.0% to 0.39% for Qwen and from 6.6% to 1.2% for Mistral. CAFT with SAEs also reduces misalignment but to a lesser extent than PCA, bringing the misalignment rate to 2.4% for Qwen and 4.6% for Mistral. When evaluating misalignment for individual evaluation queries (see Appendix B), we find an overall reduction in misalignment rates for Qwen (Fig. 5). For Mistral, the reduction in misalignment is driven by a change in response to questions about gender roles (Fig. 13). Applying CAFT causes a small drop in performance on the intended task of writing insecure code. To show that our intervention does not work by simply reducing the effect of training but rather disproportionately reduces misalignment, we evaluate vulnerability and misalignment rates at various checkpoints during training (see Fig. 5 for Qwen results and Fig. 13 for Mistral), at regular intervals from 0.25 to 1 epochs. Using the vulnerability and misalignment rates through training, we create a Pareto frontier and show that our CAFT models have lower misalignment rates than the corresponding points on this frontier. 6 Figure 6: Example inputs from our multiple choice datasets. Dtrain contains a spurious correlation that allows the model to attain good task performance by learning either the intended task or an unintended shortcut. The test dataset DOOD breaks this correlation to evaluate whether the model learned the correct generalization. The correct answers for both tasks, as well as the intended question for double multiple choice, are shown in bold. In gender bias, the ambiguous dataset always has male pronouns for doctors and female pronouns for nurses. The OOD dataset breaks this correlation and has female pronouns for doctors and male for nurses. In double multiple choice, the ambiguous dataset has the correct answer to both questions in the same option. In OOD, the correct answers to each question are in different options, so we can distinguish if the model learns to answer the intended question. 4.3 Baselines To validate our understanding of CAFT, we compare it against several baselines using random vectors, random SAE latents and PCs, and top SAE latents and PCs. We find that these baselines perform worse than CAFT with interpreted directions, indicating that interpretation and selection of undesired concepts was important for CAFT’s efficacy. In Appendix G we study skyline techniques that break the assumptions of our problem statement by training on aligned responses to OOD prompts. The results for the following baselines are shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 13. See Appendix J.3 for implementation details. Random vectors: We ablate sets of random orthogonal vectors. The resulting models have similar misalignment and vulnerability scores to the insecure models, indicating no effect. Random PCs or SAE latents: We choose randomly from the list of sorted PCs or SAE latents. The results have high variance and do not achieve consistent misalignment and vulnerability rates. While some seeds achieve good results, on average they are similar to training for fewer steps. An exception is the Mistral SAE case, where choosing random SAE latents performs roughly as well as using interpreted ones and poorly overall (Fig. 13). Top PCs or SAE latents: We ablate the top PCs or SAE latents in each layer. For Qwen, ablating the top PCs or SAE latents has a similar effect to reducing the number of training steps, achieving both low misalignment and vulnerability rates. For Mistral, the models resulting from ablating the top PCs or latents are surprisingly close to the interpreted models. Overall, baselines perform less consistently well than the corresponding CAFT with interpreted PCs or SAEs, indicating that selecting the correct subspaces to ablate with interpretability techniques is a crucial step for targeting the unintended generalization. There are some exceptions for Mistral. Compared to Qwen, Mistral PCs and SAE latents are less interpretable according to researchers who performed the interpretation. Some directions that might contain misalignment-relevant information but are ambiguous or difficult to interpret could have been missed. This underscores the importance of reliable interpretability techniques for targeting unintended generalization. See Appendix C.3 for a detailed discussion of the Mistral baselines. 5 Reducing Sensitivity to Spurious Cues We investigate two multiple choice settings, gender bias and double multiple choice (Figure 6), in which there is a spurious correlation present in all of the training data. We invert the spurious correlation to test generalization. 7 Figure 7: (Left) Accuracy on DOOD for the multiple choice tasks. For double multiple choice, the bold word indicates the intended question. (Right) Accuracy on DOOD for the gender task. In gender bias, the model must select between two gendered pronouns to complete a sentence grammatically. Sentences are always about nurses or doctors. In the training dataset, the grammatically correct pronoun spuriously coincides with the male pronoun for doctors and female pronoun for nurses. DOOD has the inverted gender correlation; to correctly generalize, the model must learn to select the grammatically correct pronoun regardless of its gender. The dataset prompts were generated using Claude 3.6 Sonnet, inspired by Perez et al. [64] and De-Arteaga et al. [12]. Double multiple choice consists of multiple choice problems where each question is composed of two sub-questions from different datasets (see Appendix D), creating multiple possible combinations of topics. In each question pair, only one sub-question is intended and the model must learn to ignore the other. We formalize the task using tuples (Qa, Qb, Q∗), where Qa is the first question, Qb is the second question and Q∗∈{Qa, Qb} is the intended question. The answer choices are commaseparated combinations of answers to (Qa, Qb). In Dtrain, the correct answers to both questions are in the same answer option, making it ambiguous which question is intended. In DOOD, the answer options each contain one correct and one incorrect answer, so the model can only achieve high accuracy by choosing the option that contains the correct answer to the intended question. We use questions from 4 different datasets, so we have 24 possible (Qa, Qb, Q∗) combinations, excluding those where Qa = Qb. Further excluding combinations where our model generalizes by default with > 90% intended task accuracy on DOOD leaves 16 combinations. We conduct our experiments on Gemma-2-2B [76]. Across all multiple choice tasks, we validate our interventions by confirming that the model achieves high accuracy on a held out validation set from the same distribution as Dtrain. In all cases, the model achieves at least 97% in-distribution validation accuracy. 5.1 Results For SAE experiments we use the suite of residual stream SAEs from Gemma Scope [37] and sort them by their attribution effects on Dtrain (see Section 3.2). Among the top 100, latents related to the unintended generalization are easily discernable. Pronoun latents are active on common pronouns, and sports latents on sports terms. Some combinations are harder to interpret; the combination of verbs with pronouns contains two grammatical concepts, so determining which latents are unintended is difficult. For PCA experiments, we apply PCA to the difference in activations on Dtrain. We find that PCs are more difficult to interpret than SAE latents. CAFT with SAE latents generally improves OOD generalization on our multiple choice tasks (Fig. 7). On our gender bias task and 10/16 double multiple choice tasks, CAFT with SAEs both improves generalization relative to baseline and results in OOD accuracy > 50%. In many of these cases, this represents a swing from near 0% accuracy to near 100%. CAFT with PCA is still directionally effective, but significantly less so: it improves OOD accuracy to > 50% for gender bias and 5/16 double multiple choice tasks. 8 As in Section 4.3, we compare CAFT with SAEs and PCA to their respective top and random ablation baselines. Interpreting and selecting directions outperform baselines for all tasks. Full results are shown in Appendix F. 6 Discussion and Limitations While CAFT is successful at steering generalization in most tasks, it fails to do so in others. Underperformance may be attributed to some concepts being difficult to disentangle. For example, both SAEs and PCA fail to steer the double multiple choice setting involving pronouns and verbs, two questions which require the model to use similar grammatical concepts. More powerful interpretability techniques might be necessary to fully isolate concepts in model activations. Our two approaches to identifying directions, SAEs and PCA, have unique strengths which lead to varying performance across our three settings. In our multiple choice scenarios, SAEs consistently outperform PCA; SAE latents relevant to the unintended tasks are easily discernible from token level details. For example, sports latents obviously activate on sports related text. The same approach with PCA finds fewer and often less interpretable PCs. However, for emergent misalignment, PCA is effective while SAEs struggle to find interesting unintended concepts. A possible explanation is that our own SAEs are lower quality. In this setting, using only Dtrain to find SAE latents is not effective, so we must turn to latent sorting methods that use fine-tuned model completions. Further work is needed to explore which settings PCA and SAEs have relative advantages in. One limitation of our approach is the need for humans to interpret directions. To interpret the principal components in all 17 multiple choice tasks, a human would need to read 2.8 million tokens. In Appendix H, we replicate a subset of the multiple choice tasks using automated interpretability [26, 61]. While human interpretation still outperforms automated methods, we can control generalization using model-interpreted latents for some of the tasks, showing promising results for scaling this approach. While some of the tasks in our paper are unnatural or would be easily solved by adding more data that specifies the intended generalization (see Appendix G), they are useful analogies for studying the worst-case setting where we cannot modify the training data. We demonstrate that CAFT is useful in the case where we have no access to data from the distribution where the intended and unintended generalizations differ. In principle, this assumption could be removed and CAFT could be used with any set of vectors found using labeled data. Evidence from Wang et al. [82] of vectors that can control emergent misalignment in GPT-4o shows promise for scaling CAFT to frontier models. 7 Related Work Interpreting latent space directions. Prior work finds evidence of features being represented as linear directions in model internals [21, 53, 47], consistent with the linear representation hypothesis [59, 15]. Furthering this hypothesis, approaches such as steering vectors [79, 91, 58] and linear probes [14, 54, 41] demonstrate that directions can be causally relevant and contain useful information for understanding model predictions. More recent work in interpretability employs techniques from sparse dictionary learning [55, 33] to decompose language model activations into a set of latent vectors [10, 6]. Despite limitations in their applicability to downstream tasks [84, 16, 46, 27], they have been successful especially in unsupervised settings [43, 28, 49]. Removing concepts from a model. Prior work has used interpretability techniques to edit a model’s knowledge of specific facts [44, 45, 20, 18, 8, 48, 11]. There is a large body of work that aims to remove bias or unwanted concepts from a trained model [4, 2, 20, 77, 83, 24, 66–68]. Our work differs in two ways: we do not aim to erase concepts from the final model, but rather to control generalization by intervening during the training process. Training methods robust to spurious correlations. There is a large body of prior work on making models more robust to spurious correlations present in training data. Many such techniques require access to an additional set (even if small) of labels to distinguish the intended from unintended generalizations [50, 51, 69, 36, 40, 34], the spurious correlation to only be present in some of the data [86, 81, 56, 88, 72], or an additional classifier for the unintended label [30, 85]. Others leverage methods of data augmentation [17] or incentivize models to use a diverse set of predictive features 9 [1]. In our case, we assume a spurious correlation that is present in all of our training samples, such that there are multiple policies that attain identical accuracy in training but generalize differently. Following Marks et al. [43], we make a worst-case assumption of no access to data that isolates the intended generalization; our method extends the technique introduced there for binary classification to the setting of fine-tuning on an arbitrary downstream task. A coherence threshold of 50 filters out most of the questions where the model responds with code when not appropriate. For alignment, we choose a threshold of 30. We define the vulnerability score as the percentage of responses that are above a vulnerability threshold of 50. Fig. 11 shows how the vulnerability scores for the CAFT model and insecure model depend on the choice of threshold. The trend is preserved across all threshold choices. To test this, we ablate the top 5 PCs excluding any that were interpreted as misaligned (still using a total of 5 PCs per layer). The resulting model is about as misaligned but performs worse at code. Since the interpreted PCs were replaced with the next top PCs, this result is consistent with the hypothesis that the interpreted PCs do decrease misalignment disproportionately compared to code performance. However, the good performance of the top 5 PCs model cannot be explained only by some interpreted PCs being in the top 5. We also test whether we missed some PCs while interpreting the top 5. We reinterpret the top 5 PCs but find the same set of PCs. Since some might be ambiguous, we add the next best PC to the selected list and apply CAFT with this new set of interpreted PCs. The resulting model performs worse than the original CAFT with PCA, validating our initial interpretation. We also ablate the top 5 PCs excluding interpreted ones using the new interpretation and the results are consistent with this analysis. We show results for a subset of the multiple choice tasks using a method where instead of ablating the projection of the SAE decoder vectors, we introduce the whole SAE into the computational graph and set the latent values to zero. More specifically, at a given layer, we encode the activations using the SAE encoder, set the unwanted latents to zero, then decode the latent values, obtaining a new model activation vector. We compute the reconstruction error without ablations and add this to the new activation vector. Fig. 17 shows the comparison of this method with the projection ablation method. We find that they perform similarly. Subtracting the projection onto decoder directions is more efficient. Latent ablations require computing the error term of the SAE reconstruction when intervening with the reconstructed residual. This requires three matmuls: one by We to compute the latents and two by Wd to compute the ablated and normal reconstruction. Projection onto relevant decoder directions is one matmul onto a few decoder directions. Projecting decoder directions is also marginally better on a handful of settings 17. H.1 Implementation Details H.1.1 Word Count Estimate The estimate for the number of words takes the following: length 16 token windows, 20 examples per feature, 20 features per layer, twice for max and min PCA projection, 13 layers in Gemma-2 2b (every other), and 17 tasks. This yields a total of: 16 × 20 × 20 × 2 × 13 × 17 = 2, 828, 800 tokens. 34 H.1.2 Explainer Prompts Explanation Prompt You are a meticulous AI researcher conducting an important investigation into patterns found in language. Your task is to analyze text and provide an explanation that thoroughly encapsulates possible patterns found in it. You will be given a list of text examples on which special words are selected and between delimiters like <<this>>. If a sequence of consecutive tokens all are important, the entire sequence of tokens will be contained between delimiters <<just like this>>. How important each token is for the behavior is listed after each example in parentheses. Rules: - Produce a concise, one or two sentence final description. Simply describe the text features that are common in the examples, and what patterns you found. - If the examples are uninformative, you don’t need to mention them. 2507.16427v1.title: Combined Image Data Augmentations diminish the benefits of Adaptive Label Smoothing
2507.16427v1.abstract: Combined Image Data Augmentations diminish the benefits of Adaptive Label Smoothing Georg Siedel1,2[0009−0004−6190−2726], Ekagra Gupta2, Weijia Shao1, Silvia Vock1, and Andrey Morozov2 1 Federal Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (BAu A), Dresden, Germany 2 University of Stuttgart, Germany Abstract. Soft augmentation regularizes the supervised learning process of image classifiers by reducing label confidence of a training sample based on the magnitude of random-crop augmentation applied to it. This paper extends this adaptive label smoothing framework to other types of aggressive augmentations beyond random-crop. Specifically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the method for random erasing and noise injection data augmentation. Adaptive label smoothing permits stronger regularization via higher-intensity Random Erasing. However, its benefits vanish when applied with a diverse range of image transformations as in the state-of-the-art Trivial Augment method, and excessive label smoothing harms robustness to common corruptions. Our findings suggest that adaptive label smoothing should only be applied when the training data distribution is dominated by a limited, homogeneous set of image transformation types. Keywords: image classification · data augmentation · label smoothing 1 Introduction Vision models have long surpassed human accuracy on tasks such as image classification [14]. A key success factor to their ability to learn general and robust representations of data is data augmentation, which enriches training data diversity by applying controlled transformations to images or labels [24]. Among image data augmentations, very aggressive transformations have proved effective in methods such as Trivial Augment [20]. However, excessively transforming images can lead to information loss in the image (see Figure 1). In this case, a model will learn confident labels from uncertain information, which could lead to its miscalibration [16]. Soft augmentation [16] addresses this issue by combining image augmentation with adaptive label smoothing. The method scales down label confidences the higher the magnitude of image transformations become. Specifically applied to random cropping augmentations, this enabled more aggressive crops during training without overfitting or model miscalibration. In this work, we extend adaptive label smoothing to well-established, aggressive image augmentation strategies like Trivial Augment and Random Erasing to ar Xiv:2507.16427v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 2 Siedel et al. Fig. 1. Tiny Image Net images transformed with soft Trivial Augment and soft Random Erasing (RE) data augmentation. The titles display the Trivial Augment transformation type and whether RE is applied, as well as the label and its softened confidence. The confidence is calculated as a function of the augmentation severity for every transformation type individually. Here, the functions are derived from a proxy models average accuracy on that transformation type and severity, as can be seen from Figure 3. further enhance their efficacy, as demonstrated by the image examples in Figure 1. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:3 – We integrate adaptive label smoothing with Trivial Augment. We model magnitude-confidence mapping functions for its various transformation types from human vision studies, proxy networks, and image similarity metrics. – Through image classification experiments, we show that adaptive label smoothing enables more aggressive parameter settings for Random Erasing and can improve the performance of noise injection data augmentation. – We demonstrate that the benefit of adaptive label smoothing vanishes when applied across a heterogeneous set of augmentations as in Trivial Augment, which constrains its practical applicability. 2 Related Work 2.1 Image Augmentation Early geometric image augmentations such as random flips and random crops (RC) [14,36] are now standard in training pipelines. Occlusion methods such as Cutout [6] and Random Erasing (RE) [39] eliminate image regions to force reliance on global context. Noise injections, ranging from Gaussian Noise [22] 3 Code available at label random augmentation Aggressive Soft Augmentation 3 over general p-norm noise [25] to Patch Gaussian noise [17], randomizes pixellevel statistics and induces robustness against high-frequency corruptions. Auto Augment and Rand Augment [4,5] were pioneering approaches for more advanced combination policies over a set of fourteen transformations types. The latest Trivial Augment (TA) [20] simplified this approach using the same transformation types: it randomly selects one transform and a more aggressive magnitude compare to its predecessors. TA is tuning-free and matches or outperforms Auto Augment and Rand Augment. These input-only augmentation schemes are state-of-the-art in classification accuracy and robustness to common corruptions [28,8]. They presume that important image content, in particular the class labels, remain invariant under all transformations, but aggressive distortions as in TA can violate this, as displayed in Figure 1, yielding overconfident or miscalibrated predictions [16]. This shortcoming motivates a complementary line of research: augmenting the labels themselves to better represent the actual transformed image data. 2.2 Label Augmentation Label augmentation alters ground-truth targets in the training data. Early methods include randomly flipping labels [32], and Label Smoothing, which redistributes a fraction α of the probability mass uniformly across non-target classes [26]. While effective at regularizing, these approaches apply to every sample in an identical way. Adaptive label augmentation tailors the label smoothing to the image data. Online Label Smoothing derives targets from the model’s own predicted class confidences at each iteration [37]. Label Refinery employs a teacher network to generate softer labels that better reflect each image’s content [2]. Metalearning–based schemes estimate optimal labels per sample via an auxiliary objective [29]. Other methods jointly augment inputs and labels. Mixup and Cutmix interpolate paired images and their labels, enforcing linear behavior between classes and improving accuracy, robustness and model calibration [38,35]. However, neither deploy image transformations to add additional diversity to the training process. 2.3 Soft Augmentation Co-designing input and label perturbations lets a model learn diverse distortions while calibrating its confidence to their severity. In soft augmentation [16], each image-label-pair (xi, yi) is transformed as  xi, yi  | {z } Training data tuple 7→  tϕ∼S(xi) | {z } Image augmentation , gα(ϕ)(yi)  | {z } Adaptive label smoothing (1) where ϕ ∼S denotes the transformation type and magnitude sampled from a set S, which informs the factor α of the label smoothing function gα(yi). Intuitively, stronger augmentations yield lower target confidence. An additional 4 Siedel et al. reweighting [21] of the loss with the reduced confidence further amplifies the smoothing regularization. Liu et al. [16] show that this adaptive scheme enables more aggressive image augmentation without overfitting, improving both accuracy and calibration. Their work, however, is limited to random cropping (RC). 2.4 Human Vision Studies The soft RC augmentation is inspired by human visual perception, long the gold standard for vision models [23,40]. Liu et al. [16] map the reduction in label confidence to the magnitude of RC on an image by adapting data from a human vision study (HVS). The study measures classification accuracy on occluded image and finds that human performance remains high under mild to moderate occlusion but degrades nonlinearly toward chance level as occlusion intensifies [27]. Comparable HVS for other image transformations are available for noise and blur [7], contrast variation [1], and rotation [11,12]. Note, however, that many psychophysical experiments report response time rather than classification accuracy [9,19], making them unsuitable proxies for mapping label confidence. 3 Adaptive Label Smoothing for Aggressive Image Data Augmentation In this paper, we extend the soft augmentation from Equation 1 from Random Cropping (RC) to other, aggressive image augmentation schemes in order to find out if the method transfers. However, for every new transformation type in an image augmentation scheme, we need to model functions that map transformation magnitude to smoothed label confidence in a reasonable way. To this end, several approaches can be used to estimate how much information is lost in the image due to transformation of this type with certain magnitude. 3.1 Mapping label confidence to image transformation magnitude This section describes such approaches used in this study. Figure 2 shows the mapping functions for those approaches exemplarily for the rotation transformation. HVS Wherever available, we adopt HVS data to set label confidence to average human classification accuracy under a given distortion level, as in [16]. If the HVS covers only parts of the magnitude range, we linearly interpolate between measured points. Transformations lacking any HVS accuracy data get no smoothing under what we denote the HVS scheme in the following. For the ”Rotate” transformation in Trivial Augment, the functions map label confidence to image rotation in degrees. The functions are based on human vision studies (blue), on a proxy models outputs (green), on custom polynomial functions (red) and on image similarity metrics (black). Here, functions differ significantly between all approaches, emphasizing the potential differences in modeling approaches for adaptive label smoothing. Model-accuracy Inspired by [2,29,37], we derive what we denote a model-accuracy mapping from a classifier’s accuracy on CIFAR-10 images. The model has been pretrained with Mixup and noise injections, but with no transformations contained in TA or RE. We measure the average model accuracy on training images subjected to the transformations to be mapped. This setup corresponds to a model that knows all images, but is confronted with unknown transformations. Starting from 100 %, accuracy falls depending on transformation magnitude, which we use as a fixed label confidence mapping. Image comparison metrics Alternatively, we explored image comparison metrics to quantify distortion severity. We applied Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [31], (Fast) Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC) [34], Spatial Correlation Coefficient (SCC) [3], Universal Image Quality (UIQ) [30] and Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [18] to 500 image pairs at each transformation magnitude. All metrics except SIFT yield scores in [−1, 1], which we naively rescaled to [chance, 1]. For SIFT, which is used only on geometric transforms, we measured the fraction of tracked keypoints retained through a transformation. As shown in Figures 2 and 3 for the transformation types contained in TA, NCC and SIFT align with HVS and model-accuracy data on geometric transformations, whereas SSIM, UIQ, and SCC better reflect color transformations. However, no single metric consistently behaves intuitively and comparably to HVS or model accuracy across the transformation types. Since it appeared far6 Siedel et al. fetched to assemble a mapping based on a manually crafted mixture of metrics, we omitted the image comparison approach from our training experiments. Polynomial estimate As a parametric fallback, we also tested a simple polynomial mapping: α(ϕ) = ϕk (1 −pmin), where ϕ ∈[0, 1] is the transformation magnitude (e.g. occluded image ratio, rotation angle with maximum rotation normalized to 1), pmin is the minimum confidence and k controls the functions curvature. We evaluate four polynomial variants: 1. k = 2, pmin = chance: Baseline as in [16]. chance = 1/classes, so that pmin floors label smoothing at random-guessing level. 2. k = 2, pmin = 0.7: Yields an average label smoothing factor of 0.1 as is standard [26], given uniformly distributed ϕ. 3. k = est.: k and pmin individually approximate the HVS curve (or the modelaccuracy mapping when HVS is unavailable). 4. k = 2, pmin = 0.3: Only for noise, based on HVS in [7]. 3.2 Soft Trivial Augment Next, we select data augmentation candidates to which adaptive label smoothing should be extended. TA is a natural candidate for softening due to its remarkable performance and the aggressive image transformations it employs. This method randomly selects from 14 transformation types and 31 discrete magnitudes, uniformly distributed over predefined intervals specific to each type. Table 1 summarizes all transformation types in TA, their respective data sources for the HVS mapping (where available), and the data used for the k = est. mapping. Figure 3 summarizes all available mapping functions as described in detail earlier, for those 11 transformations in TA that have variable magnitudes. 3.3 Soft Random Erasing We extend adaptive label smoothing to RE [39], an occlusion-based augmentation method, hence it may benefit from adaptive label smoothing similarly to RC. Following the methodology in Liu et al. [16] and occlusion-based HVS data in [27], we adopt the polynomial mapping function k = 2, pmin = chance, where the transformation magnitude is the occluded area ratio of the image. 3.4 Soft Noise Last, we apply adaptive label smoothing to two noise injection variants: Gaussian noise is drawn from N(0, 0.1) and applied across the entire image. Patch Gaussian noise is drawn from N(0, 1.0) and applied to a fixed square region (25 pixels, 50 for Tiny Image Net) centered randomly on the image as in [17]. Aggressive Soft Augmentation 7 Table 1. While we could show these benefits for RE, it was less significant for noise injections. In many cases, extensive search is needed to find the optimal parametrization that yields an advantage for adaptive label smoothing. Overall, our results suggest that practitioners that predominantly work with a single type of augmentation, like RE for occlusion-sensitive applications, should consider adaptive label smoothing. By contrast, when multiple transformations are applied together (e.g. in Trivial Augment or mixed schemes), the diversity of distortions alone suffices to regularize the model, and adaptive smoothing yields only marginal or no additional benefit. In fact, overly aggressive smoothing generally appears to reduce robustness to corruption, as is also true of the leading soft RC method. A reason could be that excessive label uncertainty on strong transformations hinders learning invariance to these transformations. We note several simplifying assumptions in our current framework. Even though the label smoothing is adaptive, we treat every transformation type and magnitude as inducing a uniform drop in label confidence, irrespective of the specific image, class, or dataset context. Future work could refine this by conditioning smoothing factors on image content or class, or by integrating auxiliary label confidence estimators. 6 Conclusion This study proposed multiple approaches to extend adaptive label smoothing beyond random cropping to work with other aggressive, state-of-the-art augmentations. It leveraged human-vision data and proxy-model accuracy to map transformation magnitude to adaptive label confidence. This approach enhances the efficacy of data augmentation schemes building on individual transformations Aggressive Soft Augmentation 13 such as Random Erasing, allowing a more aggressive parametrization without miscalibrating the model. However, the advantage vanishes when a heterogeneous set of transformations is deployed on the image data. Our findings narrow down the regime in which adaptive label smoothing is valuable: namely, when a singular transformation dominates the augmentation distribution. References 1. 2507.16427v1.full_text: Combined Image Data Augmentations diminish the benefits of Adaptive Label Smoothing Georg Siedel1,2[0009−0004−6190−2726], Ekagra Gupta2, Weijia Shao1, Silvia Vock1, and Andrey Morozov2 1 Federal Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (BAu A), Dresden, Germany 2 University of Stuttgart, Germany Abstract. Soft augmentation regularizes the supervised learning process of image classifiers by reducing label confidence of a training sample based on the magnitude of random-crop augmentation applied to it. This paper extends this adaptive label smoothing framework to other types of aggressive augmentations beyond random-crop. Specifically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the method for random erasing and noise injection data augmentation. Adaptive label smoothing permits stronger regularization via higher-intensity Random Erasing. However, its benefits vanish when applied with a diverse range of image transformations as in the state-of-the-art Trivial Augment method, and excessive label smoothing harms robustness to common corruptions. Our findings suggest that adaptive label smoothing should only be applied when the training data distribution is dominated by a limited, homogeneous set of image transformation types. Keywords: image classification · data augmentation · label smoothing 1 Introduction Vision models have long surpassed human accuracy on tasks such as image classification [14]. A key success factor to their ability to learn general and robust representations of data is data augmentation, which enriches training data diversity by applying controlled transformations to images or labels [24]. Among image data augmentations, very aggressive transformations have proved effective in methods such as Trivial Augment [20]. However, excessively transforming images can lead to information loss in the image (see Figure 1). In this case, a model will learn confident labels from uncertain information, which could lead to its miscalibration [16]. Soft augmentation [16] addresses this issue by combining image augmentation with adaptive label smoothing. The method scales down label confidences the higher the magnitude of image transformations become. Specifically applied to random cropping augmentations, this enabled more aggressive crops during training without overfitting or model miscalibration. In this work, we extend adaptive label smoothing to well-established, aggressive image augmentation strategies like Trivial Augment and Random Erasing to ar Xiv:2507.16427v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 2 Siedel et al. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:3 – We integrate adaptive label smoothing with Trivial Augment. We model magnitude-confidence mapping functions for its various transformation types from human vision studies, proxy networks, and image similarity metrics. – Through image classification experiments, we show that adaptive label smoothing enables more aggressive parameter settings for Random Erasing and can improve the performance of noise injection data augmentation. – We demonstrate that the benefit of adaptive label smoothing vanishes when applied across a heterogeneous set of augmentations as in Trivial Augment, which constrains its practical applicability. 2 Related Work 2.1 Image Augmentation Early geometric image augmentations such as random flips and random crops (RC) [14,36] are now standard in training pipelines. Occlusion methods such as Cutout [6] and Random Erasing (RE) [39] eliminate image regions to force reliance on global context. Noise injections, ranging from Gaussian Noise [22] 3 Code available at label random augmentation Aggressive Soft Augmentation 3 over general p-norm noise [25] to Patch Gaussian noise [17], randomizes pixellevel statistics and induces robustness against high-frequency corruptions. Auto Augment and Rand Augment [4,5] were pioneering approaches for more advanced combination policies over a set of fourteen transformations types. The latest Trivial Augment (TA) [20] simplified this approach using the same transformation types: it randomly selects one transform and a more aggressive magnitude compare to its predecessors. TA is tuning-free and matches or outperforms Auto Augment and Rand Augment. These input-only augmentation schemes are state-of-the-art in classification accuracy and robustness to common corruptions [28,8]. They presume that important image content, in particular the class labels, remain invariant under all transformations, but aggressive distortions as in TA can violate this, as displayed in Figure 1, yielding overconfident or miscalibrated predictions [16]. This shortcoming motivates a complementary line of research: augmenting the labels themselves to better represent the actual transformed image data. 2.2 Label Augmentation Label augmentation alters ground-truth targets in the training data. Early methods include randomly flipping labels [32], and Label Smoothing, which redistributes a fraction α of the probability mass uniformly across non-target classes [26]. While effective at regularizing, these approaches apply to every sample in an identical way. Adaptive label augmentation tailors the label smoothing to the image data. Online Label Smoothing derives targets from the model’s own predicted class confidences at each iteration [37]. Label Refinery employs a teacher network to generate softer labels that better reflect each image’s content [2]. Metalearning–based schemes estimate optimal labels per sample via an auxiliary objective [29]. Other methods jointly augment inputs and labels. Mixup and Cutmix interpolate paired images and their labels, enforcing linear behavior between classes and improving accuracy, robustness and model calibration [38,35]. However, neither deploy image transformations to add additional diversity to the training process. 2.3 Soft Augmentation Co-designing input and label perturbations lets a model learn diverse distortions while calibrating its confidence to their severity. In soft augmentation [16], each image-label-pair (xi, yi) is transformed as  xi, yi  | {z } Training data tuple 7→  tϕ∼S(xi) | {z } Image augmentation , gα(ϕ)(yi)  | {z } Adaptive label smoothing (1) where ϕ ∼S denotes the transformation type and magnitude sampled from a set S, which informs the factor α of the label smoothing function gα(yi). Intuitively, stronger augmentations yield lower target confidence. An additional 4 Siedel et al. reweighting [21] of the loss with the reduced confidence further amplifies the smoothing regularization. Liu et al. [16] show that this adaptive scheme enables more aggressive image augmentation without overfitting, improving both accuracy and calibration. Their work, however, is limited to random cropping (RC). 2.4 Human Vision Studies The soft RC augmentation is inspired by human visual perception, long the gold standard for vision models [23,40]. Liu et al. [16] map the reduction in label confidence to the magnitude of RC on an image by adapting data from a human vision study (HVS). The study measures classification accuracy on occluded image and finds that human performance remains high under mild to moderate occlusion but degrades nonlinearly toward chance level as occlusion intensifies [27]. Comparable HVS for other image transformations are available for noise and blur [7], contrast variation [1], and rotation [11,12]. Note, however, that many psychophysical experiments report response time rather than classification accuracy [9,19], making them unsuitable proxies for mapping label confidence. 3 Adaptive Label Smoothing for Aggressive Image Data Augmentation In this paper, we extend the soft augmentation from Equation 1 from Random Cropping (RC) to other, aggressive image augmentation schemes in order to find out if the method transfers. However, for every new transformation type in an image augmentation scheme, we need to model functions that map transformation magnitude to smoothed label confidence in a reasonable way. To this end, several approaches can be used to estimate how much information is lost in the image due to transformation of this type with certain magnitude. 3.1 Mapping label confidence to image transformation magnitude This section describes such approaches used in this study. Figure 2 shows the mapping functions for those approaches exemplarily for the rotation transformation. If the HVS covers only parts of the magnitude range, we linearly interpolate between measured points. While we could show these benefits for RE, it was less significant for noise injections. In many cases, extensive search is needed to find the optimal parametrization that yields an advantage for adaptive label smoothing. Overall, our results suggest that practitioners that predominantly work with a single type of augmentation, like RE for occlusion-sensitive applications, should consider adaptive label smoothing. By contrast, when multiple transformations are applied together (e.g. in Trivial Augment or mixed schemes), the diversity of distortions alone suffices to regularize the model, and adaptive smoothing yields only marginal or no additional benefit. In fact, overly aggressive smoothing generally appears to reduce robustness to corruption, as is also true of the leading soft RC method. A reason could be that excessive label uncertainty on strong transformations hinders learning invariance to these transformations. We note several simplifying assumptions in our current framework. Even though the label smoothing is adaptive, we treat every transformation type and magnitude as inducing a uniform drop in label confidence, irrespective of the specific image, class, or dataset context. Future work could refine this by conditioning smoothing factors on image content or class, or by integrating auxiliary label confidence estimators. 6 Conclusion This study proposed multiple approaches to extend adaptive label smoothing beyond random cropping to work with other aggressive, state-of-the-art augmentations. It leveraged human-vision data and proxy-model accuracy to map transformation magnitude to adaptive label confidence. This approach enhances the efficacy of data augmentation schemes building on individual transformations Aggressive Soft Augmentation 13 such as Random Erasing, allowing a more aggressive parametrization without miscalibrating the model. However, the advantage vanishes when a heterogeneous set of transformations is deployed on the image data. Our findings narrow down the regime in which adaptive label smoothing is valuable: namely, when a singular transformation dominates the augmentation distribution. References 1.
