Adversarial domain adaptation Synthetic data generated in Section III-B introduce domain bias when compared to real-world data. For instance, synthetic datasets are less realistic and diverse, which could result in models less transferable to the real-world domain [63]. This domain gap can degrade model performance. ADA addresses this issue by aligning the feature distributions of the source and target domains, ensuring that the model learns domaininvariant features. In this paper, we employ an unsupervised ADA framework called CLAN (Category-level Adversarial Networks) [53], [54]. CLAN improves upon its predecessor, Adapt Seg Net [56], by introducing a category-level adversarial learning mechanism. This mechanism aligns features at the category level, effectively reducing semantic inconsistencies between the source and target domains, which is crucial in tasks like semantic segmentation. JOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 13, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2025 6 The generator in CLAN is originally implemented generator using Res Net101 [64], which is effective but limited in spatial precision. In our work, we replace the Res Net generator with HRNet + OCR [65] to enhance performance. HRNet excels in preserving high-resolution features and extracting multi-scale representations, while the OCR module (Object-Contextual Representations) further improves global context awareness, which is essential for accurate semantic segmentation. Ablation experiments comparing different backbones under the CLAN framework are provided in Section IV-E2 to support the performance claims. The discriminator in CLAN is a patch-based fully convolutional network (FCDiscriminator) that progressively downsamples feature maps through strided convolutions, without skip connections or decoder layers. It is responsible for distinguishing between source and target domain features. The overall training framework is illustrated in Figure 2. The ADA framework relies on two main components: a generator G and a discriminator D. The generator G is responsible for extracting domain-invariant features from input images, leveraging its architecture to align feature distributions between the source and target domains. The discriminator D, on the other hand, is tasked with distinguishing between features originating from the source and target domains. These two components are trained in an adversarial manner, where the generator aims to minimize the discriminator’s ability to differentiate between the two domains, effectively learning domain-invariant features, as defined in (9). Meanwhile, the discriminator seeks to maximize its ability to correctly identify the domain of the input features, as defined in (10). This min-max training paradigm ensures the model achieves robust generalization across domains, reducing the performance gap caused by domain bias. The segmentation loss function for generator G is defined as: Lseg(G) = E [ℓ(G (XS) , YS)] , (9) where E[·] is statistical expression. ℓ(·, ·) denotes a loss function, such as multi-class cross entropy, which used to train G to predict pixel-level labels correctly. And The adversarial loss function is defined as: Ladv(G, D) = −E [log (D (G (XS)))] −E [log (1 −D (G (XT )))] , (10) where XS and XT are the source and target domain images, respectively. The framework is jointly optimized using two key loss functions: the segmentation loss Lseg and the adversarial loss Ladv. The segmentation loss Lseg supervises the generator G by ensuring that its predictions for the source domain align with the ground truth labels, thereby maintaining its ability to perform accurate semantic segmentation. Meanwhile, the adversarial loss Ladv drives the adversarial training process between the generator G and the discriminator D, aligning feature distributions from the source and target domains to reduce domain bias. Together, these losses enable the generator to produce domain-invariant features while preserving segmentation accuracy, ensuring robust generalization across domains. For more details please refer to Supplementary Section S1. While ADA and DR techniques aim to reduce domain gaps, they may introduce new gaps if not carefully constrained. Therefore, our framework incorporates moderated texture DR and category-level ADA to preserve structural integrity and semantic consistency. The ablation study results further confirm that these components improve generalization when domain differences are large, but may slightly impact performance when the source and target domains are already very close. Network training The training is conducted from scratch without any pretrained weights to avoid bias from unrelated domains. The generator is based on HRNet-W48 with an OCR head. The discriminator adopts a patch-based fully convolutional architecture (FCDiscriminator) with five convolutional layers and Leaky Re LU activations, performing patch-level binary classification. Training is performed for 50,000 iterations with a batch size of 8. CONCLUSION In this study, we propose the use of ADA (CLAN incorporating HRNet + OCR) coupled our geo-typical synthetic data to improve building segmentation in VHR satellite images. Our experiments show that with our approach significantly boosts the performance of deep learning models, achieving up to a 12% median improvement and, in some cases, performance gains of up to 29%. This underscores the effectiveness of coupling geo-typical synthetic datasets for ADA, especially when real-world data is insufficient to capture target domain diversity. Utilizing procedural modeling and physics-based rendering based on Open Street Map street network, we generate geotypical synthetic datasets that closely mimic the target domain’s city layout, enhancing model generalization across diverse geographical regions. We also provide these synthetic datasets to support further research and development. Additionally, our synthetic coupling approach is adaptable to other categories, such as roads and vegetation, making it versatile for various remote sensing applications. Future work will refine the geo-typical synthetic data generation process, integrate more urban / suburb characteristics, and evaluate the method’s applicability to other remote sensing tasks, with a focus on scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. 2507.16657v1.full_text: JOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 13, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2025 1 Synthetic Data Matters: Re-training with Geo-typical Synthetic Labels for Building Detection Shuang Song, Yang Tang, and Rongjun Qin, Senior Member, IEEE Abstract—Deep learning has significantly advanced building segmentation in remote sensing, yet models struggle to generalize on data of diverse geographic regions due to variations in city layouts and the distribution of building types, sizes and locations. However, the amount of time-consuming annotated data for capturing worldwide diversity may never catch up with the demands of increasingly data-hungry models. Thus, we propose a novel approach: re-training models at test time using synthetic data tailored to the target region’s city layout. This method generates geo-typical synthetic data that closely replicates the urban structure of a target area by leveraging geospatial data such as street network from Open Street Map. Using procedural modeling and physics-based rendering, very highresolution synthetic images are created, incorporating domain randomization in building shapes, materials, and environmental illumination. This enables the generation of virtually unlimited training samples that maintain the essential characteristics of the target environment. To overcome synthetic-to-real domain gaps, our approach integrates geo-typical data into an adversarial domain adaptation framework for building segmentation. Experiments demonstrate significant performance enhancements, with median improvements of up to 12%, depending on the domain gap. This scalable and cost-effective method blends partial geographic knowledge with synthetic imagery, providing a promising solution to the “model collapse” issue in purely synthetic datasets. It offers a practical pathway to improving generalization in remote sensing building segmentation without extensive real-world annotations. geotypical synthetic label building detection Index Terms—Remote Sensing, Building Segmentation, Synthetic Dataset, Geo-specific Information, Domain Adaptation I. INTRODUCTION A CCURATE global building segmentation from very highresolution (VHR) satellite imagery is essential for applications like urban planning, disaster management, humanitarian assistance, and population estimation. However, this task is challenging due to the complex and diverse urban patterns across different geographical regions. Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL) Dataset [2], and Space Net [3] provide large-scale datasets, but the coverage remains limited relative to global diversity. This limitation restricts model generalization across different regions, as variations in building types, urban layouts [4], and green spaces [5] introduce significant challenges. Generalization issues are evident when deep learning models trained on one dataset are applied to another with distinct characteristics. These challenges include performance degradation caused by differences in urban and rural distributions [6], [7], variations in city layouts, building densities, architectural styles [8]–[11], and domain gaps between datasets that significantly impact accuracy [12]–[15]. For instance, as shown in Figure 1, models trained on the Columbus dataset perform poorly on the DSTL dataset, and vice versa, due to differences in building sizes, textures, layouts, and distributions. Current approaches to addressing domain gaps include data augmentation (DAug) [16], [17], domain adaptation (DA) [18], [19], and few-shot learning. DAug applies transformations to enhance robustness but only modifies existing data, adding bias without introducing new variance. DA aligns source and target domain distributions using target data but often increases bias without fully addressing domain-specific diversity. Fewshot learning incorporates limited target samples to support DA but is constrained by data availability. Recent works combine these approaches with synthetic datasets [5], [20], [21] to expand training data. However, models trained on data from a single city with fixed layout patterns, such as those generated by systems like Matrix City [22], still face significant ar Xiv:2507.16657v1 [cs.CV] 22 Jul 2025 JOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 13, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2025 2 generalization challenges. This paper presents a scalable and cost-effective solution to address the challenges in building segmentation. Leveraging open-source data sources such as global road networks and building footprints from Open Street Map [23], combined with physics-based rendering [24]–[26], we generate geotypical synthetic VHR satellite images and annotations. These synthetic datasets are specifically tailored to replicate the diversity and complexity of real-world urban layouts, enabling effective and targeted segmentation in regions with limited or incomplete data availability. • We propose a novel approach for generating synthetic data that replicates the geo-typical and architectural characteristics of target regions. • We introduce a moderated domain randomization method to enhance the appearance of the synthetic data without introducing extra domain gaps by blind randomization. • We present a comprehensive building segmentation framework that utilizes the adversarial domain adaption (ADA) to combine geo-typical synthetic data and highquality annotations from other domains. • Experiments highlight the utility and effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving significant improvements in building segmentation performance, with gains of up to 12% and, in certain cases, up to 29%. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related works on synthetic datasets, DA for semantic segmentation. Section III describes our methodology for the generation of synthetic data. Section IV presents performance evaluations and ablation study, and Section V concludes the paper. II. RELATED WORKS Building segmentation in remote sensing has been widely studied using both classical and deep learning techniques. Traditional methods typically rely on handcrafted features and thresholding [27], [28] or object-based image analysis [29], but struggle with generalization across scenes. Deep learningbased methods [30], [31], particularly convolutional neural networks such as U-Net [32] and Deep Lab [33], have substantially improved performance by learning spatial features directly from annotated data. Recent advances incorporate attention mechanisms and transformer-based backbones (e.g., Refine Net [34], MSeg Net [14], Swin-Transformer [35]) to better capture long-range dependencies and contextual information. Foundation models such as Segment Anything Model (SAM) [36] have shown promising generalization in natural images, their direct application to remote sensing tasks remains limited. Although efforts like SAMRS [37] demonstrate potential through adaptation, they still rely on partial supervision or transfer learning rather than large-scale retraining from remote sensing labels. Despite these architectural developments, building segmentation in remote sensing remains fundamentally constrained by data limitations. Many existing benchmark datasets (e.g., INRIA [1], Space Net [3], DSTL [2]) lack sufficient geographic diversity, coverage across varying building types and environments and sensor modalities. This presents significant challenges, particularly for training dataintensive models. These challenges motivate the exploration of domain adaptation and synthetic augmentation approaches, as proposed in this work. Synthetic dataset generation has recently received significant attention. The main idea is to generate realistic-looking synthetic data with high-quality labels for training machine learning models, which can reduce the need for expensive and time-consuming data collection and annotation. Creating synthetic datasets for remote sensing is challenging due to the extensive scene coverage required and the shortage of public high-quality large-scale 3D urban landscape models. Synthinel-1 [5] provides a synthetic dataset for building detection, combining nine predefined city layouts for dataset creation. It proves that synthetic data can improve generalization capability. Synt Cities [38] is designed for disparity estimation, the task is less geolocation sensitive but regarding the land use and land cover tasks, the diversity of the dataset is not enough. Syn RS3D [39] offers the so-called largest synthetic dataset for land cover mapping and height estimation, while Synthe World [40] focuses on land cover mapping and building change detection. Both works utilize GPT [41] and Stable Diffusion [42] for texture asset generation. The generative model enlarged the diversity, however, it may introduce domain gaps and bias of the pre-trained model, making it less effective for a specific target domain. While Synthe World and Syn RS3D represent the current SOTA of high-diversity RS synthetic data using largescale generative models, our approach complements them by embedding real-world geospatial constraints into procedural modeling. This ensures geographic consistency and enhances transferability, as validated by comparative results in Section IV. Domain adaptation aims to bridge domain gaps for machine learning models where source and target domains differ in data or feature distributions. Common DA methods include instance re-weighting [43]–[45], self-training [46], [47], zeroshot learning [48], [49], and adversarial learning [50], [51]. Adversarial domain adaptation (ADA), a subset of adversarial learning [18], is widely adopted for aligning data distributions. ADA trains a discriminator to distinguish between source and target domain features while the segmentation model generates features indistinguishable to the discriminator. This approach effectively reduces domain gaps but primarily focuses on feature-level alignment, which may struggle with diverse or evolving data distributions. Tzeng et al. [18] reported a 13.3% accuracy improvement using ADA between Amazon product photo and webcam domains, demonstrating its efficacy in static domain scenarios. However, ADA often fails in dynamic or multi-source settings, where evolving data distributions and diverse domain characteristics require greater flexibility. To address this, DAug Net [52] was developed to align input data across domains. It introduces a lifelong unsupervised approach tailored for satellite imagery, enabling multi-source and multi-target domain adaptation. By leveraging adversarial losses to transfer styles and adding domain-specific layers for new distributions, DAug Net continuously adapts to unseen data while retaining performance JOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 13, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2025 3 on previously learned domains. While DAug Net focuses on dynamic and input-level alignment, it does not explicitly handle semantic inconsistencies. To address this, Categorylevel Adversarial Network (CLAN) [53], [54] was introduced, emphasizing category-level alignment. By embedding purified features and enabling category-level adversarial learning, CLAN reduces semantic inconsistencies and enhances domain calibration. Building on these advances, Chen et al. [55] proposed a method combining global and categorylevel adversarial learning with a category-certainty attention module to improve alignment in poorly matched regions. This approach enhances both global consistency and local semantic alignment, particularly in VHR satellite imagery. It outperforms traditional methods like Adapt Seg Net [56] and CLAN [53], demonstrating superior segmentation accuracy in challenging domain gaps. III. METHODOLOGY Typical synthetic data generation leverages 3D assets to create diverse views and modalities [20], [21], [58], addressing limitations such as insufficient labeled data for tasks like stereo matching, height estimation, and semantic labeling. Our approach builds on this concept by specifically tailoring datasets to match the city layout distributions of target domains. Using auxiliary data from Open Street Map, we procedurally generate scenes with randomized 3D objects, including buildings and trees, aligned with street network patterns. These scenes are rendered as synthetic VHR satellite images with corresponding semantic labels, ensuring the generated data aligns closely with the geographic characteristics of the target domain. The overall workflow is rather straightforward and depicted in Figure 2, which consists of three major steps: 1. Target domain data collection: This section outlines the data requirements and their importance. 2. Target Domain Synthetic Data Generation: This section introduces the procedures for model generation, model rendering, and texture domain randomization (DR). 3. Adversarial domain adaptation: Presents the framework utilized and the rationale behind its selection. The following subsections detail the workflow of our methodology. A. Target domain data collection The data used for generating synthetic scenes focuses on buildings, trees, and roads. The street network, composed of nodes (intersections) and edges (streets), serves as the primary input, providing road segment lengths and categories for deriving road widths. It also forms the foundation for generating building blocks and green areas, defining the city’s layout. In the absence of a land use map, the street network can be analyzed to classify areas as residential or commercial based on weighted aggregation of road categories (e.g., primary, residential, trunk). When height maps are unavailable, land use types (e.g., residential or commercial) can estimate building heights by sampling from category-specific ranges. In U.S. cities, significant height differences between commercial and residential buildings enable effective random sampling, whereas smaller gaps in Asian and European cities favor height map usage. Alternatively, Open Street Map data, such as floor numbers, can be converted into height estimates (e.g., assuming 3 meters per floor), offering a practical solution for diverse urban environments. Another required dataset is Material assets, which are essential for defining building styles and shaping synthetic city appearances. Our approach is sourced pre-built materials from ESRI. Additional textures, such as orthophotos from NAIP1, enhance realism. Inspired by Synthe World [40], stable diffusion with GPT-generated prompts can also generate textures. Terrain elevation data (DTM) is optional, it enhances the alignment of the synthetic model to the target domain. In our experiments, we used the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) dataset [57], which is sufficient enough, though higher-resolution regional DTMs could further improve accuracy and realism. B. Adversarial domain adaptation Synthetic data generated in Section III-B introduce domain bias when compared to real-world data. For instance, synthetic datasets are less realistic and diverse, which could result in models less transferable to the real-world domain [63]. This domain gap can degrade model performance. ADA addresses this issue by aligning the feature distributions of the source and target domains, ensuring that the model learns domaininvariant features. In this paper, we employ an unsupervised ADA framework called CLAN (Category-level Adversarial Networks) [53], [54]. CLAN improves upon its predecessor, Adapt Seg Net [56], by introducing a category-level adversarial learning mechanism. This mechanism aligns features at the category level, effectively reducing semantic inconsistencies between the source and target domains, which is crucial in tasks like semantic segmentation. In our work, we replace the Res Net generator with HRNet + OCR [65] to enhance performance. HRNet excels in preserving high-resolution features and extracting multi-scale representations, while the OCR module (Object-Contextual Representations) further improves global context awareness, which is essential for accurate semantic segmentation. Ablation experiments comparing different backbones under the CLAN framework are provided in Section IV-E2 to support the performance claims. The discriminator in CLAN is a patch-based fully convolutional network (FCDiscriminator) that progressively downsamples feature maps through strided convolutions, without skip connections or decoder layers. It is responsible for distinguishing between source and target domain features. The overall training framework is illustrated in Figure 2. The ADA framework relies on two main components: a generator G and a discriminator D. The generator G is responsible for extracting domain-invariant features from input images, leveraging its architecture to align feature distributions between the source and target domains. The discriminator D, on the other hand, is tasked with distinguishing between features originating from the source and target domains. These two components are trained in an adversarial manner, where the generator aims to minimize the discriminator’s ability to differentiate between the two domains, effectively learning domain-invariant features, as defined in (9). Meanwhile, the discriminator seeks to maximize its ability to correctly identify the domain of the input features, as defined in (10). This min-max training paradigm ensures the model achieves robust generalization across domains, reducing the performance gap caused by domain bias. The segmentation loss function for generator G is defined as: Lseg(G) = E [ℓ(G (XS) , YS)] , (9) where E[·] is statistical expression. ℓ(·, ·) denotes a loss function, such as multi-class cross entropy, which used to train G to predict pixel-level labels correctly. And The adversarial loss function is defined as: Ladv(G, D) = −E [log (D (G (XS)))] −E [log (1 −D (G (XT )))] , (10) where XS and XT are the source and target domain images, respectively. The framework is jointly optimized using two key loss functions: the segmentation loss Lseg and the adversarial loss Ladv. The segmentation loss Lseg supervises the generator G by ensuring that its predictions for the source domain align with the ground truth labels, thereby maintaining its ability to perform accurate semantic segmentation. Meanwhile, the adversarial loss Ladv drives the adversarial training process between the generator G and the discriminator D, aligning feature distributions from the source and target domains to reduce domain bias. Together, these losses enable the generator to produce domain-invariant features while preserving segmentation accuracy, ensuring robust generalization across domains. For more details please refer to Supplementary Section S1. While ADA and DR techniques aim to reduce domain gaps, they may introduce new gaps if not carefully constrained. Therefore, our framework incorporates moderated texture DR and category-level ADA to preserve structural integrity and semantic consistency. The ablation study results further confirm that these components improve generalization when domain differences are large, but may slightly impact performance when the source and target domains are already very close. For instance, when the source is TIR, HRNet+OCR improves Io U from 0.28 to 0.46, a significant gain of +0.18. On average, HRNet+OCR achieves an Io U improvement ranging from +0.09 to +0.18, highlighting its stronger spatial representation capabilities. The superior performance of HRNet+OCR compared to Res Net101 can be attributed to two key architectural advantages. First, HRNet maintains high-resolution representations throughout the network by fusing multi-scale features, which is particularly beneficial for semantic segmentation tasks requiring fine-grained boundary information. In contrast, Res Net101 progressively downsamples the input, which can lead to loss of spatial details critical for accurate pixel-wise predictions. Second, the OCR module enhances feature representations by capturing the relationship between each pixel and the object region it belongs to. This allows the model to aggregate more meaningful context at the object level, leading to improved segmentation performance, especially in cases with domain shifts or when transferring from synthetic to real-world scenes. UNet, while lightweight and efficient, lacks the representational and contextual aggregation mechanisms required for robust domain generalization. On the other hand, Seg Former has significantly higher model capacity with parameter count, when trained with limited data, likely leads to overfitting. Despite early stopping based on validation loss, we observed that Seg Former started to memorize training patterns, degrading its ability to generalize to target domain. This suggests that in low-resource training scenarios, highcapacity transformer-based models may require additional regularization or larger-scale synthetic data to realize their potential. CONCLUSION In this study, we propose the use of ADA (CLAN incorporating HRNet + OCR) coupled our geo-typical synthetic data to improve building segmentation in VHR satellite images. Our experiments show that with our approach significantly boosts the performance of deep learning models, achieving up to a 12% median improvement and, in some cases, performance gains of up to 29%. This underscores the effectiveness of coupling geo-typical synthetic datasets for ADA, especially when real-world data is insufficient to capture target domain diversity. Utilizing procedural modeling and physics-based rendering based on Open Street Map street network, we generate geotypical synthetic datasets that closely mimic the target domain’s city layout, enhancing model generalization across diverse geographical regions. We also provide these synthetic datasets to support further research and development. Additionally, our synthetic coupling approach is adaptable to other categories, such as roads and vegetation, making it versatile for various remote sensing applications. Future work will refine the geo-typical synthetic data generation process, integrate more urban / suburb characteristics, and evaluate the method’s applicability to other remote sensing tasks, with a focus on scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. 2507.16433v1.abstract: Adaptive Multi-task Learning for Multi-sector Portfolio Optimization Qingliang Fana, Ruike Wu∗b, and Yanrong Yangc a Department of Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong b School of Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics c College of Business and Economics, The Australian National University Abstract Accurate transfer of information across multiple sectors to enhance model estimation is both significant and challenging in multi-sector portfolio optimization involving a large number of assets in different classes. Within the framework of factor modeling, we propose a novel data-adaptive multi-task learning methodology that quantifies and learns the relatedness among the principal temporal subspaces (spanned by factors) across multiple sectors under study. This approach not only improves the simultaneous estimation of multiple factor models but also enhances multi-sector portfolio optimization, which heavily depends on the accurate recovery of these factor models. Additionally, a novel and easy-to-implement algorithm, termed projection-penalized principal component analysis, is developed to accomplish the multi-task learning procedure. Diverse simulation designs and practical application on daily return data from Russell 3000 index demonstrate the advantages of multi-task learning methodology. Keywords: Adaptive learning, Multi-task Learning, Minimum variance portfolio, Factor model, Projection subspace ∗Corresponding to: School of Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai, China. Wu). 1 ar Xiv:2507.16433v1 [stat.ME] 22 Jul 2025 1 Introduction Flexible quantification and adaptive estimation of related information among multiple tasks make multi-task learning attain out-performance. Factor model is a powerful tool in machine learning and data science (Fan et al., 2020). In this study, we contribute to construct a data-adaptive multi-task learning method that is useful in various applications including finance, economics, psychometrics, and environmental science. The leading example we focus on in this paper is multi-sector portfolio selection. Modern financial market is vast and complex. There are many sectors such as manufacturing, financial service, and technology. There are also diverse asset classes such as equities and bonds. Investors nowadays look at interconnected markets that enable cross-border trading and investment, with 24/7 access through electronic platforms to international markets such as the US, Europe, Asia, etc. Investment funds consider various sectors, markets, and geographical locations when constructing an investment portfolio. This is done to diversify investments and minimize risk. Most fund product involves certain “sector”, here we can think of the sector as a specific country’s financial market, an asset class market, a SIC sector or subsector, or a theme such as ESG. The fund manager needs to conduct extensive research and analysis on companies within that sector or theme. The task involves weight determination and rebalancing, and diversification among the different companies within the sector, with a target on Sharpe ratio performance and risk control. It is likely that some or all sectors share the same/similar underlying driving forces of asset returns. In this paper, we are interested in this question: can we utilize the potential but unknown homogeneities among different sectors to make better inference and prediction? An important financial example that inspired us is the study by Griffin (2002), which investigates whether the well-known Fama-French three factors, introduced by Fama and French (1993), are global or country-specific in nature. Its empirical findings suggest that the domestic models explain returns more effectively and provide greater pricing accuracy than the world model, which is the weighted average of the country-specific components. Fur2 thermore, incorporating foreign factors into a domestic factor model yields only a marginal increase in explanatory power. The paper concluded that extending the three-factor model into an international context offers no significant benefits. However, we note that the results in Griffin (2002) also indicate that the country-specific factors from foreign regions share a substantial amount of information with the domestic country-specific factors of interest. Similarly, Kose et al. (2003) employ a Bayesian dynamic latent factor model to estimate common components in macroeconomic aggregates in a 60-country sample covering seven main regions of the world. Their findings reveal that a common world factor is an important source of volatility for aggregates in most countries, providing evidence for the existence of a global business cycle. Bollerslev et al. (2014) investigate how the variance risk premium predicts stock market returns in the U.S. and several other countries through country-specific regressions. They uncover strong predictability and nearly identical patterns across countries, indicating the presence of homogeneous information across multiple country-specific markets. Additionally, it is natural to classify individual stocks based on their broad industry categories. However, it is worth noting that many commonly used factors in stock markets are constructed without accounting for industry distinctions (for example, Fama and French (1993, 2015)), indicating that different industrial sectors may share substantial information. 1.1 Literature Review Analyzing multiple datasets jointly can improve efficiency by leveraging their commonalities. This approach is often referred to as multi-task analysis. Common multi-task approaches regularize task-specific parameters through regularization terms (Evgeniou and Pontil, 2004; Evgeniou et al., 2005), as well as cluster or pooled datasets based on their similarities (Crammer et al., 2008; Jacob et al., 2008; Mc Donald et al., 2016). Recently, Duan and Wang (2023) and Knight and Duan (2023) study the multi-task learning for linear regression problem by using l2-norm-based penalties; Huang et al. (2025) and Xu and Bastani (2025) study multi-task learning and bandits under sparse heterogeneity, where the 3 source/task-associated parameters are equal to a global parameter plus a sparse task-specific term. Earlier studies on multi-task learning can be found in the references of the aforementioned works. To the best of our knowledge, no existing research has investigated multi-task learning for portfolio decision analysis in high-dimensional setups. Our work also connects to the studies of transfer learning and integrative analysis. For example, Tang and Song (2016) introduce a fused lasso regression method to identify heterogeneity patterns of coefficients and to merge the homogeneous parameter clusters across multiple datasets; Fang et al. (2018) propose an integrative sparse principal component analysis approach for multiple independent datasets, where the similarities between datasets are measured by the distance between factor loadings or by the signs of the loadings; Li and Sang (2019) propose the spatially clustered coefficient regression method, which incorporates spatial neighborhood information via regularization; Li et al. (2022) consider estimation and prediction of a high-dimensional linear regression in the setting of transfer learning; Zhang and Zhu (2022) examine high-dimensional quantile regression under a transfer learning framework; Cai et al. (2022) propose an integrative estimation procedure for data-shielding high-dimensional regression, which protects individual-level data by leveraging a summary-statistics-based integration method; Tian and Feng (2023) study the transfer learning problem under high-dimensional generalized linear models; Li et al. (2023) focus on high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models; Zhang et al. (2024) study how to improve estimation efficiency in clustered coefficient regression for distributed network systems by aggregating information from neighboring nodes; Cai et al. (2024) employ minimax rate theory to study the estimation of the mean of random functions; Gu et al. (2024) propose an angle-based approach to exploit the similarity between two linear regression models; Cao et al. (2023) study the application of transfer learning techniques to financial portfolio optimization problem by penalizing the distance between the pre-trained portfolio and the transferred portfolio; Mörstedt et al. (2024) propose a novel covariance estimator and the corresponding portfolio strategy based on non-linear shrinkage, where historically optimal 4 shrinkage parameters are transferred to the current estimation task. Be different with them, we focus on the multi-task factor model and utilize the potential interconnected features of different sectors in a data-adaptive manner. On one hand, if all assets share the completely same factors, pooling them together is expected to be the most beneficial. However, assets worldwide can be grouped into various regions and the assets in each region are likely to be affected by the region-specific factors. Assets within the same market can be categorized into various sectors and the assets in each sector may be influenced by sector-specific factors (Hawawini et al., 2003, and its references). Pooling all data together when groups do not share complete information can even be detrimental to the statistical analyses conducted individually, as demonstrated in our simulation. On the other hand, fully separating stocks into groups and analyzing each group independently would also degrade performance, since different groups may share common information that would not be utilized in separate analyses. Therefore, it is crucial to develop a method that effectively leverages information across sectors while avoiding the model misspecification inherent in the pooling strategy. Moreover, standard financial practices often involve managing multiple related sectors (here the “sector” can be one industrial sector/market/asset class). In practice, the analysis of each task (throughout the rest of the paper, the “task” means the estimation of factor models for each sector) is often conducted independently, with specialized analysts assigned to each set of assets. However, analyzing these related tasks simultaneously would enhance efficiency and yield superior performance. 1.2 Contribution In this study, we consider a multi-task learning problem in a framework that simultaneously analyzes multiple (financial) sectors by leveraging the potential homogeneous information embedded across them, with the goal of improving performance in portfolio allocation. Specifically, we propose a projection-penalized factor model (PPFM), which jointly performs factor analysis for multiple financial groups, utilizing the potential commonality in their la5 tent factors. The proposed method is data-adaptive, automatically adjusting to the degree of homogeneity across the considered groups. Under certain regularization conditions, we first establish the asymptotic properties for estimations of factor loadings and common factors (and their product) for each groups from PPFM. With the estimations of factor loading and common factors in each sector, we further derive the asymptotic consistency of the sector-specific estimators for covariance matrix and precision matrix of assets return, and then establish the consistency of portfolio risk and the Sharpe ratio for each sectors. Simulation results demonstrate that, when the included sectors share a proportion of information, the PPFM-based MVP outperforms both individually constructed MVP and those derived from a pooled strategy (a single model including all stocks) in terms of the average out-ofsample Sharpe ratio and out-of-sample risk.1 When sectors exhibit complete heterogeneity or homogeneity, the performance of PPFM-based portfolios closely aligns with that of individually constructed portfolios and those from a pooled strategy, respectively, indicating the adaptiveness of the proposed strategy. Finally, we conduct an empirical analysis using individual stock data from multiple industries in the U.S. stock market. The results show that the PPFM-based portfolio achieves the best overall performance in terms of the aggregated Sharpe ratio and risk across all sectors, outperforming individual strategy and pooled strategy. Furthermore, our empirical results also show that if one is interested in a specific sector, incorporating highly related sectors allows the PPFM-based MVP to achieve significantly better performance in terms of Sharpe ratio compared to the MVP from individual strategy. The contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We propose a novel projection-penalized factor model, which jointly performs factor analysis for multiple groups, utilizing the potential commonality in their latent factors. Significant challenges arise from the "interconnections" among multi-sector datasets. We quantify the homogeneity among different sectors by utilizing the common subspace across multiple sectors, expanded by stochastic 1The average out-of-sample Sharpe ratio and portfolio risk across all considered groups. 6 trends, or the common serial trends. (2) To solve the proposed PPFM, we further develop a homogeneity-guided iterative principal component algorithm, which is easy to implement in practical applications. (3) We further propose a data-adaptive approach to quantify the extent of homogeneity, which is characterized by a penalization coefficient selected through cross-validation. (4) We establish the theoretical properties of the proposed PPFM, along with the estimators for the covariance matrix, precision matrix, portfolio risk, and Sharpe ratio. (5) To our knowledge, a multi-sector version of MVP is novel in the literature, which can achieve better aggregated performance across all considered sectors when there is a certain degree of shared information among the sectors. In particular, by including the sectors that are highly related to a specific sector of interest, the PPFM-based MVP can achieve significantly better performance than the individual sector strategy. (6) The proposed MVP extends the POET estimator in Fan et al. (2013) for portfolio optimization, to a multi-sector setting by learning factors through incorporating across-sector homogeneity. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the multi-sector factor model and the associated estimation procedures. Section 3 presents the main theoretical results. Simulation studies are reported in Section 4. Section 5 conducts empirical analyses using stock returns from the Russell 3000 index components. Section 6 concludes the paper. The detailed steps for solving the multi-task optimization problem (2.8), along with the full proofs of the main theoretical results, is provided in the Supplementary Material. 2 Multi-sector Factor Model 2.1 MVP Preliminaries In this paper, we consider an adaptive homogeneity learning for multi-sectors based on minimum variance portfolio (MVP) in high-dimensional setup with the help of factor structure. The minimum variance portfolio optimization has a surging appearance in recent studies on portfolio management (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003; De Miguel et al., 2009; Fan 7 et al., 2012; Bodnar et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2024) pioneered by Markowitz’s mean-variance model (Markowitz, 1952). Specifically, the classic MVP problem is: min W ⊤Σr W, s.t. W ⊤1p = 1. If A is a column vector, both ∥A∥and ∥A∥F equal the Euclidean norm ∥A∥2. 2.2 Two-sector Case We first consider the simplest multi-sector model with two sectors. Throughout this section, the terms “sector” and “market” are used interchangeably to refer to the conglomeration of data from one sector. We collect two datasets R1 and R2 from two different markets (de8 noted market 1 and market 2), the underlying structures of two markets can be arbitrarily related. We are interested to see whether the common information shared between the two markets can lead to improved statistical estimation for markets 1 and 2, on average, compared to using only the individual datasets R1 and R2. In asset pricing studies, the factor model is the main workhorse (Fama and French, 1992; Bai and Ng, 2002; Fan et al., 2013) that draws from the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). The theoretical work of arbitrage pricing theory (APT, Ross, 1976) laid the foundation for approximate factor models, which conveniently decompose the return data matrix to a lowrank component and a sparse component (Chamberlain and Rothschild, 1983). Specifically, we model the (excess) assets return from two markets m = 1, 2 by r(m) it = b(m)⊤ i F (m) t + e(m) it , i = 1, 2, . . . , pm; t = 1, 2, . . . , Tm; m = 1, 2, (2.5) where r(m) it is the (excess of the risk-free, often ignored in notations for simplicity) return of asset i in market m at time t, F (m) t is the Km-dimensional vector of common factors in market m at time t, Km is the number of common factors in market m, b(m) i = (b(m) i1 , . . . , b(m) i Km)⊤ is the Km × 1 factor loading, which captures the relationship between common factors and financial asset i in market m; and e(m) it is the idiosyncratic error. In practice, factors can be either observed or not2. In this paper, we assume unobserved factors as the default setting. The vector form of model (2.5) is r(m) t = B(m)F (m) t + e(m) t , t = 1, 2, . . . , Tm, m = 1, 2 (2.6) where r(m) t =  r(m) 1t , r(m) 2t , . . . , r(m) pmt ⊤ is the vector of returns, B(m) =  b(m) 1 , b(m) 2 , . . . , b(m) pm ⊤ is the factor loading matrix, et = (e1t, e2t, . . . , epmt)⊤, and we further define F (m) = (F (m) 1 , · · · , F (m) Tm )⊤. 2Some of those factors are commonly used by practitioners (Fama and French, 1992, 1993, 2015), while others might not be universally accepted. Harvey and Liu (2021), Feng et al. (2020) have good discussions on this “zoo of factors”. 9 In factor model, the information of asset returns is captured by the following parts: the underlying common factors, the factor loadings, and the idiosyncratic errors. The factor loadings and idiosyncratic errors are specific to individual assets, while the common factors driving the co-movement of a basket of assets, effectively reflecting marketand sector-level information. As such, in the following we first discuss the degrees of homogeneity of two factor spaces. Motivated by the principle of factor modeling, it is natural to use a “distance measure” between the common factors of two markets to measure their similarity in information and hence the usefulness of joint modeling for estimation. In this paper, we use the distance measured by the Frobenius norm between the projection matrices spanned by the common factors of two markets to assess the degrees of homogeneity between the two markets. We note that utilizing the distance between projection matrices accommodates all cases of different factor space, including same number of factors but different factors and varying numbers of common factors across different markets. As a result, we can consider the following projection-penalized optimization problem, which utilizes the homogeneous information between two markets, to estimate the factor loading and common factors in each sector: min B(1),F (1),B(2),F (2) L(B(1), B(1), F (1), F (2)) = 1 T T X t=1 r(1) t −B(1)F (1) t 2 + 1 T T X t=1 r(2) t −B(2)F (2) t 2 + λ T P (1) −P (2) 2 F , (2.7) subject to the identification conditions that F (m)⊤F (m)/T = IK and B(m)⊤B(m) is a diagonal matrix for m = 1, 2. Here, P (m) is the projection matrix of common factors, defined as P (m) = F (m)(F (m)⊤F (m))−1F (m)⊤, m = 1, 2. Note that the data from two markets are required to share the same sample size T since we penalize the discrepancy of T (m) × T (m) projection matrix from two markets. The restriction for the same sample size across multiple datasets is easy to meet, as multiple datasets can be viewed as divisions (categorized by sectors such as the industry classification and the markets where the equities are traded) 10 of a single pooled market dataset analyzed by conventional methods. The dimensions of assets in two market are allowed to be different, which facilitates practical implementation, as matching the number of stocks across multiple sectors can sometimes be challenging. Remark 1. The similarity measure between the projection matrices of two markets in (2.7) provides a more general form of similarity in terms of joint estimation. Suppose that market 1 and market 2 have K1 and K2 common factors, where K1 may differ from K2, and the common factors in the two markets may also differ. For simplicity, let us first consider an asset i that belongs to market 1. The term P (1)(ri1, . . . , ri T)⊤represents the return which is explained by the common factors in market 1, i.e., the asset’s expected return under the market 1 factor structure. Similarly, P (2)(ri1, . . . , ri T)⊤represents the return explained by the common factors in market 2. If the projection matrices of the two markets are similar, it implies that the expected return of asset i in market 1 and 2 are close. This, in turn, indicates that the factors in market 1 and market 2 explain similar patterns of risk premium and thus share considerable common information. Note that it is natural for one factor to be largely explained by other factors derived from different markets in financial field (Feng et al., 2020). The positive constant λ is called the regularization parameter, which controls the trade-off between the prediction error we make on the two factor models and the complexity of the solution. When λ = 0, the optimal solutions are the same as those derived from classic principal component analysis (PCA) of each market independently, and λ makes two tasks unrelated. When λ is sufficiently large, ˆF (1) is forced to be close to ˆF (2), effectively enforcing the two market models to be identical. Note that in this situation, ˆB(1) is not close to ˆB(2), as the factor loadings of assets in two different sectors can differ significantly. For the optimization problem (2.7), the process can be described as follows: we leverage the information from sector 2 to enhance the estimation for sector 1, while simultaneously using the information from sector 1 to improve the estimation for sector 2. If sectors 1 and 2 exhibit a sufficient degree of homogeneity, both tasks can be better completed, resulting in 11 an overall improvement in the average performance across all tasks. Remark 2. As an alternative to the ℓ2-norm based penalty, we can penalize the difference between two projection matrices using the ℓ1-norm. This approach may yield common factor estimations F (1) and F (2) (and corresponding projection matrices) that are exactly equal. Note that, on one hand, the ℓ2 penalty yields an explicit solution to the optimization problem (2.7), see Algorithm 1 below, which is often preferred by practitioners and is computationally simpler. On the other hand, since the primary focus is on similarity rather than exact equality, analysis based on the ℓ2 penalty suffices. The problem (2.7) can be solved using first-order conditions, as detailed in Appendix A. Algorithm 1 is proposed to numerically estimate factor loadings and common factors for two sectors. It requires five inputs: the return matrices of two sectors R1, R2, the number of common factors K, the tuning parameter λ, the maximum steps Max I and the tolerance level tol. The goal is to simultaneously estimate the factor models for each market while accounting for the relatedness among various markets. Accordingly, for each task m ∈[1, 2, . . . , M], return data are collected for pm assets over a sample size T. The following projection-penalized factor model (PPFM) minimization problem is then proposed: min B(1),F (1),··· ,B(M),F (M) L(B(1), F (1), · · · , B(M), F (M)) = M X m=1 1 T T X t=1 r(m) t −B(m)F (m) t 2 + λ T M X m=1 X m′>m P (m) −P (m′) 2 F . (2.8) It is worth noting that the same degree of regularization is applied to all projection discrepancies, as no prior information indicates which markets are similar. Additionally, the approach allows the data to reveal relationships among the markets under consideration, thereby avoiding subjective judgments by practitioners. From the perspective of statistical inference, only a single tuning parameter, λ, needs to be selected, which is highly appealing. It is often unclear whether and how a task can be better addressed by incorporating information from other tasks. Clearly, the proposed strategy offers a novel way to tackle this challenge. Remark 3. Let ˆK1 and ˆK2 denote the estimated value by applying the above two penalty functions, respectively, and we set the final ˆK as the integer part of ( ˆK1 + ˆK2)/2. 2.5 Selection of Regularization Parameter In practice, we use k-fold cross-validation to select value for regularization parameter λ. Specifically, let R(m) denote the sample data available at decision point for sector m, m = 1, 2, . . . , M. Then we randomly split R(m) into k groups to form k validation sets, denote as {R(m) 1 , . . . , R(m) k }. For each validation set, the training set is taken to be the rest of R. For each training set, based on a pre-specified λ, we can obtain estimations of factor loadings and common factors for all sectors via optimization (2.8), thus obtaining the minimum variance portfolios for each sector, denoted as ˆw(m) i (λ), i = 1, . . . , k. Thus, λcv is selected to minimize the out-of-sample portfolio risk on the validation set as follows: λcv = argminλ 1 k M M X m=1 k X i=1 risk( ˆw(m) i (λ), R(m) i ) (2.13) where risk( ˆw(m) i , R(m) i ) = PTi t=1  ˆw(m)⊤ i (λ)rt −¯r(m) i (λ) 2 /(Ti −1), and ¯r(m) i (λ) = PTi t=1 ˆw(m)⊤ i (λ)rt/Ti, Ti is the number of observations in i-th validation set. Note that the criterion (2.13) minimizes the average out-of-sample portfolio risk across all considered sectors. Thus, this tuning parameter selection is adopted from a holistic perspective encompassing all sectors. If investors are interested only in a specific sector, it is natural to select a λ that minimizes the out-of-sample risk solely for that sector. In empirical applications, specifying an appropriate value for Cτ is required to carry out adaptive shrinkage estimation for error covariance matrices. In this paper, we apply a datadriven N-fold cross-validation procedure to determine values for Cτ in each sector individu16 ally. More precisely, with the residual ˆe(m) t from our multi-sector PCA estimation procedure, we randomly divide it into two subsets, which are denoted as {ˆe(m) t }t∈A and {ˆe(m) t }t∈B. The sample sizes of each subset are T(A) and T(B), and T(A) + T(B) = T. Subset A is used for training and subset B is used for validation purpose. Therefore, we choose the threshold Cτ by minimizing the following objective function over a compact interval: C∗ τ = argmin Cτ,min<Cτ≤Cτ,max 1 N N X j=1 ˆΣ(m),A,j e (Cτ) −S(m),B,j e 2 F (2.14) where Cτ,min is the minimum constant that guarantees the positive definiteness of ˆΣ(m),A,j e (Cτ), Cτ,max is a large constant such that ˆΣ(m),A,j e (Cτ) is diagonal matrix, ˆΣ(m),A,j e (Cτ) is the threshold residual covariance estimator by using subset A in j-th loop with threshold Cτ for sector m, and S(m),B,j e is sample covariance matrix by using subset B in j-th loop for sector m. For the i-th common factor in m sector, we assume it follow a stationary AR(1) process as f (m) i,t = α(m) i f (m) i,t−1 + u(m) i,t for i = 1, . . . , Km and m = 1, . . . , M with f (m) i,0 = 0, and u(m) i,t ∼N(0, 1 −α(m)2 i ) indicates the covariance matrix of common factors in all sectors are identity matrix. The similar setup for autoregressive common factors can be found in Fan et al. (2013), Fan et al. (2024). In our simulation, we set the number of common factors Km = 2, m = 1, . . . , M for simplicity. For factor loadings bi =  b(m) i,1 , b(m) i,2 ⊤ , i = 1, 2, · · · , p, m = 1, 2, . . . , M which capture the relationship between common factors and individual assets, we draw them from normal distribution, that bi,j ∼ N(µb,j, σ2 b,j), j = 1, 2. Clearly, factor loadings are different across sectors. For idiosyncratic error et = (e1t, . . . , ept)⊤, we generate them from the normal distribution N(0, Σe). For parameter values in the above model setup, we calibrate them from the real data. In details, we select largest 250 stocks measured by market values in the components of S&P 500 index, then we apply POET estimation proposed by Fan et al. (2013) (with thresholding parameter 0.5) to daily excess return data to obtain the estimations of factor loading ˆB, common factors ˆF and sparse error covariance matrix ˆΣe. The period of data is from 01/2006 to 12/2009, containing 1008 observations total. Then, we set µ(m) b,1 = 0.018, µ(m) b,2 = −0.001, σ(m) b,1 = 0.0072, σ(m) b,2 = 0.0084 according to the mean and variance of ˆB. For the coefficients α(m) i , we randomly sample them from N(0, 0.1) based on 22 the observation that the estimated autocoefficients from the Fama-French five factors3 (as well as our estimated factors) typically fall within the range of approximately -0.1 to 0.1. For Σ(m) e across various sectors, we set them as the sparse residual covariance matrix estimators ˆΣe, computed using p randomly selected stocks over any one-year period. We first evaluate the performance of our PPFM-based (joint) portfolios under varying degrees of homogeneity. As a baseline, we consider M = 16 sectors that share the same two common factors. For simplicity, we denote these two baseline factors as F1 and F2, such that F (m) i = Fi for i = 1, 2 and m = 1, . . . , 16 in this baseline setting. Then we gradually increase the heterogeneity among sectors. Specifically, we sequentially replace a block of five factors in {F (2) 1 , F (3) 1 , . . . , F (16) 1 , F (2) 2 , F (3) 2 , . . . , F (16) 2 } with five differently generated factors, one block at a time. For example, during the first replacement, the first five factors F (2) 1 , F (3) 1 , . . . , F (6) 1 , which are initially all F1 in the baseline setting, are replaced by newly generated factors F (2)∗ 1 , F (3)∗ 1 , . . . , F (6)∗ 1 . After six such replacements (6 × 5 = 30 factors are replaced), all 16 sectors are completely distinct from each other. Therefore, our data has gradually transformed from highest homogeneity to highest heterogeneity. 4.2 Performance Measures To assess the (out-of-sample) performance of the proposed estimator, we divide the data of length T into the training set Rtrain and testing set Rtest with sub-sample size Ttrain and Ttest, respectively. The training data set is used for estimating factor loadings and common factors, and testing data set is employed to compute out-of-sample measures. We apply the following three measures. (1) Weight error (WE): the ℓ1 norm of the difference between the estimated and oracle weights WE(m) = ∥c W (m) −W ∗(m)∥1, where c W (m) is the vector of estimated portfolio weights and W ∗(m) is true minimum variance weights calculated by using true Σ(m) r . (3) Out-of-sample risk error (Risk E): the absolute difference between the standard deviation of the out-of-sample oracle portfolio returns and the standard deviation SD(m) of the out-of-sample estimated portfolio returns, where SD(m) = r (Ttest −1)−1 PTtest t=1  r(m),p t −ˆµ(m),p 2 and ˆµ(m),p = T −1 test PTtest t=1 r(m),p t , r(m),p t = c W (m)⊤r(m) t , and r(m) t ∈R(m) test. (4) Out-of-sample Sharpe ratio error (SRE): the absolute difference between the out-ofsample Sharpe ratios of the estimated portfolio and the infeasible oracle portfolio, where the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio for each sector is calculated as SR(m) = ˆµ(m),p/SD(m). For benchmarks, we compare the performance of the proposed method with those of the individual strategy and the pooled strategy. The individual analysis constructs POET-based minimum variance portfolio (MVP) for each sector separately, while the pooled strategy constructs a POET-based MVP using the combined dataset. The regularization parameter for the proposed PPFM model is selected via the cross-validation procedure described in Subsection 2.5, and the sparse threshold parameter Cτ is set to 0.5 for all considered portfolios. We assume that the number of factors is known in this section, to eliminate the influence of incorrect estimation of factor number. The sample sizes of training data and testing data are set to 100 and 300, respectively. 2507.16433v1.full_text: Adaptive Multi-task Learning for Multi-sector Portfolio Optimization Qingliang Fana, Ruike Wu∗b, and Yanrong Yangc a Department of Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong b School of Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics c College of Business and Economics, The Australian National University Abstract Accurate transfer of information across multiple sectors to enhance model estimation is both significant and challenging in multi-sector portfolio optimization involving a large number of assets in different classes. Within the framework of factor modeling, we propose a novel data-adaptive multi-task learning methodology that quantifies and learns the relatedness among the principal temporal subspaces (spanned by factors) across multiple sectors under study. This approach not only improves the simultaneous estimation of multiple factor models but also enhances multi-sector portfolio optimization, which heavily depends on the accurate recovery of these factor models. Additionally, a novel and easy-to-implement algorithm, termed projection-penalized principal component analysis, is developed to accomplish the multi-task learning procedure. Diverse simulation designs and practical application on daily return data from Russell 3000 index demonstrate the advantages of multi-task learning methodology. Keywords: Adaptive learning, Multi-task Learning, Minimum variance portfolio, Factor model, Projection subspace ∗Corresponding to: School of Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai, China. Wu). 1 ar Xiv:2507.16433v1 [stat.ME] 22 Jul 2025 1 Introduction Flexible quantification and adaptive estimation of related information among multiple tasks make multi-task learning attain out-performance. Factor model is a powerful tool in machine learning and data science (Fan et al., 2020). In this study, we contribute to construct a data-adaptive multi-task learning method that is useful in various applications including finance, economics, psychometrics, and environmental science. The leading example we focus on in this paper is multi-sector portfolio selection. Modern financial market is vast and complex. There are many sectors such as manufacturing, financial service, and technology. There are also diverse asset classes such as equities and bonds. Investors nowadays look at interconnected markets that enable cross-border trading and investment, with 24/7 access through electronic platforms to international markets such as the US, Europe, Asia, etc. Investment funds consider various sectors, markets, and geographical locations when constructing an investment portfolio. This is done to diversify investments and minimize risk. Most fund product involves certain “sector”, here we can think of the sector as a specific country’s financial market, an asset class market, a SIC sector or subsector, or a theme such as ESG. The fund manager needs to conduct extensive research and analysis on companies within that sector or theme. The task involves weight determination and rebalancing, and diversification among the different companies within the sector, with a target on Sharpe ratio performance and risk control. It is likely that some or all sectors share the same/similar underlying driving forces of asset returns. In this paper, we are interested in this question: can we utilize the potential but unknown homogeneities among different sectors to make better inference and prediction? An important financial example that inspired us is the study by Griffin (2002), which investigates whether the well-known Fama-French three factors, introduced by Fama and French (1993), are global or country-specific in nature. Its empirical findings suggest that the domestic models explain returns more effectively and provide greater pricing accuracy than the world model, which is the weighted average of the country-specific components. Fur2 thermore, incorporating foreign factors into a domestic factor model yields only a marginal increase in explanatory power. The paper concluded that extending the three-factor model into an international context offers no significant benefits. However, we note that the results in Griffin (2002) also indicate that the country-specific factors from foreign regions share a substantial amount of information with the domestic country-specific factors of interest. Similarly, Kose et al. (2003) employ a Bayesian dynamic latent factor model to estimate common components in macroeconomic aggregates in a 60-country sample covering seven main regions of the world. Their findings reveal that a common world factor is an important source of volatility for aggregates in most countries, providing evidence for the existence of a global business cycle. Bollerslev et al. (2014) investigate how the variance risk premium predicts stock market returns in the U.S. and several other countries through country-specific regressions. They uncover strong predictability and nearly identical patterns across countries, indicating the presence of homogeneous information across multiple country-specific markets. Additionally, it is natural to classify individual stocks based on their broad industry categories. However, it is worth noting that many commonly used factors in stock markets are constructed without accounting for industry distinctions (for example, Fama and French (1993, 2015)), indicating that different industrial sectors may share substantial information. 1.1 Literature Review Analyzing multiple datasets jointly can improve efficiency by leveraging their commonalities. This approach is often referred to as multi-task analysis. Common multi-task approaches regularize task-specific parameters through regularization terms (Evgeniou and Pontil, 2004; Evgeniou et al., 2005), as well as cluster or pooled datasets based on their similarities (Crammer et al., 2008; Jacob et al., 2008; Mc Donald et al., 2016). Recently, Duan and Wang (2023) and Knight and Duan (2023) study the multi-task learning for linear regression problem by using l2-norm-based penalties; Huang et al. (2025) and Xu and Bastani (2025) study multi-task learning and bandits under sparse heterogeneity, where the 3 source/task-associated parameters are equal to a global parameter plus a sparse task-specific term. Earlier studies on multi-task learning can be found in the references of the aforementioned works. To the best of our knowledge, no existing research has investigated multi-task learning for portfolio decision analysis in high-dimensional setups. Our work also connects to the studies of transfer learning and integrative analysis. For example, Tang and Song (2016) introduce a fused lasso regression method to identify heterogeneity patterns of coefficients and to merge the homogeneous parameter clusters across multiple datasets; Fang et al. (2018) propose an integrative sparse principal component analysis approach for multiple independent datasets, where the similarities between datasets are measured by the distance between factor loadings or by the signs of the loadings; Li and Sang (2019) propose the spatially clustered coefficient regression method, which incorporates spatial neighborhood information via regularization; Li et al. (2022) consider estimation and prediction of a high-dimensional linear regression in the setting of transfer learning; Zhang and Zhu (2022) examine high-dimensional quantile regression under a transfer learning framework; Cai et al. (2022) propose an integrative estimation procedure for data-shielding high-dimensional regression, which protects individual-level data by leveraging a summary-statistics-based integration method; Tian and Feng (2023) study the transfer learning problem under high-dimensional generalized linear models; Li et al. (2023) focus on high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models; Zhang et al. (2024) study how to improve estimation efficiency in clustered coefficient regression for distributed network systems by aggregating information from neighboring nodes; Cai et al. (2024) employ minimax rate theory to study the estimation of the mean of random functions; Gu et al. (2024) propose an angle-based approach to exploit the similarity between two linear regression models; Cao et al. (2023) study the application of transfer learning techniques to financial portfolio optimization problem by penalizing the distance between the pre-trained portfolio and the transferred portfolio; Mörstedt et al. (2024) propose a novel covariance estimator and the corresponding portfolio strategy based on non-linear shrinkage, where historically optimal 4 shrinkage parameters are transferred to the current estimation task. Be different with them, we focus on the multi-task factor model and utilize the potential interconnected features of different sectors in a data-adaptive manner. On one hand, if all assets share the completely same factors, pooling them together is expected to be the most beneficial. However, assets worldwide can be grouped into various regions and the assets in each region are likely to be affected by the region-specific factors. Assets within the same market can be categorized into various sectors and the assets in each sector may be influenced by sector-specific factors (Hawawini et al., 2003, and its references). Pooling all data together when groups do not share complete information can even be detrimental to the statistical analyses conducted individually, as demonstrated in our simulation. On the other hand, fully separating stocks into groups and analyzing each group independently would also degrade performance, since different groups may share common information that would not be utilized in separate analyses. Therefore, it is crucial to develop a method that effectively leverages information across sectors while avoiding the model misspecification inherent in the pooling strategy. Moreover, standard financial practices often involve managing multiple related sectors (here the “sector” can be one industrial sector/market/asset class). In practice, the analysis of each task (throughout the rest of the paper, the “task” means the estimation of factor models for each sector) is often conducted independently, with specialized analysts assigned to each set of assets. However, analyzing these related tasks simultaneously would enhance efficiency and yield superior performance. 1.2 Contribution In this study, we consider a multi-task learning problem in a framework that simultaneously analyzes multiple (financial) sectors by leveraging the potential homogeneous information embedded across them, with the goal of improving performance in portfolio allocation. Specifically, we propose a projection-penalized factor model (PPFM), which jointly performs factor analysis for multiple financial groups, utilizing the potential commonality in their la5 tent factors. The proposed method is data-adaptive, automatically adjusting to the degree of homogeneity across the considered groups. Under certain regularization conditions, we first establish the asymptotic properties for estimations of factor loadings and common factors (and their product) for each groups from PPFM. With the estimations of factor loading and common factors in each sector, we further derive the asymptotic consistency of the sector-specific estimators for covariance matrix and precision matrix of assets return, and then establish the consistency of portfolio risk and the Sharpe ratio for each sectors. Simulation results demonstrate that, when the included sectors share a proportion of information, the PPFM-based MVP outperforms both individually constructed MVP and those derived from a pooled strategy (a single model including all stocks) in terms of the average out-ofsample Sharpe ratio and out-of-sample risk.1 When sectors exhibit complete heterogeneity or homogeneity, the performance of PPFM-based portfolios closely aligns with that of individually constructed portfolios and those from a pooled strategy, respectively, indicating the adaptiveness of the proposed strategy. Finally, we conduct an empirical analysis using individual stock data from multiple industries in the U.S. stock market. The results show that the PPFM-based portfolio achieves the best overall performance in terms of the aggregated Sharpe ratio and risk across all sectors, outperforming individual strategy and pooled strategy. Furthermore, our empirical results also show that if one is interested in a specific sector, incorporating highly related sectors allows the PPFM-based MVP to achieve significantly better performance in terms of Sharpe ratio compared to the MVP from individual strategy. The contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We propose a novel projection-penalized factor model, which jointly performs factor analysis for multiple groups, utilizing the potential commonality in their latent factors. Significant challenges arise from the "interconnections" among multi-sector datasets. We quantify the homogeneity among different sectors by utilizing the common subspace across multiple sectors, expanded by stochastic 1The average out-of-sample Sharpe ratio and portfolio risk across all considered groups. 6 trends, or the common serial trends. (2) To solve the proposed PPFM, we further develop a homogeneity-guided iterative principal component algorithm, which is easy to implement in practical applications. (3) We further propose a data-adaptive approach to quantify the extent of homogeneity, which is characterized by a penalization coefficient selected through cross-validation. (4) We establish the theoretical properties of the proposed PPFM, along with the estimators for the covariance matrix, precision matrix, portfolio risk, and Sharpe ratio. (5) To our knowledge, a multi-sector version of MVP is novel in the literature, which can achieve better aggregated performance across all considered sectors when there is a certain degree of shared information among the sectors. In particular, by including the sectors that are highly related to a specific sector of interest, the PPFM-based MVP can achieve significantly better performance than the individual sector strategy. (6) The proposed MVP extends the POET estimator in Fan et al. (2013) for portfolio optimization, to a multi-sector setting by learning factors through incorporating across-sector homogeneity. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the multi-sector factor model and the associated estimation procedures. Section 3 presents the main theoretical results. Simulation studies are reported in Section 4. Section 5 conducts empirical analyses using stock returns from the Russell 3000 index components. Section 6 concludes the paper. The detailed steps for solving the multi-task optimization problem (2.8), along with the full proofs of the main theoretical results, is provided in the Supplementary Material. 2 Multi-sector Factor Model 2.1 MVP Preliminaries In this paper, we consider an adaptive homogeneity learning for multi-sectors based on minimum variance portfolio (MVP) in high-dimensional setup with the help of factor structure. The minimum variance portfolio optimization has a surging appearance in recent studies on portfolio management (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003; De Miguel et al., 2009; Fan 7 et al., 2012; Bodnar et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2024) pioneered by Markowitz’s mean-variance model (Markowitz, 1952).
